"He shall certainly attain the self-arisen wisdom of all Buddhas;
having subdued Māra and sat at the site of enlightenment, he shall extensively deliver boundless multitudes.

At that time, having heard this verse, the youth Sudhana immediately ascended the mountain of blades and threw himself into the mass of fire; before he had even reached the middle, he attained the Bodhisattva samādhi called "Firmly Abiding in Pure Stability."
As soon as he touched the flames, he further attained the Bodhisattva samādhi called "The Door of Supernormal Power of Tranquil Bliss.
Sudhana said: "How marvelous!"
"Noble One!
When my body touches such sword-blades and great flames, it is peaceful and blissful.
Then, the brahmin said to Sudhana:

“Good son! I have attained only this Bodhisattva liberation of the Universally Perfect and Inexhaustible Wheel. As for those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who possess the great blazing flames of merit capable of incinerating all the afflictions and views of sentient beings; who dwell in the Bodhisattva’s non-regressive mind, inexhaustible mind, tireless mind, and undaunted mind; whose minds are like the Vajra-treasury of Nārāyaṇa; whose minds are free from pride and indolence as they swiftly cultivate all practices; and who, with the wind-wheel of great vows, universally sustain all things, possessing courageous and firm pledges that never regress—[I do not know their conduct].”
How could I possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct?

Good son! To the south there is a city named Siṃhapraśvāsa; in that city there is a king named Abhayatārakaketu, who has a young girl named Maitrīcaryā. Go to her and ask: how should a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?
Then, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, gazed up at him with earnest devotion, and took his leave.
At that time, Sudhana conceived a mind of inconceivable and supreme reverence toward the spiritual friend;
he gave rise to a mind of vast, pure faith and understanding.
Constantly mindful of the Mahāyāna, never abandoning the resolve;
single-mindedly seeking the Buddha-wisdom, always free from divergent thoughts;
contemplating the realm of dharmas without any doubt or confusion.

With single-minded focus, they follow spiritual friends; unobstructed wisdom is ever present before them; they dwell with certainty at the limit of true reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); they are skillfully able to discern the limit of reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; they universally enter the limits of every *kṣaṇa* throughout the three periods of time; they accord with and understand the limit that is like space; they directly perceive that all phenomena are eternally without the limit of duality; they abide in the non-conceptual limit of the *dharmadhātu*; they enter the unobstructed limit of all meanings; they abide in the limit of all eons without decay or destruction; they accord with and subdue the limits of the nature of all karma; they abide in the limit of the Tathāgata’s most supreme, uncommon qualities; and they understand the limit of the Tathāgata’s limitlessness.

With supreme wisdom, they are able to utterly destroy all nets of attachment and inverted perceptions; they do not grasp at the signs of distinctions between identical or different buddha-fields, nor do they grasp at the signs of the harmonious assemblies and sites of enlightenment of all Buddhas;
they do not grasp at the signs of the purity of Buddha-fields, for they understand that all sentient beings are devoid of a self or the characteristic of a sentient being.
He also knows that all sounds and speech are like echoes in an empty valley, and he knows that all diverse forms are like reflections; contemplating thus, he observes with right mindfulness.
Traveling south by stages toward the city of Siṃhapralamba, he inquired everywhere for the maiden Maitrāyaṇī.
He heard people say:
"She is the king’s daughter; she resides in the royal palace, attended by five hundred maidens."
"Residing in the Vairocana-maṇi-garbha Palace, upon a seat of Nāga-jaya-candana wood with feet of gold-threaded netting and celestial garments, he is preaching the sublime Dharma.
Having heard this, Sudhana went to the gate of the royal palace, his mind single-pointedly filled with longing and reverence, seeking to see her.
At that time, he saw an immeasurable multitude of people entering the palace.
Sudhana asked them, "Where are you all going now? They all replied:
“We wish to go to the maiden Maitrīyaśas to hear and receive the sublime Dharma.
Sudhana then thought:
“Since there are no obstructions at this royal palace gate, I too should enter.”

He then entered the royal palace and beheld its jeweled hall: its floor was made of crystal, its pillars of lapis lazuli, and its walls of diamond; it had a perimeter wall of Jambūnada gold, with railings of various jewels and hundreds of thousands of diverse gems, while windows were formed by light shining everywhere.
It was adorned with incalculable, supreme maṇi-jewels, and beautified by perfect mirrors of maṇi-treasures;
it was illuminated day and night by the radiance of the world’s most supreme *prabhāgarbha* (light-treasury) maṇi-jewels.
Countless jeweled nets spread all around and covered it above; windows and lattices reflected one another, and various jewels shone in mutual brilliance.
Hundreds and thousands of golden bells were suspended upon it, emitting subtle and wondrous sounds when stirred by a gentle breeze.
There were such inconceivable adornments of various jewels.

The maiden Maitrāyaṇī was of a body the color of pure gold, with deep blue eyes and hair; her appearance was upright and majestic, endowed with all the marks and signs of excellence, as she expounded the Dharma with a Brahma-like voice.
Having seen him, Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, and standing to one side with palms joined in reverence, addressed him, saying: "Noble One!
I have already set my mind on Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice, nor how a bodhisattva should cultivate the bodhisattva path.
"I have heard that the Noble One is skilled at providing instruction;
I pray that you will speak for me. The young woman replied, "O son of good family!
“You should observe the various adornments within and without the palace where I dwell.
Sudhana prostrated himself and, as instructed, observed; he saw them within every wall, within every mirror, within every pillar, within every sign, within every image, and within every...
Within each of the jeweled nets, within each of the railings, within each of the golden bells, within each of the jewel trees,
within each of the jewel necklaces, within each of the ornaments, within each of the jewel images,
and within each of the maṇi gems, Vairocana illuminates the world with his radiance.

Within these jewels, one sees all the Tathāgatas of all dharma-realms throughout the ten directions— from their initial generation of the mind of enlightenment and their cultivation of the bodhisattva path,
through each of their individual practices and vows, each of their respective realms, each of their appearances as they attain equal and perfect enlightenment,
and each of their manifestations of vast supernormal powers and turning of the wondrous wheel of Dharma, and so forth.
Each manifests entry into nirvana.
Such reflected images and various realms are like figures in a mirror, and also like the sun, moon, and stars seen throughout the sky in clear water.
All of this was due to the power of the great roots of goodness cultivated by the maiden Maitrāyaṇī in the past, whereby all these various forms appeared within it.

At that time, Sudhana recalled everything he had observed—the adornments of the lands of all Buddhas, the signs of their meritorious conduct, vows, and spiritual transformations—and with palms joined in reverence, he gazed single-mindedly up at the maiden Maitrāyaṇī.
Then, that maiden said to Sudhana: "Noble son!

This gateway of the universal adornment of the *prajñāpāramitā* is a dharma that I have sought and attained in the presence of as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in thirty-six Ganges Rivers."
"Those Tathāgatas each, by means of various and diverse skillful gates, have enabled me to enter that which was expounded by one Buddha,
so that others need not repeat it. Sudhana said, "Noble One!"
“What is the scope of this Universal Adornment Gate of the Prajñāpāramitā?
The maiden replied, “Noble son!

Having entered this Gate of Universal Adornment of the Prajñāpāramitā, I followed, inclined toward, contemplated, observed, retained, and analyzed all its spheres, all its modes of conduct, all its characteristics, and all its realizations; at that very moment, I attained the dhāraṇī-gate of universal production, and one million asaṃkhyeya dhāraṇī-gates all manifested before me.
They appear with the rapid whirling of a water vortex,
namely: the dhāraṇī-door of the Buddhas, the dhāraṇī-door of the Dharma, the dhāraṇī-door of Buddha-fields,
the dhāraṇī-door of sentient beings, the universal dhāraṇī-door, and the dhāraṇī-door of the past.
The gate of dhāraṇī of the future, the gate of dhāraṇī of the present, the gate of dhāraṇī of the limit of permanence, the gate of dhāraṇī of merit,
the gate of dhāraṇī of the accumulation of merit, the gate of dhāraṇī of wisdom,
the gate of dhāraṇī of the accumulation of wisdom, the gate of dhāraṇī of all vows, and the [gate of dhāraṇī] of distribution...
The gateway of the dhāraṇī that distinguishes all vows; the gateway of the dhāraṇī of practice; the gateway of the dhāraṇī of pure practice;
the gateway of the dhāraṇī of the cultivation and accumulation of practice; the gateway of the dhāraṇī of perfect practice; the gateway of the dhāraṇī of karma;
the gateway of the dhāraṇī of the non-destruction of karma; and the gateway of the dhāraṇī of the purity of karma.
The dharani-door of the streaming of karma; the dharani-door of the manifestation of what is performed by karma;
the dharani-door of abandoning and leaving evil karma; the dharani-door of cultivating right karma;
the dharani-door of mastery over karma; the dharani-door of wholesome conduct; and the dharani-door of constantly maintaining wholesome conduct.
The dharani-gate of samādhi, the dharani-gate of conforming to samādhi, the dharani-gate of observing samādhi,
the dharani-gate of the realm of samādhi, the dharani-gate of arising from samādhi,
the dharani-gate of supernormal powers, the dharani-gate of the ocean of mind, and various [other dharanis].
The dharani-gate of the mind, the dharani-gate of the straightforward mind, the dharani-gate of the pure mind,
the dharani-gate of illuminating the dense forest of the mind, the dharani-gate of the purity of the ground of the mind,
the dharani-gate of knowing the places where the minds of sentient beings arise, and the dharani-gate of knowing the subtle minds of sentient beings.
The gate of knowing the afflictive conduct of sentient beings; the dhāraṇī gate of knowing the habitual tendencies of afflictions;
the dhāraṇī gate of knowing the expedient means regarding afflictions; the dhāraṇī gate of knowing the actions performed by afflictions;
the dhāraṇī gate of knowing the faith of sentient beings; and the dhāraṇī gate of knowing the understanding of sentient beings.
The dharani-door of knowing the conduct of sentient beings; the dharani-door of knowing the distinctions among the various conducts through which sentient beings find faith and understanding;
the dharani-door of knowing the natures of sentient beings; the dharani-door of knowing the desires of sentient beings;
the dharani-door of knowing the perceptions of sentient beings; and the dharani-door of knowing the origins of worlds.
The dharani-door of universally beholding the ten directions; the dharani-door of universally beholding all dharmas;
the dharani-door of expounding the Dharma; the dharani-door of great loving-kindness; the dharani-door of great compassion; the dharani-door of tranquility;
the dharani-door of the path of language; and the dharani-door of liberation.
The gate of the female principle, the universally produced dhāraṇī gate, the unattached limit dhāraṇī gate,
the skillful means and non-means dhāraṇī gate, the conforming dhāraṇī gate, the differentiated dhāraṇī gate,
the universally entering dhāraṇī gate, the unobstructed limit dhāraṇī gate, and the universal...
The gate of dhāraṇīs pervading all things; the gate of dhāraṇīs of the Buddha-dharma; the gate of dhāraṇīs of the Bodhisattva-dharma;
the gate of dhāraṇīs of the Śrāvaka-dharma; the gate of dhāraṇīs of the Pratyekabuddha-dharma;
the gate of dhāraṇīs of mundane dharmas; the gate of dhāraṇīs of the formation of worlds; the gate of dhāraṇīs of the destruction of worlds...
The dharani-door of world-entrances, the dharani-door of world-abodes, the dharani-door of world-adornments,
the dharani-door of world-shapes, the dharani-door of narrow worlds, the dharani-door of vast worlds,
the dharani-door of defiled worlds, and the dharani-door of pure worlds.
The dhāraṇī gate of manifesting defiled worlds within pure worlds; the dhāraṇī gate of manifesting pure worlds within defiled worlds;
the dhāraṇī gate of entirely defiled worlds; the dhāraṇī gate of entirely pure worlds;
the dhāraṇī gate of defiled and pure worlds; and the dhāraṇī gate of pure and defiled worlds.
The dharani-door of level worlds, the dharani-door of high-and-low worlds,
the dharani-door of inverted worlds, the dharani-door of upright worlds,
the dharani-door of sideways worlds, the dharani-door of world-nets, and the dharani-door of revolving worlds.
The dhāraṇī-door of abiding according to the distinct perceptions of various worlds; the dhāraṇī-door of the conduct of worlds; the dhāraṇī-door of the subtle entering the coarse;
the dhāraṇī-door of the coarse entering the subtle; the dhāraṇī-door of the large entering the small;
the dhāraṇī-door of the small entering the large; and the dhāraṇī-door of beholding all Buddhas.
The dharani-door of discerning the Buddha-body; the dharani-door of seeing the Buddha’s light as an array of majestic nets;
the dharani-door of hearing the Buddha’s perfect and wondrous voice; the dharani-door of the Buddha turning the wheel of Dharma;
the dharani-door of the accomplishment of the Buddha’s wheel of Dharma; and the dharani-door of the distinctions of the Buddha’s wheel of Dharma.
The dharani-door of the entry into the Buddha’s wheel of Dharma, the dharani-door of the etymological explanation of the Buddha’s wheel of Dharma,
the dharani-door of the revolution of the Buddha’s wheel of Dharma, the dharani-door of the universal pervasion of the Buddha’s body,
the dharani-door of the perfection of the Buddha’s assembly, and the dharani-door capable of performing the buddha-work.
The dharani-door of knowing the distinct characteristics of the various Buddha-assemblies; the dharani-door of universally entering the oceans of Buddha-assemblies;
the dharani-door of the light-radiance of all Buddhas; the dharani-door of the samadhis of all Buddhas;
the dharani-door of the sovereign application of the samadhis of all Buddhas; and the dharani-door of the dwelling places of all Buddhas.
The gate of the nirmāṇa of all Buddhas, the dhāraṇī-gate of the empowerment of all Buddhas, the dhāraṇī-gate of the transformations of all Buddhas,
the dhāraṇī-gate of the playful manifestations of all Buddhas, the dhāraṇī-gate of the Buddhas’ knowledge of the differences in the mental activities of sentient beings,
and the dhāraṇī-gate of the various miraculous displays of the supernatural powers of all Buddhas; [the state of] dwelling in the Tuṣita palace.
The dharani-door of performing all deeds, up to the dharani-door of manifesting entry into nirvana;
the dharani-door of benefiting sentient beings; the dharani-door of entering the profound Dharma;
the dharani-door of entering the subtle and wondrous Dharma; the dharani-door of the characteristics of the bodhicitta; the bodhicitta...
The dhāraṇī gate of that from which [all] arises; the dhāraṇī gate of the signs of the bodhicitta that aids the path;
the dhāraṇī gate of all vows; the dhāraṇī gate of all practices; the dhāraṇī gate of the signs of supernormal powers;
the dhāraṇī gate of the signs of renunciation; the dhāraṇī gate of the signs of the purity of total retention; and wisdom.
The dhāraṇī-door of the mark of purity of the wheel, the dhāraṇī-door of the mark of purity of wisdom,
the dhāraṇī-door of the mark of immeasurable liberation, the dhāraṇī-door of the purity of the power of mindfulness,
and the dhāraṇī-door of the purity of one’s own mind.

“Good son! I know only this Gate of Universal Adornment of the Prajñāpāramitā. As for the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, their minds are vast, equal to the realm of empty space; they enter the Dharma-realm, their wisdom is broad and expansive, and their merit is fully perfected, firm and immovable.”
Abiding in supramundane dharmas and remaining far removed from the world, they diligently seek and cultivate practice, directing themselves toward all-knowledge;
their eye of wisdom is pure, free from all defilements and obscurations, and their physical, verbal, and mental actions are entirely pure;
through discerning wisdom, they universally enter into all phenomena, and their unobstructed insight is like space.

They have thoroughly penetrated all realms of the world and attained the great treasury of light of the stage of non-obstruction; they are skillfully adept at discerning the meanings of all phenomena, such that nothing in any world can eclipse them.
Constantly acting within the world, they are unstained by worldly dharmas; they are able to benefit the world and cannot be destroyed by the world.
They serve as the ultimate refuge for all sentient beings, skillfully understanding the languages of all sentient beings and clearly comprehending their various customs and rituals.
Knowing the karmic habits, faculties, and capacities of all sentient beings, they teach the Dharma according to their mental inclinations and conduct as is appropriate.
Manifesting their bodies universally in all places and attaining constant mastery at all times—
how could I possibly know or describe such meritorious conduct?
"Good son! To the south of here, there is a land called Trimukha.
There dwells a bhikṣu named Sudarśana; go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path."
Then, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, and gazing up at him with longing devotion, took his leave and traveled south.
At that time, Sudhana reflected upon the profound nature of the bodhisattva’s dwelling-place;
he reflected upon the profound limit of the dharma-realm realized by the bodhisattva; and he reflected upon the bodhisattva’s subtle wisdom regarding sentient beings.

Profound! One contemplates the profundity of the bodhisattva’s wisdom regarding the perceptions and activities of the world; one contemplates the profundity of the non-active nature of sentient beings;
one contemplates the profundity of the continuous flow of the minds of sentient beings; one contemplates the profundity of the limit of dependent origination of all phenomena;
one contemplates the profundity of the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of sentient beings; one contemplates the suchness (*tathatā*) of sentient beings...
The realm of light and shadow is profoundly deep; the limit of the distinctions among the names of sentient beings is profoundly deep;
the limit of the languages of sentient beings is profoundly deep; the limit of the adorned dharmas of sentient beings is profoundly deep;
the limit of the secrets of sentient beings is profoundly deep; the limit of the radiance of sentient beings is profoundly deep.

Proceeding by stages, he arrived at the kingdom of Trimukha; there, throughout the cities, marketplaces, villages, mountains, rivers, forests, marshes, and the dwellings of rishis, he searched everywhere for the bhikṣu Sudarśana.

Suddenly, he beheld [the Buddha] walking back and forth in a grove; his skull was like a parasol, and his crown was adorned with a fleshly protuberance (uṣṇīṣa), most excellent and majestic. His eyes were long and wide like blue lotus petals; his nose was high, straight, and upright like polished pure gold; the color of his lips was crimson and clean like the *bimba* fruit; and his teeth were white, even, closely set, and complete in forty.

His cheeks were like those of a lion; his jaw and chin were full and rounded; his eyebrows were high and long; his forehead was broad, level, and straight; the *ūrṇā-kośa* mark was brilliantly translucent, like white lapis lazuli; his ears had well-defined lobes, shaped like hanging pearls; and his face was like the full moon, such that those who beheld it never grew weary.

His neck is rounded and straight, marked with three graceful lines; his chest displays the marks of virtue, adorned by the wondrous urna-treasure. His breast is like that of a lion, his shoulders are well-rounded, and his waist and flanks are deep and slender like a vajra-pestle.
His arms and elbows are smooth and straight, hanging down past the knees when standing; his fingers are joined by webbed membranes, like those of a white goose king.
The palms of his hands and the soles of his feet bear the mark of the vajra-wheel; they are soft, delicate, and smooth like *tūla* cotton.
His calves are like those of the eni-deer; he is full and even in seven places; his fingers are slender and long; and his heels are flat and round.
His skin is golden in color, with a constant radiance extending one fathom; the hairs of his body point upward, each curling to the right.
His body is perfectly proportioned like a nyagrodha tree, adorned with the marks and signs of excellence, as pure and majestic as the King of Snow Mountains.
The sense faculties are serene and still, and the eyes do not blink; regarding all objects of perception, the mind is free from agitation.
His wisdom is profound and vast like the great ocean; whether sinking or rising, whether it be wisdom or non-wisdom, all shifting movements and conceptual proliferations have entirely ceased.

They attain the impartial realm practiced by the Buddhas, enter the gateway of the differentiated dharmas of dependent origination, and bring sentient beings to maturity with a mind that is never weary.
They are able to give rise to profound, vast, and perfect great compassion, teaching, transforming, and guiding others with a mind that never for a moment abandons them.

Desiring to uphold the true Dharma-eye of all Tathāgatas, desiring to cause all sentient beings everywhere to give birth to the eye of wisdom, and desiring to constantly tread upon the path traversed by the Tathāgatas, he walked with careful attention, neither too slowly nor too quickly.
Tranquil and dignified, he was like the full moon; his majestic deportment was solemn and grave, like that of the Śuddhāvāsa devas.
He was surrounded before and behind by countless devas, nāgas, gandharvas, Śakras, Brahmās, world-protectors, humans, and non-humans.
The presiding deity of each direction turns according to that quarter to guide them from before;
the deities who attend upon their feet hold precious lotus flowers, supporting their feet as they walk;
and the fire deity, Lord of Infinite Light, holds a precious torch, spreading its radiance to illuminate the way.
The forest spirit Jambudhvaja constantly rains down various exquisite kusuma flowers;
the earth spirit Acalagarbha manifests treasuries of jewels at will; the space spirit Samantaprabha adorns the void;
and the ocean spirit Mañjuśrī rains down mani-jewels.
The mountain spirit Sovereign of the Treasury of Mount Sumeru joined his palms in prostration;
the wind spirit Sovereign of Unobstructed Power scattered various fragrant flowers;
and the night spirit Sovereign of Spring’s Mild and Serene Air bowed her body in respectful homage.
Constantly Perfectly Awakened, the Lord of the Day, holding a mani-jewel banner that illuminates the ten directions, dwelt in the midst of space emitting great radiance.
Sudhana approached him, prostrated at his feet with his head, joined his palms, and said: "Noble One!
I have already first resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and I further desire to diligently seek the path of all bodhisattvas.

Having heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction and guidance, I pray that you will tell me how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
The Wondrous Vision replied, “Good son!

Although my years since leaving home are few, during this present life of mine, I have approached, made offerings to, and purely cultivated the Brahma-faring under as many Tathāgatas as there are grains of sand in thirty-eight Ganges Rivers.”
In the presence of some Buddhas, they purely cultivate the Brahma-faring for one day and one night;
in the presence of others, they purely cultivate the Brahma-faring for seven days and seven nights;
and in the presence of still others, for half a month or one month.
For one year, a hundred years, a thousand years, a hundred thousand years, ten million (*nayuta*) years, or even unspeakably unspeakable numbers of years;

or at the abodes of certain Buddhas, for a minor eon (*kalpa*), a medium eon, or a great eon, or even for unspeakably unspeakable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas—there they draw near to and make offerings to [the Buddhas], purely cultivating the holy life (*brahmacarya*), hearing the sublime Dharma, and practicing in accordance with the teachings. They purify and adorn their great vows, enter the profound realms of all Buddhas, cultivate and accumulate all the wondrous practices of Bodhisattvas, and bring to perfection all the gates of the *pāramitās*.

They also see the perfect enlightenment attained by those Buddhas, the supernatural powers they manifest, the wheels of Dharma they turn, the nirvana they display, and all their bequeathed teachings—even down to the various distinctions until the end of the Dharma—and are able to receive and uphold them all without any confusion or disorder.
He also knew that those Buddhas, by the power of the great vows they had originally made, universally adorned and purified all Buddha-lands;
by the power of the various samādhis they had originally entered, perfected the profound and wondrous practices of Bodhisattvas;
and by the power of the Universal Worthy (Samantabhadra) conduct they had originally cultivated, purified the ocean of the Buddhas' pāramitās.
"Furthermore, noble son!

I am never apart from this place of walking meditation; in a single thought-moment, all the ten directions appear before me, for I have attained pure and wondrous wisdom that observes and understands them without obstruction.

In a single thought-moment, all worlds appear before me, for I have attained the power of swiftness to traverse unspeakably unspeakable numbers of worlds in a single thought-moment without obstruction."
In a single thought-moment, unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields all appear before them, because they have attained the power of the Bodhisattva’s vows to universally adorn and purify;

in a single thought-moment, the diverse activities of unspeakably unspeakable numbers of sentient beings all appear before them, because they have attained fulfillment in the ocean of Samantabhadra’s gateways of teaching;

in a single thought-moment, the pure bodies of unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddhas all appear before them, because they have attained the power to universally draw near and accomplish the practices and vows of Samantabhadra.

In a single thought-moment, Tathāgatas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields all appear before me; this is because of my vow-power to attain a supple mind and to make offerings to and serve all Tathāgatas.

In a single thought-moment, unspeakably unspeakable Tathāgatas pour down the rain of Dharma into the hearts of sentient beings, all appearing before me; this is because of my vow-power to comprehend incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) Dharma-gates and to accord with *dhāraṇīs*.

In a single thought-moment, oceans of Bodhisattva practices as numerous as unspeakably unspeakable [atoms] all appear before me; this is because of my supreme vow-power to purify all Bodhisattva practices, which are like the net of Indra.

In a single thought-moment, unspeakably unspeakable oceans of samādhis all manifest before them, because they have attained the power of the vow to freely enter and emerge from all samādhis within a single samādhi;

in a single thought-moment, unspeakably unspeakable oceans of faculties all manifest before them, because they have attained the power of the vow to know the limit of all faculties and perceive all faculties within a single faculty;

in a single thought-moment, unspeakably unspeakable periods of time all manifest before them, because they have attained the power of the vow that as long as the realms of sentient beings are not exhausted, the turning of the wheel of Dharma shall never cease throughout all time.

Within a single thought-moment, unspeakably unspeakable oceans of the three periods of time all appear before one, because of the light of wisdom and the power of vows that thoroughly understands the temporal divisions within all worlds.

"Good son! I know only this bodhisattva liberation door of the 'Inexhaustible Lamp of Accordance. As for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, their mental conduct is as firm and solid as a diamond; they are born into the lineage of the Tathāgata’s family and truly accomplish the indestructible, eternally abiding life-force; they constantly kindle the lamp of wisdom, which never reaches exhaustion or extinction."

His body is firm and solid, incapable of being obstructed or destroyed; he is able to universally manifest an illusory form-body, with features so dignified and majestic that they have no peer in the world.

According to the minds of sentient beings, it appears in infinite varieties; like the law of dependent origination, its transformations are inexhaustible, and it cannot be harmed by poisons, blades, or fires.
He subdues the hosts of Māra’s armies and crushes those of heterodox paths; his physical form is wondrous and beautiful, like Jāmbūnada gold, surpassing all in the world and being peerless.

He emits a great net of light that universally illumines the ten directions; whoever beholds it will surely shatter the great mountains of all obstructions, surely uproot all unwholesome roots, and surely plant vast and supreme roots of goodness.
Such persons are difficult to encounter and difficult to appear in this world, like the udumbara flower.
How then could I know or describe their meritorious conduct?
"Noble son! To the south of here, there is a land named Pūrṇaśruta; in it is a city called Suvaktra, where there dwells a youth named Indriyeśvararāja."
"Go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
At that time, the youth Sudhana, desiring to bring all bodhisattva practices to fulfillment and desiring to cultivate the inexhaustible merit of a bodhisattva, [set out].
Desiring to don the armor of the Bodhisattva’s great vow;
desiring to radiate the Bodhisattva’s light of great power;
desiring to accomplish the Bodhisattva’s power of profound faith and understanding;

Desiring to give rise to the immeasurable and supreme practices of a bodhisattva, their mind never tires of the bodhisattva teachings; they delight in entering all the merits of a bodhisattva, vow to always guide and sustain all sentient beings, and wish to transcend the dense forest and wilderness of birth and death;
regarding spiritual friends, they always delight in seeing, hearing, serving, and making offerings to them, their hearts never wearying.

Conceiving a sense of profound respect for the immeasurable Dharma, he prostrated himself before Sudarśana, circumambulated him countless times, gazed upon him with earnest devotion, and then took his leave and departed.

At that time, having received the instructions of the bhikṣu Sudarśana, the youth Sudhana retained them without forgetting, contemplated and practiced them until they were certain and clear, and accordingly entered into realization of that Dharma-gate.
Surrounded by a retinue of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others,
he proceeded step by step toward the country of Paripūrṇaśruta and entered the city of Suvilokitamukha, searching everywhere for the youth Indriyeśvara.
At that time, the devas, nāgas, spirits, and others in the void addressed Sudhana, saying: "Good son!
This boy is now on a sandbank by the river, playing with other boys, piling up sand."
At that time, having heard these words, Sudhana went to where he was; there he saw the boy surrounded before and behind by ten thousand other boys, playing by piling up sand.
Having seen him, she approached and prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, and stood before him with palms joined, saying: "Noble One!
I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice or cultivate the bodhisattva path."
"I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction; I only pray that you will take pity on me and explain this for my sake.
The Lord of Mastery said, "Good son!

In the past, I studied the methods of calculation, numeration, seals, and signs under the youth Mañjuśrī, whereby I immediately attained entry into the gateway of all knowledge regarding the supernormal powers of craftsmanship.

"Good son! Because of this, I know all the verbal treatises of the world, including the inner sciences (adhyātma-vidyā), logic (hetu-vidyā), and medicine (cikitsā-vidyā), as well as their written characters; I also know calculation, mudrās, and various treatises on the wisdom of giving and receiving. Furthermore, I know all medicinal herbs and poisons, how to compound them and neutralize them, and I am also able to cure diseases such as epilepsy, consumption, and possession by malevolent spirits—indeed, all such ailments."

He is also able to establish cities, towns, and villages, as well as various adornments such as marketplaces, residential wards, gardens, ponds, halls for the righteous, charitable shelters, terraces, pavilions, towers, palaces, houses, windows, doors, and gateways;
he is also skilled in driving four-horse chariots, the arts of warfare, strategic retreats and advances, and the discernment of victory and defeat;
furthermore, he is adept at compounding various elixirs of the immortals and performing transformations through illusory arts.
He was also skilled in managing various occupations such as agriculture, commerce, and trade;
he was proficient in the rituals and the proper order of social ranks;
and he understood the auspicious or inauspicious physical characteristics of sentient beings, as well as the nature of their karmic actions—whether virtuous or evil.
They also know that sentient beings are endowed with all roots of goodness and unwholesome roots;
they also know the distinctions between the various types of rebirths in the fortunate realms and the miserable realms.

They thoroughly understand the pure paths of action of all noble ones: that this person should attain the path of the Śrāvaka vehicle, that this person should attain the path of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, that this person should attain the path of the Bodhisattva vehicle, and that this person should enter the ground of the Tathāgata’s wisdom. In this way, they are able to know everything, even the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional.

He also knows the rules of conduct and ritual procedures for all those in states of tranquility, as well as what constitutes timely and untimely eating, and what is appropriate or inappropriate for their self-sustenance and prolongation of life;
he also knows the worldly methods of livelihood, the management of assets, and the relative value of goods in terms of their origin and destination;
and he also knows the distinctions regarding the stages of entering the womb, remaining in the womb, and being born throughout his own and others' past successions of bodies.

He also knows all future sentient beings—how they die here and are born there, die there and are born here, pass away from that place and are reborn in that same place, or pass away from this place and are reborn in this same place.

He also knows the various distinct Dharma-gates of all Buddhas of the past and present, their manifold arrangements, instructions, and admonitions for taming sentient beings; how he can cause them to become steadfast, practice accordingly, transcend the flow of birth and death, reach the shore of Nirvana, and attain the purity of body and mind like refined gold, with light shining everywhere in vast accomplishment.

"Good son! I further possess thorough knowledge of the eighteen crafts and various technical arts, along with the sixty-two auxiliary treatises (vidyā-sthāna) and all methods of inner science (adhyātma-vidyā) for subduing internal afflictions."
What are called the internal afflictions of the body?
There are four causes and conditions:

first, the visual faculty apprehending the object of form; second, the habitual tendencies of grasping from beginningless time; third, the intrinsic nature of that consciousness itself; and fourth, mental attention directed toward the object of form.

I hope that by virtue of these four kinds of causal conditions, the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) undergoes transformation, and the waves of consciousness arise—like a torrential stream, continuing in an uninterrupted succession.
"Good son! Just as when visual consciousness arises, all the sensory consciousnesses are born simultaneously within every pore and atom, so it is likewise here.
For example, just as a bright mirror suddenly manifests all images, so too do the various consciousnesses sometimes manifest all at once."

Good son! It is like a fierce wind blowing upon the waters of the great ocean, causing the waves to ceaselessly surge. Driven by the winds of sense objects, the ocean of the tranquil mind is tossed, giving rise to the waves of consciousness that flow on in uninterrupted succession. These causes and conditions act in mutual dependence, neither abandoning nor separating one another; they are neither identical nor different, just as water and its waves. Through the manifestation of characteristics produced by karma, deep bondage arises.

Unable to understand that the five groups of consciousness arise from the intrinsic nature of form and so forth, the ālayavijñāna never says of itself, "I give rise to the seven consciousnesses," nor do the seven consciousnesses say, "We are born from the ālaya. Rather, they arise through the conceptual differentiation of the objective aspects grasped by one's own mind.

Such profound ālayavijñāna, with its subtle modes of activity and ultimate limits, is realized only by the Tathāgatas and the Bodhisattvas dwelling on the stages; it is entirely unknown to Śrāvakas who follow the Dharma of the ignorant, to Pratyekabuddhas, to ordinary worldlings, and to followers of external paths.

The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha’s Great Vaipulya, Scroll Nine: Beholding all Tathāgatas throughout the entire Dharma-realm—from their first aspiration, their cultivation of bodhisattva practices, the fulfillment of their great vows, the perfection of their merits, the attainment of equal and right enlightenment, the turning of the wondrous wheel of Dharma, and even the manifestation of entry into nirvana.

In this way, there was no such image that did not appear; it was as if all the various forms of the sun, moon, and stars were universally seen within clear water. All of this was due to the power of the roots of goodness cultivated by the maiden Maitrāyaṇī in her past lives.
At that time, the youth Sudhana, recollecting the marks of all the Buddhas he had beheld, joined his palms and gazed up at the maiden Maitrāyaṇī.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra, Scroll Ten, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā of Kapiśa by Imperial Decree.
From the "Chapter on the Vows and Practices of Samantabhadra for Entering the Realm of Inconceivable Liberation": "Good son!

I also thoroughly know all treatises on sound (*śabda-vidyā*), as well as voices, languages, internal and external origins, names, and etymological explanations—all of which are universal and inexhaustible. Even if Śakra were to listen to and receive the science of grammar (*śabda-vidyā*) from a Brahmā King for the full span of his celestial lifespan, reaching a complete thousand years, he still could not know the limits of the treatises on sound. Yet, within a single thought-moment, by means of this method of calculation, I am able to fully comprehend them, exhausting their very source and foundation."
“Good son! He further taught me the bodhisattva method of calculation, namely:
one hundred thousand is one lakṣa;”
One hundred lakṣas constitute one koṭi;
one koṭi multiplied by itself constitutes one ayuta;
one ayuta multiplied by itself constitutes one nayuta.
One nayuta multiplied by nayuta is one bimbara;
one bimbara multiplied by bimbara is one kiṅkara;
one kiṅkara multiplied by kiṅkara is one agara.
Agāra multiplied by agāra is one *viśvavara*;
*viśvavara* multiplied by *viśvavara* is one *pravarā*;
*pravarā* multiplied by *pravarā* is one *pramā*.
Two *parama* make one *vavara*; two *vavara* make one *apara*; two *apara* make one *tavara*.
Ten *tāvara* make one *nāvamati*; ten *nāvamati* make one *akṣema*; ten *akṣema* make one *pramā*.
One *prumā* makes one *nīma*;
one *nīma* makes one *abhakṣa*; one *abhakṣa* makes one *vibhaga*.
One vibhava makes one vibhāṣa; one vibhāṣa vibhāṣa makes one mṛvaka; one mṛvaka mṛvaka makes one nahaḷa.
Naha-ra-naha-ra makes one virāga;
virāga-virāga makes one mivaga; mivaga-mivaga makes one vigava.
Vigava multiplied by vigava makes one saṃkhyāma;
saṃkhyāma multiplied by saṃkhyāma makes one visara;
visara multiplied by visara makes one vimāna.
Two *vibhāṣa* make one *timitiṅga*;
two *timitiṅga* make one *vibhaṅga*; two *vibhaṅga* make one *vīrut*.
One *vīrudha-vīrudha* makes one *vibhāṣā*;
one *vibhāṣā-vibhāṣā* makes one *vibhāṣāti*;
one *vibhāṣāti-vibhāṣāti* makes one *vikhaṇḍa*.
Two vikhaṭas make one droṇa; two droṇas make one āḍhaka; two āḍhakas make one vāraṇa.
One *valana-valana* makes one *vipalana*;
one *vipalana-vipalana* makes one *samaya*;
one *samaya-samaya* makes one *vitudula*.
Two *mīdru* make one *khepara*; two *khepara* make one *dhavara*; two *dhavara* make one *mīdurina*.
Two *mṛdvīṇā* make one *śamita*; two *śamitas* make one *nirbhara*; two *nirbharas* make one *vicitra*.
Two *mīcara* make one *mīśara*; two *mīśara* make one *mīnitsata*; two *mīnitsata* make one *abhavātta*.
One *arbuda* and one *arbuda* make one *ni-kharva*;
one *ni-kharva* and one *ni-kharva* make one *mahā-nikharva*;
one *mahā-nikharva* and one *mahā-nikharva* make one *padma*.
Parikṣata, parikṣata makes one vimukha; vimukha, vimukha makes one prita; prita, prita makes one hrida.
One *hrīdha* is equal to one *aruka*; one *aruka* is equal to one *indriya*;
one *indriya* is equal to one *kṣiruka*.
One *kṣiruka* makes one *nūvana*; one *nūvana* makes one *haruṇa*; one *haruṇa* makes one *varuda*.
One *varuṭa-varuṭa* makes one *mṛduṭa*; one *mṛduṭa-mṛduṭa* makes one *kṣaṇya*;
one *kṣaṇya-kṣaṇya* makes one *acaramta*.
One *acaramta* is equal to one *īrupaya*; one *īrupaya* is equal to one *vimāruya*;
one *vimāruya* is equal to one *manupuya*.
One manupāya-manupāya is one visada; one visada-visada is one samata; one samata-samata is one paramatara.
Two *paramatara* make one *aramatara*; two *aramatara* make one *bhamatara-bhama*;
two *tara-bhamatara* make one *apamātara*.
Two apamātras make one gāmatra; two gāmatras make one nāmatra; two nāmatras make one himātra.
Two *kṣema-dvāra* make one *vimātra*; two *vimātra* make one *paramātra*; two *paramātra* make one *śimātra*.
Śimātara, śimātara makes one īra; īra, īra makes one vīra; vīra, vīra makes one tīra.
Two *tīra* make one *gīra*;
two *gīra* make one *sūphura*; two *sūphura* make one *cillaya*.
Two *cīrāya* make one *nīra*; two *nīra* make one *kīra*; two *kīra* make one *sīra*.
Two *sira* make one *hira*; two *hira* make one *mīra*; two *mīra* make one *salāṭa*.
One *salata* makes one *salata*; one *salata* and another *salata* make one *meruta*;
one *meruta* and another *meruta* make one *miruta*;
one *miruta* and another *miruta* make one *kheruta*.
Two *kṣurudha* make one *māndhara*;
two *māndhara* make one *dhuruda*; two *dhuruda* make one *samudra*.
Two *samudra* make one *ayuta*; two *ayuta* make one *kamara*; two *kamara* make one *maghava*.
One maghavā-maghavā is one apara; one apara-apara is one kṣīrodaka;
one kṣīrodaka-kṣīrodaka is one vairocana.
Velo-velo makes one kaśvāla; kaśvāla-kaśvāla makes one havya; havya-havya makes one vibhara.
Vipara-vipara makes one nāvara; nāvara-nāvara makes one niṣpanda; niṣpanda-niṣpanda makes one māvara.
Mabara-mabara constitutes one sarana; sarana-sarana constitutes one brahma;
brahma-brahma constitutes one brahmāna.
Two *brahmāṇa* make one *vigama*; two *vigama* make one *upavarta*; two *upavarta* make one *nirniśa*.
Two *nir-ni-śa* make one *acaya*; two *acayas* make one *samudra*; two *samudras* make one *ayuta*.
Two apantās make one avamānā; two avamānās make one utpala; two utpalas make one padma.
One padma is equal to one asaṃkhyeya; one asaṃkhyeya asaṃkhyeyas is equal to one avavāminya;
one avavāminya avavāminyas is equal to one nirvīra.
Nye-nyen nye-nyen constitutes one asaṃkhyeya;
an asaṃkhyeya asaṃkhyeyas constitute one asaṃkhyeya-parivarta;
an asaṃkhyeya-parivarta asaṃkhyeya-parivartas constitute one aprameya.
An immeasurable multiplied by an immeasurable constitutes one immeasurable-turn;
an immeasurable-turn multiplied by an immeasurable-turn constitutes one boundless;
a boundless multiplied by a boundless constitutes one boundless-turn.
An infinite turn and another infinite turn constitute one incomparable;
an incomparable and another incomparable constitute one incomparable turn;
an incomparable turn and another incomparable turn constitute one incalculable.
One asaṃkhyeya multiplied by an asaṃkhyeya is one asaṃkhyeyaparivarta;
one asaṃkhyeyaparivarta multiplied by an asaṃkhyeyaparivarta is one acintya;
one acintya multiplied by an acintya is one acintyaparivarta.
One incalculable turn of an incalculable [number] constitutes one inconceivable;
one inconceivable turn of an inconceivable [number] constitutes one inconceivable-turn;
one inconceivable-turn of an inconceivable-turn constitutes one immeasurable.
An immeasurable multiplied by an immeasurable constitutes one "immeasurable-turn";
an immeasurable-turn multiplied by an immeasurable-turn constitutes one "unspeakable";
an unspeakable multiplied by an unspeakable constitutes one "unspeakable-turn."
An unspeakable number of unspeakable numbers constitutes one unspeakably-unspeakable;
furthermore, an unspeakably-unspeakable number constitutes one unspeakably-unspeakable turn.
“Good son! Furthermore, by means of this method of calculation known to Bodhisattvas, I am able to distinguish and calculate the number of grains in countless *yojana*-wide heaps of sand;
I can also calculate and know the various arrangements and sequential distinctions of all worlds throughout the entirety of space in the ten directions.”
They are also able to calculate and know the various dimensions—whether broad or narrow, large or small—and the distinct differences in the names of all worlds throughout the ten directions.
That is to say:

they thoroughly know and penetrate without obstruction all names of kalpas, all names of Buddhas, all names of dharmas, all names of truths, all names of karmas, all names of bodhisattvas, and all names of sentient beings.

“Good son! I know only this Dharma-gate of the Light of Wisdom of Great Supernatural Powers in All Crafts. As for the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, they are able to know the number of all sentient beings and the names of all sentient beings;
they are able to know the number of categories of all phenomena and the names of all categories of phenomena.”
They are able to know the number of all time-periods and kalpas throughout the three periods of time, as well as the names of all those time-periods and kalpas;
they are able to know the number of all Tathāgatas, as well as the names of all those Tathāgatas;
they are able to know the number of all Bodhisattvas, as well as the names of all those Bodhisattvas.
They are also able to calculate and know the sequential order of the formation, destruction, and continuity of all worlds, both defiled and pure;
the sequential order of the succession of time, days, months, years, and kalpas; the sequential order of the names and successions of the appearance of all Buddhas;
and the sequential order of the turning of the wheel of Dharma by all Buddhas. One...
The continuous sequence of all bodhisattvas’ resolve to attain enlightenment and their practice of the path;
the continuous sequence of all bodhisattvas’ maturing of sentient beings; the continuous sequence of the causal karma created by all sentient beings;
the continuous sequence of the karmic retributions experienced by all sentient beings; and likewise, even unto all names and signs.
Through the successive arising of the inexhaustible continuity of dependent origination,
this Dharma-door of mastery in calculation attained by the Bodhisattva brings vast benefit to both self and others; it enables sentient beings to follow and enter into realization,
maturing them step by step until ultimate liberation is reached.
How could I possibly describe their merits, demonstrate their practices, reveal their spheres of activity,
manifest their supreme powers, discern their aspirations, proclaim their aids to the Path, inspire their great vows, expound their wondrous conduct,
elaborate upon their various perfections, praise their purity, or open up their extraordinary wisdom?
Even the light of such merit possessed by a bodhisattva cannot be known even in its slightest portion;
how much less could one fully know the ocean of supreme and wondrous majestic spiritual power and great merit of all Buddhas,
the fulfillment of the fruits of the perfections of the jewel-treasury of merit and wisdom of all Buddhas, and the realization of all Buddhas who shine like lamps?
How do you manifest the unobstructed realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*), proclaim the vast, pure, and sovereign wheel of Dharma of all Buddhas,
sport within the most supreme and profound samādhi-realms of all Buddhas, and awaken to the gates of liberation through the supernormal powers and wise insights of all Buddhas?

"Good son! To the south there is a city named Samudravetadīpa. There dwells an upāsikā named Prabhūtā. Go to her and ask: how should a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?"

At that time, having heard these words, the youth Sudhana leaped for joy; he gave rise to a mind of reverence and attained a rare jewel-like mind of faith and delight, accomplishing a vast mind for the benefit of sentient beings.

They are able to clearly perceive the sequential emergence of all Buddhas—their descent into birth, attainment of the Way, preaching of the Dharma, and entry into Nirvana—supremely pure, ultimately perfect, and having awakened to and entered into profound and subtle wisdom.

Manifesting bodies in accordance with all realms of existence, he thoroughly understood the distinct spheres of the three periods of time; having attained an inexhaustible treasury of great merit and emitted the sovereign radiance of great wisdom, he opened the locks of all cities within the triple world to advance toward Buddha-knowledge and reach ultimate Bodhi. He prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, gazed upon him with earnest devotion, and then took his leave and departed.

At that time, the youth Sudhana followed and reflected upon the instructions of the spiritual friends; observing with right mindfulness, he was earnest and yearning, his mind never weary or satisfied, just as the great ocean receives the rain from massive clouds and swallows up all flowing streams.
They formed this thought:
"The instruction of a spiritual friend is like the spring sun, causing all the roots and sprouts of wholesome dharmas to grow;
the instruction of a spiritual friend is like the full moon in autumn, such that wherever it shines and touches, body and mind become cool and serene."
The instruction of a virtuous friend is like the snowy mountains in summer, able to remove the heat and thirst of all wild beasts;
the instruction of a virtuous friend is like the sun over a fragrant pond, able to open the lotus flowers of all wholesome minds;
the instruction of a virtuous friend is like the orb of the sun-jewel, illuminating and guiding sentient beings to the place of the Dharma-treasure.
The instruction of a spiritual friend is like the Jambu tree, which brings forth the flowers and fruits of all merit and wisdom;
the instruction of a spiritual friend is like a great dragon king, who freely summons and spreads the cloud-rain of the sublime Dharma;
the instruction of a spiritual friend is like Mount Sumeru, where various untainted merits are accumulated, serving as the majestic abode for the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
"The instruction of a spiritual friend is like Śakra, Lord of the Devas, surrounded by all the devas of merit; it can destroy the asura armies of craving and false views.
Thinking thus, he proceeded gradually until he reached the city of Sāgaramati, where he searched everywhere for this upāsikā.
Then, all those people said to him:
"Good son! That upāsikā is here within this city, dwelling in her own home."

Having heard this, Sudhana went immediately to her door and stood with palms joined. He beheld her residence, which was vast, magnificent, and adorned in every way; it was surrounded on all sides by walls made of various jewels, and each of its four sides had a gate decorated with precious gems.

Having entered, Sudhana saw the laywoman seated upon a jeweled throne; she was in the prime of her youth with a radiant complexion, her features were dignified and beautiful, she wore no flowers or necklaces but dressed in plain garments with her hair hanging loose, and her majestic splendor was so extraordinary that all who beheld her were filled with joy.
Except for the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, no others can equal them;
possessing supreme power and a vast mind, they cause all sentient beings who see, hear, or draw near to them to give rise to feelings of respect and loving reverence.
Within that residence, ten billion seats were laid out, surpassing all that exists among humans and devas; these were all produced by the karmic power of the bodhisattva.

Inside the residence there were no garments, food, drink, or other ornaments; instead, a single small vessel was placed before it, and ten thousand young maidens surrounded it, their bodies adorned with every kind of exquisite jewel.
His speech was harmonious and elegant; he constantly attended at [the Buddha's] side, gazing up with reverence and following his instructions without ever feeling weary or indolent.
His body emitted a wondrous fragrance that perfumed the entire city and pervaded all of space; all humans and devas who smelled this fragrance never regressed from their resolve for Bodhicitta.
Other sentient beings who encounter this fragrance find their bodies and minds become supple and gentle;

they are free from thoughts of anger or harm, free from thoughts of resentment or enmity, free from thoughts of stinginess or jealousy, free from thoughts of flattery or deception, free from thoughts of treachery or crookedness, free from thoughts of greedy attachment, free from thoughts of malice, free from thoughts of illusion or hypocrisy, free from thoughts of inferiority, free from thoughts of arrogance, free from thoughts of deviance, free from thoughts of obstruction, and free from thoughts of clinging. They abide in a mind of equanimity, give rise to a mind of great compassion, develop a mind intent on benefiting others, abide in a mind of self-restraint, and remain free from a mind of covetous seeking.
Those who hear her voice rejoice and leap for joy;
those who behold her form are entirely freed from lustful defilement.
At that time, Sudhana went forward, prostrated at the feet of the upāsikā, circumambulated her to the right with reverence, and stood before her with palms joined.
He addressed him, saying: "Noble One!

I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice or cultivate the bodhisattva path. I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction; I pray that you will explain this to me."
He then replied: "Good son!

I have attained the Bodhisattva liberation door called 'The Treasury of Adornments of Inexhaustible Merit. Within this single small vessel, I can produce various kinds of sweet, excellent food and drink according to the diverse desires and inclinations of sentient beings, such that their color, fragrance, flavor, and texture are all fully sufficient."

Good son! Within this vessel of mine, the food and drink produced could serve even a hundred beings, a thousand beings, a hundred thousand beings, a hundred million beings, ten billion beings, a hundred billion beings, a trillion beings, a nayuta of beings, and even up to unspeakably unspeakable numbers of beings.

Suppose there were as many sentient beings as there are atoms in Jambudvīpa; as many sentient beings as there are atoms in one four-continent world system (cāturdvīpaka); as many sentient beings as there are atoms in a small thousand-world system, a medium thousand-world system, or a great trichiliocosm; even as many sentient beings as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields; and suppose there were as many sentient beings as there are atoms in all worlds throughout the ten directions—may they all be fully satisfied according to their respective desires and inclinations.
Hunger and thirst were eliminated, and their bodies and minds became peaceful and joyful;
their wisdom increased, yet the food and drink remained inexhaustible and never diminished.
Just as they produced food and drink, they were even able to produce various kinds of couches and seats, various kinds of bedding, various kinds of silken fabrics, and various kinds of garments.
Various types of vehicles, various banners and pennants, various canopies and parasols, various flower garlands,
various necklaces and ornaments, various precious jewels, various scattered incenses, various pellet incenses, various ointment incenses,
various burning incenses, various powdered incenses, and even various other things in accordance with the Dharma.
Regarding material requisites, he gives them to all who come with a universal mind, making no distinction between enemy and friend, noble and lowly, or rich and poor;
according to their wishes and desires, he causes them all to be fully satisfied.
They all conceived toward me a mind of respect, a mind of reverence, a mind of tireless devotion, and a mind of submissiveness. "Good son!

Suppose that all sentient beings in a single world-system in the eastern direction who practice the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, having eaten my food, were all to realize the fruits of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles and abide in their final bodies.
As with one world, so it is successively for a hundred worlds, a thousand worlds, a hundred thousand worlds,
ten million worlds, a billion worlds, ten billion worlds, a hundred billion worlds,
a hundred thousand billion worlds, a hundred thousand billion nayuta worlds, and worlds as numerous as the atoms in Jambudvīpa.
...worlds as numerous as the atoms in one set of four continents, worlds as numerous as the atoms in a small chiliocosm,
worlds as numerous as the atoms in a medium chiliocosm, worlds as numerous as the atoms in a great trichiliocosm,
and even up to worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields;...
In all the realms, whatever sentient beings there may be who practice the vehicles of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas,
having eaten my food, they shall all realize the fruits of Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha-hood and abide in their final bodies;
the same applies to the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
Furthermore, good son!

Just as in one world in the eastern direction, even up to worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields—whatever bodhisattvas in their final existence dwell therein, having partaken of my food, they all proceed to the most excellent site of enlightenment, subdue the armies of Māra, and attain equal and perfect awakening.

In the south, west, and north, in the four intermediate directions, and above and below—in every world, even as many worlds as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields—all those bodhisattvas in their final existence who have partaken of my food shall all go to the most excellent site of enlightenment, subdue the armies of Māra, and attain perfect awakening.
"Good son! Do you see these ten thousand maidens who are my retinue? He replied:
"I have seen it! the upāsikā said.
"O son of good family!..."
Now, my retinue of bodhisattvas consists of a hundred thousand asaṃkhyeyas, with these ten thousand maidens as their leaders;
they all practice the same conduct as I, share the same great vow, possess the same roots of goodness,
follow the same path of renunciation, and have the same pure understanding and the same pure faith.
Pure mindfulness; identical purity of inclination; identical purity of wisdom; identical immeasurable awakening;
identical purification of the faculties; identical universal mind; identical vast mind; identical sphere of activity; identical realized principle;
identical resolute understanding; identical clarity regarding the Dharma; identical pure and wondrous form; identical...
Equal in immeasurable power, equal in supreme diligence, equal in the sound of the True Dharma, equal in sounds according to the species [of beings],
equal in pure sound, equal in the foremost sound, equal in praising merit, equal in pure karma,
equal in pure retribution, equal in vast loving-kindness, equal in universal compassion, equal in universal protection, and equal in...
They bring all beings to full maturity.
Purifying their bodily actions in common with others, they manifest according to conditions so that all may see them as appropriate and be filled with joy;
purifying their verbal actions in common with others, they possess mastery over the Dharma, providing conventional explanations and disseminating the transformative teachings of the Dharma.
They are alike in being able to go universally to the sites of enlightenment of all Buddhas, and alike in being able to go to the abodes of all Buddhas to make offerings and serve them;
they are alike in manifesting awakened wisdom and fully understanding the various distinct Dharma-gates of all Buddhas;
and they are alike in attaining stable dwelling in the stages of pure conduct of all Bodhisattvas.

"Noble son! These ten thousand maidens are able to take this food and, in a single instant, reach everywhere throughout the ten directions to make offerings to all the great bodhisattvas dwelling in their final bodies, as well as to all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, even extending throughout the realms of hungry ghosts in the worlds of the ten directions, causing them all to be fully satisfied and removing their hunger and thirst."
“Good son! These ten thousand maidens shall also take my food and, within the realm of devas, provide sufficient deva-food;

likewise, within the realm of nāgas, they shall provide sufficient nāga-food; and even among humans and non-humans, they shall bestow various foods and drinks according to their needs, causing all to be fully satisfied.”
"In this vessel of mine, there has never been any decrease; how much less could there be any exhaustion? Good son!
Wait but a moment, and you shall see for yourself."

When these words were spoken, Sudhana immediately saw immeasurable sentient beings entering through the four gates; all had been invited by the original vows of the laywoman (upāsikā). Once they had assembled, she prepared seats for them to sit upon and provided them with food and drink according to their needs;

even down to various kinds of superior and exquisite requisites, she supplied them all in full abundance, causing the hearts of those sentient beings to be filled with joy, peace, and delight as they congratulated one another.
Furthermore, the items produced within this vessel neither diminish nor are ever exhausted.
At that time, having made this offering, the upāsikā said to Sudhana: "Noble son!..."

I know only this bodhisattva liberation door of the treasury of inexhaustible adornments of merit. As for the inexhaustible treasury of great adornments of merit of all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, it is profoundly deep and bottomless like the great ocean;
it is vast and boundless like space;
and it fulfills the hearts of sentient beings like a wish-fulfilling jewel.
All that is sought is obtained, like a great mass of jewels;
it protects all beings, like the Cakravāḍa mountains;
and it causes all roots of goodness to grow, like a great rain from the clouds.
Guarding the treasury of the Dharma is like a lock and key;
gathering the jewels of the Dharma universally is like Mount Sumeru;
destroying the darkness of ignorance is like a lamp or candle.
He universally shelters all living beings, like a lofty parasol.
How could I possibly know or describe his meritorious conduct? Good son!
To the south there is a city named Mahānta; therein dwells an elder named Jñānasampanna. Go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
Then, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, gazed up at him with deep reverence, and took his leave. At that time,

having attained the bodhisattva liberation door of the inexhaustible treasury of merit and adornment, Sudhana reflected upon that ocean of merit in accordance with its nature and contemplated that space of merit.
They turn toward that mass of merit;
they ascend that mountain of merit;
they gather that treasury of merit.
Drink from that spring of merit;
sport in that pool of merit;
purify that field of merit.
Behold that treasury of merit;
enter that teaching of merit;
open those eyes of merit.
Practicing that path of merit and planting those seeds of merit,
he proceeded by stages until he reached the great city of Mahāvana, where he searched everywhere for the wise householder.

One should give rise to a heart of yearning for spiritual friends; maintain mindfulness of spiritual friends without interruption; cultivate a firm resolve and aspiration for spiritual friends; and through skillful means, seek to meet all spiritual friends with never-ceasing satisfaction.
One should vow to serve all spiritual friends with diligent effort and tirelessness, using them to perfume and cultivate one's own mind.
One knows that by relying on a spiritual friend, one can fulfill all virtues;
one knows that by relying on a spiritual friend, one can generate all blessings;
one knows that by relying on a spiritual friend, one can increase all practices.
One knows that by relying on spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), one is able to serve all virtuous associates spontaneously, without being taught by others;
one knows that by relying on spiritual friends, all the faculties (*indriya*) of a bodhisattva are purified.

Reflecting in this way, they cause their roots of goodness to grow, deepen their aspiration and joy, augment the foundation of their virtue, broaden their great compassion, draw near to all-knowledge, fulfill the path of Samantabhadra, illuminate the true Dharma of all Buddhas, increase all the practices and vows of Bodhisattvas, and radiantly manifest the light of wisdom of the Tathāgata’s ten powers.
At that time, Sudhana saw the householder within the city, at the crossroads of the marketplace, atop a terrace of the seven treasures, seated upon a throne adorned with various jewels;

that throne was exquisite and infinitely pure, its body fashioned from the king of wish-fulfilling gems (*cintāmaṇi-rāja*), its feet from various *vajras* and *indranīla* mani-jewels, draped with nets of jeweled cords and pearls, and embellished with *vimalagarbha* mani-jewels.
Furthermore, it was adorned with five hundred exquisite images of precious jewels;
celestial jewel-garments were spread out, celestial banners and pennants were erected, great jewel-nets were stretched, and great jewel-canopies were hung, with Jambūnada gold forming their covers;
pure lapis lazuli jewels formed their poles.
He caused people to hold it up to cover its top;
the wings and feathers of the king of geese served as its fan,
and the tails of white yak-cows served as its whisk.
It was entirely adorned with stainless, wondrous jewels.

Celestial youths stood on the left and right, burning various exquisite incenses and raining down various celestial flowers. Day and night, five hundred musical instruments were constantly played; their sounds were so exquisite that they surpassed those of the heavens, and among all sentient beings who heard them, there was none who did not rejoice.
Surrounded before and behind by ten thousand followers, their physical forms were upright and majestic, pleasing to all who beheld them.

Adorned with celestial ornaments, they surpassed even the gods and humans, being most excellent and peerless; having fully accomplished the aspirations of Bodhisattvas, they shared the same past roots of goodness as the householder, standing in attendance and gazing upon him while receiving his instructions.

At that time, all sentient beings within that city, as well as all the hosts of devas in the sky, conceived a mind of compliance, a mind of affection, and a mind of joy toward the householder. Because their minds were compliant with, joyful in, and affectionate toward this spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), they immediately gave rise to clouds of all kinds of exquisite celestial *kusuma* jewel-flowers and rained down a universal shower of all kinds of exquisite celestial *kusuma* jewel-flowers.
These gods and humans had also planted pure roots of goodness together with the householder in the past.
At that time, having witnessed this, Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, and stood with palms joined, saying: "Noble One!"
For the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, I have resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
for the sake of causing all sentient beings to eliminate suffering and hardship;
and for the sake of causing all sentient beings to achieve ultimate peace and happiness.
In order to cause all sentient beings to emerge from the ocean of birth and death;
in order to cause all sentient beings to enter the island of the Dharma-treasure;
and in order to cause all sentient beings to dry up the river of craving.
In order to cause all sentient beings to give rise to great compassion;
in order to cause all sentient beings to abandon and leave behind greedy attachment;
and in order to cause all sentient beings to thirst for and yearn after the Buddha’s wisdom.
In order to cause all sentient beings to cross over the great wilderness of birth and death;
in order to cause all sentient beings to love and delight in the supreme merits of all Buddhas;
and in order to cause all sentient beings to exit the city of the triple world.
In order to cause all sentient beings to enter the city of omniscience, they resolve upon bodhicitta through such various benefits as these;

yet they do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practices, nor how they should cultivate the bodhisattva path, so as to be able to gather and protect all sentient beings and serve as a place of reliance for them.
"I have heard that the Noble One is skilled at providing instruction;
I pray that you will speak for me. The householder replied, "Excellent!"
Excellent! Son of good family,
it is well that you have been able to resolve your mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of such benefit.
"Good son! It is rare to find one who resolves to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

If such a person can resolve their mind upon it, they will then be able to seek the bodhisattva practices with an unshakable mind, and having encountered spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), their heart will never grow weary or satisfied."
Approaching spiritual friends with a mind free from weariness;
serving spiritual friends with a mind free from sorrow or distress;
making offerings to spiritual friends without ever regressing.
One cherishes spiritual friends and never abandons them;
one thirsts for spiritual friends without a moment’s respite;
one seeks spiritual friends without ceasing at any time.
One follows the instructions of spiritual friends without ever becoming indolent;
one receives the commands of spiritual friends with a mind free from error.

Spiritual friends possess great majestic power and are difficult to encounter, serve, or make offerings to. If one can attend to them, pay them homage, and praise them with a heart free from anxiety or regret, then one will attain all merits in full and the poisons of afflictions shall not disturb the mind.
“Good son! Do you see these ten thousand members of my retinue and assembly? He replied:
“I have seen it!
the householder said.
“O son of good family!

I have already caused them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, to be born into the family of the Tathāgatas, to increase their pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma*), and to dwell securely in the immeasurable *pāramitās*;
they study the ten powers of the Buddha, leave behind the seeds of the mundane world, and abide in the lineage of the Tathāgatas;
they shatter the wheel of birth and death and turn the pure wheel of Dharma.
They extinguish the three evil destinies and abide in the destiny of the True Dharma.
Capable of accomplishing all such bodhisattva practices, they are universally able to rescue and protect all sentient beings.

"Good son! I have attained the liberation door called 'The Treasury of Merit Produced According to One's Wishes,' by which all sentient beings have their every need fulfilled and their vows completely satisfied."

That is to say: providing food to those who need food, drink to those who need drink; likewise, various kinds of clothing, necklaces, flower garlands, silken fabrics, burning incense, unguents, powdered incense, gold, silver, pearls, and all manner of rare treasures; various banners and streamers, various canopies and parasols, houses, dwellings, and furnishings for reclining and resting; various lamps and candles, medicinal decoctions and drugs for the treatment of illness; various boats and ships, elephants, horses, carriages, slaves, oxen, sheep, and all manner of attendants—every such requisite for life.

Furthermore, he is able to give away celestial crowns and precious ornaments, the bright jewel within his topknot, and even his beloved wives, concubines, sons, and daughters, as well as his eyes, ears, nose, tongue, skin, flesh, marrow, bones, body, hands, and feet—without discriminating between the poor and the wealthy, the noble and the humble, or the beautiful and the ugly—but according to the intentions of those who come to him, he gives them all. He even preaches the true, wondrous Dharma for their sake, causing them to practice and realize it until they reach ultimate perfection.
"Good son! Wait but a moment, and you shall see for yourself.

As these words were spoken, immeasurable sentient beings—from various locations, various worlds, various lands, various cities, various villages, and various dwellings—differing in form and kind, with diverse inclinations and attachments, and numbering in the infinite, all gathered together by the power of the Bodhisattva’s past vows.

At that time, the householder, knowing that the assembly had gathered, surveyed them all with a steady gaze; after reflecting for a brief moment, he looked up into the void, and whatever was required descended from the sky, flowing continuously into the householder’s palms.
According to the various assemblies and all their aspirations, he bestows everything with his own hands, causing them all to be fully satisfied.

Once their wishes are fulfilled, they give rise to great joy; their physical complexion becomes radiant and pleasant, their minds become harmonious and supple, and they become capable of receiving transformation. Only then does he preach for them the various sublime Dharmas.
That is to say:
for those who seek to obtain an abundance of all kinds of fine foods, he teaches various gateways for accumulating merit;

he expounds upon the practice of leaving all poverty behind, the practice of the nectar-like wealth of abundance, the practice of the great reverence of Dharma-knowledge, the practice of adorning the body with the marks and signs of excellence, the practice of achieving majestic power to subdue demonic adversaries, and the practice of the food of Dharma-joy and the delight of dhyāna.

They increase and accomplish practices that are difficult to subdue; they are well able to thoroughly understand the practice of the unsurpassed nutriment, which grants eternal life, physical strength, peace, and eloquence, and brings about the full possession of the Dharma-gates.

To satisfy those who desire various fine drinks, he preaches the Dharma for them, causing them to abandon craving within birth and death, to rejoice in the Buddha Vehicle, and to enter the profound flavor of the Dharma;

to satisfy those who desire various superior flavors, he preaches the Dharma for them, causing them all to be fully endowed with and filled by the flavor of the Dharma, so that they may realize the supreme flavor among the flavors of the Tathāgata;

to satisfy those who desire various boats and vehicles, he proclaims for them the Dharma-gate of renunciation, causing them all to cross over the great ocean of birth and death and to be carried upon the most excellent, unsurpassed Mahāyāna.

For those who desire to be fully provided with clothing, he preaches the Dharma for them so that they may obtain the raiment of pure shame and modesty, and even the Tathāgata’s pure and wondrous marks and golden-hued skin; all such articles of livelihood he bestows according to their wishes, providing for them without exception.

Thereafter, he preached the Dharma to them all according to what was appropriate for each, causing them all to awaken to and enter the gateway of the unsurpassed, pure wisdom as suited to their needs; having heard the Dharma, they returned to their respective abodes.
