At that time, having revealed to the youth Sudhana the inconceivable realm of liberation of the bodhisattvas, the householder said to him: "Noble son!

I know only this liberation door of the treasury of merit produced at will; as for the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who have accomplished the "Precious Hand," which covers all worlds throughout the ten directions, making universal offerings to the Buddhas and bestowing gifts upon all sentient beings, they use their power of mastery to raise clouds of various colored jewels and rain down showers of various colored jewels—namely:
various colored necklaces, various colored jeweled crowns, various colored exquisite garlands, and various...
Various colors of worldly garments, various colors of Dharma robes, various colors of ornaments,
various colors of precious flowers, various colors of exquisite incenses, various colors of unguents, various colors of powdered incenses,
various colors of pavilions, various colors of precious parasols, and various colors of banners and streamers.
The sounds of music were exquisite, singing praises of the Buddha-dharma;

even the various articles of daily life pervaded the dwellings of all sentient beings and filled the sites of enlightenment in all buddha-fields, making offerings to all Buddhas and bringing all sentient beings to maturity. And...
How could I possibly know or describe those various merits and sovereign spiritual powers?
Son of good family!

To the south of here there is a great city named Siṃhaghoṣa; therein dwells an elder named Dharmaratnoṣṇīṣa. Go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path.

At that time, the youth Sudhana leaped for joy and exulted, feeling profound personal gratitude. He realized that it was through all the spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) that his merits were brought to fulfillment; thus, he paid homage to the spiritual friends with respect and humility, performing the rites due to a disciple.
He formed this thought:
"It is because of this householder that I have been awakened; it is he who has enabled me to hear this rare Dharma.

Reflecting thus, he never ceased his affectionate regard for the spiritual friend, never faltered in his heart of reverence for the spiritual friend, always delighted in receiving and practicing the spiritual friend’s instructions, maintained resolute faith and compliance with the spiritual friend’s words, increased his respect for the spiritual friend ever further, and served the spiritual friend with a mind free from regression. He prostrated at the householder’s feet, circumambulated him countless times, gazed up at him with earnest devotion, and then took his leave and departed.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Ten;
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Eleven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā of Kaśmīra by Imperial Decree.
The Chapter on Entering the Sphere of the Inconceivable Liberation and the Vows and Practices of Samantabhadra.
At that time, after the youth Sudhana had heard this profound gate of liberation from the householder, he contemplated and practiced it with unwavering persistence.

They roam that ocean of merit; they purify that field of merit; they proceed toward that ford of merit; they look up to that mountain of merit; they open that treasury of merit; they turn that wheel of merit; they contemplate those dharmas of merit; they plant those causes of merit; they generate that power of merit; they increase that momentum of merit; they cultivate that mind of merit; and they awaken to that gateway of merit.
Gradually proceeding to the city of Śrāvastī, he searched everywhere for the elder Ratnaśikhin.
Seeing him in the marketplace, he immediately prostrated himself before him.
Circumambulating him countless times, he stood before him with palms joined and said:

“Noble One! I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice, nor how a bodhisattva should cultivate the bodhisattva path.”
Excellent, O Noble One!
I pray that you will explain to me the path of the bodhisattvas, so that by riding upon this path I may proceed toward omniscience.
At that time, the elder took Sudhana by the hand, led him to his home, showed him his residence, and said to Sudhana: "Noble son!
“You should now observe the house in which I dwell.
At that time, Sudhana looked all around and saw that the house was vast, magnificent, and beautiful; it had two gates on each of its four sides, all constructed of Jāmbūnada gold.
Walls of white silver encircle it on all sides;
palaces of crystal are adorned with various jewels;
and towers are made of deep-blue lapis lazuli.
Its pillars were made of exquisite *śaṅkha* gems;
its steps, courtyards, balconies, railings, doors, windows, and lattices were all fashioned from various jewels, adorned and embellished with hundreds of thousands of kinds of precious stones.
There were agate gem-pools filled to the brim with fragrant water, and on all four sides were railings draped with pearls.
Forests of various jewel trees stood in rows all around.
Lion thrones were made of red pearl-maṇi jewels, adorned with the intermingling of incalculable gems;
canopies were fashioned from the king of maṇi jewels, the Vairocana.
To the left and right of his seat, he established jeweled banners of mani-gems with blazing flames;
a net made of wish-fulfilling jewel-kings of variegated light covered them above.
Within that residence was a great multi-storied pavilion, ten stories high, with eight gates opening on each level.
Having entered, Sudhana observed them in succession.
On the lowest level, he saw various kinds of superior flavors of food and drink being distributed.
Upon seeing the second tier, he bestowed various precious garments and manifold wealth.
Upon seeing the third tier, he universally bestowed all manner of precious ornaments.
Upon seeing the fourth tier, he bestowed female attendants who were skillful in speech, as well as retinues who followed his will, along with the finest and most exquisite treasures for their use.
Upon seeing the fifth tier, bodhisattvas of the fifth stage were gathered there in clouds, expounding the sublime Dharma for the sake of bringing peace to sentient beings.

All their activities were nothing other than the accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s most supreme discourse on the *dhāraṇī* gates and the ocean of *samādhis*, as well as the various worldly forms of brilliant wisdom, radiance, seals, and practices.
Upon seeing the sixth level, there were various bodhisattvas who had all already accomplished profound wisdom;
they thoroughly understood the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and attained great dhāraṇī;
they were fully endowed with the three types of higher knowledge and the six supernormal powers.
Entering the gate of the universal treasury, they emerge from obstructive realms;
abiding in the non-dual dharma, they manifest the majestic deportment of Buddhas.
Thus they gather together amidst the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment throughout the unspeakably wondrously adorned oceans of worlds.
Each, by means of distinct names, separately reveals the gateways of the *prajñāpāramitā*;
that is to say:
the gateway of the *prajñāpāramitā* of the treasury of tranquility, and the gateway of the wisdom that skillfully discriminates the knowledge of all sentient beings.

The gate of the pāramitās: the gate of the pāramitā of unshakable wisdom, the gate of the pāramitā of the light of detachment from desire, the gate of the pāramitā of the treasury that cannot be overcome,
the gate of the pāramitā of illuminating the wheel of sentient beings, and the gate of the pāramitā of conforming to the net of teachings.
The *prajñāpāramitā* gate of the treasury of the ocean of merit; the *prajñāpāramitā* gate of universal vision’s relinquishing and attaining;
the *prajñāpāramitā* gate of entering the inexhaustible treasury and practicing in accordance with it;
the *prajñāpāramitā* gate of entering the inexhaustible ocean of skillful means for all worlds; and the *prajñāpāramitā* gate of entering in accordance with all worlds...
The gate of Prajñāpāramitā that is the ocean of all teachings; the gate of Prajñāpāramitā of unimpeded eloquence;
the gate of Prajñāpāramitā that universally illumines according to the needs of sentient beings without obstruction;
the gate of Prajñāpāramitā of stainless radiance; and the gate of Prajñāpāramitā that constantly contemplates past conditions and spreads the clouds of Dharma.
The Gate of Honey.

He preached such hundreds of thousands of *asaṃkhyeya* gates of the *prajñāpāramitā*, pervading the assembly at the site of enlightenment beyond description, manifesting the adornment of profound wisdom.
Upon seeing the seventh layer, they attained the patience of an echo-like resonance (*pratibhāsa-kṣānti*).

Bodhisattvas filled its entirety, employing the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*) to analyze and expound the various gateways of transcendence (*nairyāṇika-mukha*), and were able to hear, retain, and uphold all the true Dharma (*saddharma*) preached by all Tathāgatas.
Upon seeing the eighth layer, one attains the power of non-retrogressive supernatural knowledges and wisdom.
Immeasurable bodhisattvas gather therein, observing all worlds with subtle wisdom.
They know that the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment in all Buddha-fields are like illusions, like mirages, like shadows, and like reflections, lacking any inherent nature.

They perceive the non-conceptual realm of all Tathāgatas, manifesting the universal form-bodies of all Buddhas; they are able to pervade the worlds of the ten directions with a single voice, their bodies reaching all sites of enlightenment throughout the entire Dharma-realm, leaving nothing unpenetrated.

They universally enter the realm of the Buddhas, universally behold the bodies of the Buddhas, and are universally able to receive and uphold all Buddha-dharmas; they universally serve as the foremost leaders within the assemblies of all Buddhas, expounding the essential points of the Dharma.
He saw the ninth level, where the assembly of Bodhisattvas bound to one more birth had gathered;
he saw the tenth level, which was filled with all the Tathāgatas.

From the first generation of the mind of enlightenment, they cultivate the bodhisattva practices, transcend the wheel of birth and death, fulfill the ocean of great vows, possess supreme supernormal powers, and attain supreme mastery.
By means of supreme power, he purifies Buddha-fields with sublime adornments;
he appears universally in the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment throughout the ten directions, expounding the True Dharma, and even manifesting his final nirvana.
"Throughout the limits of the future, you shall tame, benefit, and transform sentient beings, causing all such things to be clearly seen.
At that time, having witnessed these and other such extraordinary events, Sudhana said: "Noble One!"
"In what place in the past did you plant such roots of goodness that you have obtained these kinds of sublime rewards and brought about this entire assembly of purity?
The elder replied, "O son of good family!"
I recall that in the past, beyond as many eons as there are atoms in a buddha-field, there was a world named Wheel Adorned with Various Colors;

the Buddha’s name was King of Universal Adornment of the Boundless Light Perfecting the Dharma Realm, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
Together with an assembly of hundreds of billions of śrāvakas, with Jñānavairocana as their leader;
and together with an assembly of hundreds of billions of bodhisattvas, with Jñānasūryatejaprabha as their leader.

At that time, there was a king named Dharmeśvara. Having accepted the king's invitation, the Buddha entered the Maṇidhvaja-vyūha Garden; I played exquisite music on the road and offered worship by burning a single pellet of incense.

Because that Tathāgata, together with the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, has accepted my offerings, this incense smoke shall rise as great clouds of fragrance, pervading the entirety of space to form a protective canopy. For seven days and seven nights throughout Jambudvīpa, it shall rain down everywhere various boundless multicolored clouds of exquisite fragrance, corresponding to the physical forms of sentient beings.

Furthermore, they cause musical sounds to produce all manner of exquisite and wondrous tones that pervade the void, manifesting the Tathāgata’s inconceivable, unimpeded, and vast accumulation of wisdom regarding the three periods of time, so that those who hear them may eliminate all defilements and obstructions of affliction,
increase all true roots of goodness, and swiftly perfect the knowledge of all-knowledge.

I was able to universally manifest various supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). At that time, I dedicated the roots of merit from these offerings toward three goals: first, the vow to forever be free from poverty and suffering; [the second was to]... [the third was to]...; and to [attain] the state of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). Furthermore, I vowed that all sentient beings might likewise attain such roots of merit as these. Having made this vow, I immediately attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*) and became able to manifest the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*). Subsequently, I proceeded to the presence of the Buddha Śālendrarāja and, having heard his teaching, I attained the stage of Non-Returner (*anāgāmin*). Thereafter, I passed away from that life and was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven. From there, I descended to be born in the human world, where I encountered the present Buddha Śākyamuni and attained the fruit of Arhatship. My lifespan has now reached eighty thousand years, yet my physical appearance remains like that of a youth of sixteen. I am currently residing at the Jetavana Monastery in Śrāvastī, where I preach the Dharma for the sake of the fourfold assembly. All those who hear my teaching will never again fall back into the realms of the three evil destinies. This is called the first root of merit for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Akṣayamati. The Buddha said to the Venerable Ānanda, “The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Akṣayamati possesses such inexhaustible roots of merit. You should know that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Akṣayamati is one who has long cultivated the roots of goodness under many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas. The Buddha then spoke a verse: “The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, having served many Buddhas, has perfected the practice of giving and attained the stage of non-retrogression. Second, they vowed to always see all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
third, they vowed to constantly hear the True Dharma of all Buddhas.
Due to these causes and conditions, they have obtained this retribution.
“Good son! I know only this bodhisattva liberation door called ‘The Treasury of Merit Universally Adorned by Unobstructed Vows.
As for those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have attained the inconceivable treasure-trove of merit and produce inconceivable and immeasurable virtues;”
They enter the ocean of the Tathāgatas' bodies, which is free from discrimination; they are sheltered by the cloud of the supreme Dharma, which is free from discrimination;
they cultivate the aids to the path of merit, which are free from discrimination;
and they give rise to the net of Samantabhadra’s practices, which is free from discrimination.
They realize the state of non-conceptual samādhi, which is equal to the roots of goodness of non-conceptual Bodhisattvas;
they abide in the non-conceptual dwelling of the Tathāgatas;
and they perceive the equality of the three periods of time as non-conceptual, never becoming weary or fatigued throughout all kalpas.
They dwell on the stage of sovereign mastery over the realm of the indestructible universal eye.
How could I possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct? Noble son!
In the south there is a land named Mūlamūla;
in that land there is a city named Samantamukha;
within it dwells an elder named Samantanetra.
"Go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
Then, the youth Sudhana prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, gazed up at him with deep reverence, and took his leave to depart.
At that time, having heard this liberation from the householder Ratnaśikhin, the youth Sudhana deeply entered the immeasurable knowledge and vision of all Buddhas,
dwelt securely in the immeasurable supreme practices of Bodhisattvas, thoroughly mastered the immeasurable skillful means of Bodhisattvas,
sought after the immeasurable Dharma-gates of Bodhisattvas, and purified the immeasurable... of Bodhisattvas.
Measuring their faith and understanding, clarifying and sharpening the immeasurable faculties of bodhisattvas, accomplishing the immeasurable aspirations of bodhisattvas,
penetrating the immeasurable gates of bodhisattva practice, increasing the immeasurable power of bodhisattva vows,
establishing the boundless banner of victory of bodhisattvas, and giving rise to the boundless wisdom of bodhisattvas, they realize...
The Bodhisattva’s boundless light of Dharma universally enters the boundless great assemblies of Bodhisattvas;
they are certain and free from doubt regarding the Bodhisattva Dharma, seeking the pure liberation of Bodhisattvas, dwelling in the Bodhisattva mind,
possessing deep faith and delight, and applying their attention in accordance with it.

Proceeding by stages, he arrived at the kingdom of Veṇṭaka. He searched everywhere for the location of that city; though he encountered many hardships, he did not shrink from toil or suffering, his body felt no fatigue and his mind never grew weary or despondent.

He kept only the instructions of the spiritual friend in right mindfulness, vowing to always remain close to, serve, and make offerings to him. He thoroughly disciplined all his faculties and remained free from all negligence.

With a mind of constant love and joy toward spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), he then arrived at the city-gate of Universal Entrance (*Samantamukha*), surrounded by hundreds of thousands of villages; that city was vast and adorned with every kind of ornament.
The battlemented walls are lofty and steep, while the thoroughfares are broad and level.
The marketplace is lined with artisans of a hundred crafts, and its wares consist mostly of rare and exotic treasures.
Caravans of goods pass to and fro in abundance, and the scene of men and things is most impressive to behold.
At that time, Sudhana searched throughout the city for the residence of the elder, and everyone replied to him:
"He dwells in the marketplace, at the place where incense and medicines are sold."
Having heard this, he went there.
Seeing him situated upon the fragrant platform seat, he immediately approached, prostrated at his feet, stood with palms joined, and said: "Noble One!"
I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
The elder said: "Excellent! Excellent!"
"Good son! You have already been able to resolve upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Good son!"

In the past, I studied under the youth Mañjuśrī, where I learned the sublime medical prescriptions for understanding the root causes of the arising of illnesses, as well as the essential methods for various fragrances; by means of this knowledge, I am able to understand the diverse causal conditions of the illnesses of all sentient beings and can provide healing for them all.
That is to say:
wind-disorders, jaundice, phlegm-fever, demonic possession, poisonous charms, and even injuries caused by water or fire;

all such internal and external ailments, of infinite varieties, I am able to treat according to the Dharma with various prescriptions and medicines within a single thought-moment, causing them all to be cured and bestowing upon them peace and happiness.
"You should study and practice this Dharma-gate.
Sudhana spoke again: "Noble One!"
"I asked the Bodhisattva about the sublime practices he cultivates; why then do you speak of these worldly medical prescriptions?
The Elder replied, "Good son!..."
When a bodhisattva first begins to train in the cultivation of enlightenment, one should know that illness constitutes the greatest obstacle.
If sentient beings have physical illnesses, their minds will be unsettled; how then could they cultivate the various pāramitās?
Therefore, when a bodhisattva cultivates enlightenment, they should first treat all illnesses of the body.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva observes that all sentient beings in every world—whether they are engaged in worldly affairs and enjoy sensual pleasures, or even those who have left the home life to diligently practice and attain the fruits of the Noble Path—all do so because of the king’s civilizing influence and governance, which must depend upon freedom from illness.
Why is this? Because human kings are the very foundation of peace and happiness for all sentient beings.
When Bodhisattvas manifest their transformative power, they first treat the king and subsequently heal the sentient beings.
"Only after ensuring they are free from affliction and suffering shall you preach the Dharma to subdue their minds. 'Good son!

If a bodhisattva wishes to treat various illnesses, he should first carefully observe the origins of those diseases—their categories, increases, and decreases are infinite and boundless; I shall now explain a small portion of them for you.'"
“Good son! All sentient beings take the four great elements as the basis for their bodies; from these four-element bodies, four types of illness can arise.
They are as follows:”
There are bodily illnesses, mental illnesses, adventitious illnesses, and illnesses that are both bodily and mental.
Regarding bodily illnesses, wind, bile, phlegm, and heat are their primary causes;
regarding mental illnesses, insanity and mental derangement are their primary causes.
Regarding "guest illnesses," these are primarily caused by injuries from weapons or staffs, or by excessive physical exertion.
Regarding "inherent illnesses," these are primarily caused by hunger and thirst, cold and heat, suffering and pleasure, and sorrow and joy.
Other categories of diseases arise from one another in succession, causing sentient beings to experience suffering of body and mind. "Good son!
Such various illnesses are rare among the poor and lowly because they undergo much labor; they are more common among the wealthy and noble because they indulge in excessive pleasure."

“Good son! All sentient beings form their bodies through the aggregation of immeasurable, extremely subtle great elements (*mahābhūta*), just as the great ocean is composed of countless drops of water.
Likewise, the human body has three *koṭis* of body hairs and three *koṭis* of pores, each of which serves as a dwelling place for three *koṭis* of worms.”

Observing this with clarity: within the pores of the skin, inside both eyes, on the palms of the hands and soles of the feet, and at the places where fat and grease accumulate, hair-insects do not grow;
as for the rest of the body parts, there is no space between them that is empty.
“Good son! Furthermore, contemplate this body as consisting solely of the nature of the five great elements. What are these five?
That is to say:
solidity, moisture, warmth, motion, and the nature of space.
As for what is called "solidity," it is as follows:
The three hundred and sixty bones of the body, along with all that is firm and hard, are of the nature of the earth element;
all that is moist and humid is of the nature of the water element;
and all sensations of warmth are of the nature of the fire element.
All that is mobile is of the nature of the wind element;
all cavities and apertures are of the nature of the space element.
Yet these four great elements consist largely of atoms, which abide in mutual dependence within the realm of space.
The intrinsic nature of atoms is subtle and difficult to know; except for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, no others are able to perceive it.
"Good son! Thus, this body formed by the harmonious combination of the five great elements is like a worldly granary or basket, which ultimately ends in decay and dispersal."
Thus, this physical vessel is sustained by karma and is not something created by a sovereign god (īśvara);
nor is it produced by intrinsic nature (svabhāva), time, space, or the like.
It is, for example, like a potter who shapes clay into a vessel, fills it with foul impurities, and adorns it with colorful paintings to deceive the foolish.
Furthermore, it is like four snakes placed within a single basket; likewise, the four great elements combine to form this body.
If even one element becomes unbalanced, one hundred and one diseases arise.
Therefore, the wise person should contemplate this body as if tending to venomous snakes, or as if holding a fragile earthen vessel.
"Good son! You should further know that both the internal body and the external vessel-world are all composed of the four great elements.
From beginning to end, they undergo transformation through five stages."
What is the fivefold transformation of the external vessel-world?
It refers to that which is elicited by the sentient beings of the ten directions throughout the entirety of space and sustained by their deluded karma.
At the time when the kalpa first formed, human lifespan was immeasurable and beings were born through spontaneous transformation;
there was no sense of "I" or "mine," nor did food, morsel-food, greed, or other such afflictions manifest.
Next, by means of the "mine-ness" [of possessions], field-lords were established together to exercise governance.
Subsequently, the lifespan gradually decreased until it reached ten years.
Due to these evil karmas, the three minor calamities arose; by the time of the fifth period, the world was on the verge of destruction.
Once the fire disaster has arisen, the Brahma world becomes entirely empty; the same applies to the successive occurrence of water disasters and wind disasters.
Good son! This is called the fivefold transformation of the external vessel-world.
What are the five stages of transformation within the internal body?
They are as follows: the stage of infancy, in which the mind is devoid of conceptual discrimination;
Just as at the beginning of a kalpa, humans possessed no sense of "mine," so it was during the stage of childhood;
subsequently, they were able to distinguish right from wrong,
just as in the second period, the distinction between self and other was established.
Next is the stage of middle age, where one indulges in greed, anger, and delusion;
it is like the third period, when they collectively established a field-lord.
Next is the stage of old age, where one is assailed by manifold illnesses.
Just as in the fourth period, lifespan and other factors decline;
then, reaching the stage of death, the body disintegrates and life ends;
and just as in the fifth period, the world undergoes destruction—this is called the fivefold transformation of the internal body.
Sudhana said, "Noble One! By what causes do these five periods arise?"
The Universal Eye replied:
"Good son! Time has no inherent substance; it is produced by conceptual discrimination and revolves without end, following the wheel of deluded karma."
Just as when a person awakens from sleep, that is called the "initial period," consisting of the first *kṣaṇa* and *tat-kṣaṇa*.
Next are the *lava*, *muhūrta*, day and night, years, and *kalpas*; these are the many distinctions of time.
Alternatively, a single year may be divided into six seasons, namely:
the spring season, the hot season, the rainy season, the autumn season, the cold season, and the snowy season.
Therefore, the wise person knows the increase and decrease of diseases and is well-versed in all the seasons of various regions.
That is to say: during the snowy season of spring, phlegm disorders are provoked;
during the hot and rainy season, wind disorders arise.
During the cold season of autumn, yellow fever increases;
in general, diseases increase according to the seasons.
"O son of good family!
I have now explained to you how various ailments increase according to the seasons; such bodily illnesses arise from indigestion.

If sentient beings can know moderation and contentment regarding food and drink, weighing their age and vigor, the strength or weakness of their constitution, and the seasonal conditions of cold and heat, wind, rain, dryness, and moisture;
and if they examine their own physical exertion and rest to ensure they act appropriately, they will not err in what is suitable for them.
It enables all manner of illnesses to arise without cause. "Good son!
In this dwelling place of mine, there are always sentient beings from all ten directions who suffer from various ailments; they come to me to seek relief through medical treatment."
With the power of my wisdom, I observe the origins of their conditions and prescribe appropriate remedies according to the nature of each ailment;
I treat them with impartiality, causing all to be healed.

Furthermore, I bathe them with various kinds of fragrant waters and clothe them in fine garments, adorning them with necklaces and ornaments. I bestow upon them all manner of food and drink, as well as wealth, treasures, curiosities, and necessities, providing everything so that they are fully satisfied. Only then do I preach the Dharma to each according to their needs, enabling them to forever sever the afflictions of the mind’s disease.
That is to say:
for those with an abundance of all forms of craving, he teaches the contemplation of impurity;
for those with an abundance of malice, he teaches the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion.
For those with a predominance of delusion, teach them to discern the various characteristics of phenomena;
for those with equal proportions of the afflictions, reveal to them the sublime Dharma-gates of impurity, loving-kindness and compassion, or the concise, intermediate, and extensive teachings.

In this way, according to what is appropriate, one should sever all afflictions; to cause them to resolve upon bodhicitta, one extols the merits of all Buddhas; to cause them to give rise to great compassion, one reveals the immeasurable suffering and distress of saṃsāra;
to cause their merit to increase, one praises the cultivation and accumulation of immeasurable blessings and wisdom;
and to cause them to make great vows, one lauds the taming of all sentient beings.
In order to cause them to cultivate the conduct of Samantabhadra, he spoke of how bodhisattvas dwell in all lands and cultivate the web of practices throughout all eons;
in order to cause them to be endowed with the physical body adorned by the marks and signs of a Buddha, he extolled and praised the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā);
in order to cause them to attain the pure and stainless Dharma-body of a Buddha, he extolled and praised the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā).
To cause them to attain the inconceivable body of a Buddha’s merit, he extols and praises the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*);
to cause them to obtain the Tathāgata’s invincible body, he extols and praises the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*);
to cause them to attain the Buddha’s pure and peerless body, he extols and praises the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).
In order to cause them to attain the Buddha’s ultimate, equal Dharma-body, they extol and praise the Prajñā-pāramitā;
in order to cause them to attain the Buddha’s universally manifesting, differentiated form-body, they extol and praise the Upāya-pāramitā;
in order to cause them to abide for all kalpas for the sake of all sentient beings with minds free from weariness, they extol and praise the Praṇidhāna-pāramitā.
To cause them to universally manifest their bodies and purify all Buddha-fields, they praise and extol the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*);
to cause them to manifest pure bodies that bring joy to all sentient beings according to their inclinations, they praise and extol the perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-pāramitā*);

and to cause them to attain the ultimate, most excellent, pure, wondrous, and undefiled body, they praise and extol the permanent departure from all unwholesome dharmas and the dedication of all wholesome dharmas to the Buddhas.
In this way, he extensively bestowed various kinds of material wealth and the Dharma upon all sentient beings, fulfilling their every wish.
He caused each of them to receive his transformative guidance, and they departed with joy. "Good son!
I am also well-versed in the essential methods for compounding all types of incense, namely:

the peerless King of Incenses; the Piṇḍasāra King of Incenses—this incense is shaped like a drop of water; the Invincible King of Incenses; the Various Awakening King of Incenses; the Alūna-cchadi King of Incenses—this incense is red in color like the hue of the rising sun, its fragrance being produced from flowing tree sap; the Incense King that Manifests According to One’s Desires; the Firm and Subtle Sandalwood King of Incenses appropriate to the Seasons; the Dragon-Victorious Firm Sandalwood King of Incenses; the Brahma-sound Uragavara Incense; the Firm Black Aquatic Aromatic Wood (Aguru) King of Incenses; and the Immovable Faculties King of Incenses.
“I know the origins, functions, potencies, and the relative value—whether noble or base—as well as the methods for preparing all such incenses as these. ‘Good son!

That is to say:
the vow to rescue and protect all sentient beings;
the vow to adorn and purify all Buddha-fields;
"I make this vow to make offerings to all Tathāgatas. 'O noble son!

When I wish to offer these incenses, from each and every incense there emerge immeasurable fragrances that pervade the entire ocean of dharma-realms and the sites of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) of all Tathāgatas throughout the ten directions. These transform into various incense palaces, incense walls, incense towers, incense railings, incense parapets, incense gates, incense windows, incense crescents, incense nets, incense images, incense halos, incense ornaments, incense radiance, incense clouds and rains, incense banners, incense canopies, and incense pennants, adorning the entirety of the dharma-realms in the ten directions and filling them everywhere as an offering.'"
“Good son! I know only this Dharma-gate for causing all sentient beings to universally behold all Buddhas, serve them, and offer them worship with joy.

Just as the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas are like great medicinal kings—whether they are seen, heard, remembered, or recollected; whether one dwells together with them, travels with them, calls their names, or rejoices in their merit—all obtain benefit, and none pass by in vain.”
If there are sentient beings who even briefly encounter this, they will surely cause all afflictions to be extinguished.
They shall enter the Buddha-dharma and depart from the aggregates of suffering.
They will forever bring to rest all fears of birth and death, reaching the state of omniscience that is free from all dread.
Having demolished the great mountain of all aging and death, they dwell securely in the city of the Great Nirvana of Equality.
How could I possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct?
“Good son! To the south of here, there is a great city named Tāladdhvaja;
in that city there is a king named Amṛtāgni.”
“Go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
Then, the youth Sudhana prostrated at the feet of Samantanetra, circumambulated him countless times, gazed up at him with earnest devotion, and departed with a heart full of longing.

At that time, the youth Sudhana, having heard from the spiritual friend Samantacakṣus the teaching on the Bodhisattva dharma-door of enabling all sentient beings to universally behold all Buddhas with joy, followed it with mindfulness in a continuous succession of thoughts. Overjoyed and leaping for gladness, he reflected:

"The spiritual friend, through skillful means, is able to sustain me; through a profound and respectful heart, he is able to protect me, causing me to attain non-retrogression in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

Thus, through single-minded mindfulness, they give rise to a mind of pure faith, a mind of joyful celebration, a mind of serene contentment, a mind of disciplined compliance, a mind of courageous exertion, a mind of tranquility, a mind of vastness, a mind of adornment, a mind free from attachment, a mind free from obstruction, a mind of attainment, a mind of mastery, a mind of constancy, a mind that regards [the Buddha] as a teacher, a mind of skillful discernment, a mind that universally generates all practices, a mind that understands the Dharma upon hearing it, a mind that travels everywhere to Buddha-fields, a mind that beholds the adornments of the Buddhas, a mind that never departs from the Buddhas, a mind that single-mindedly seeks the Ten Powers, and a mind that is resolutely without retreat.

Proceeding by stages, he passed through kingdoms, cities, villages, camps, and settlements, until finally reaching the city of Tāladvaja, where he sought everywhere for an opportunity to see the king.
At that time, he encountered many learned and highly knowledgeable Brahmins conversing about worldly affairs at a crossroads; Sudhana went to them and asked how he might see King Amṛtāgni.
Then, that highly wise great Brahmin asked Sudhana:
"From where have you come?
What do you seek to request from my king that you wish to see him?"

He said, “I have come from the country of Vīraṇamūla. The elder Samantacakṣus taught me the Dharma-gate of Attaining Joy and sent me here to seek an audience with Your Majesty, to inquire about the bodhisattva’s practice of the bodhisattva path.”
The brāhmaṇa said: “That kingdom of Veṇugrāma is peaceful, secure, and prosperous.
Your physical appearance is adorned with virtue and wisdom; by leaving that place to come here, you will surely obtain great benefit.”
"By virtue of your great benevolence and wisdom, you will surely see my king.
Be seated at ease, sir, and listen to what I have to say.
My king constantly resides in the Hall of Precious Adornment and sits upon the Victorious Maṇi Lion Throne, promulgating the True Dharma and bringing sentient beings to fulfillment."
Sudhana spoke again,
"For what reason is the Great King named Amṛtāgni? He replied:

"Our King is fully endowed with the seven limbs and transforms through the Middle Way; he punishes the wicked to eliminate their transgressions, like a blazing fire, and he protects and gathers the virtuous, bestowing upon them happiness, like ambrosia."
Through this compassionate and impartial teaching, he increases their lifespans without ever feeling weary or satisfied.
Therefore, the people of my country praise the King’s magnificent virtue and sing in celebration of his governance, all calling our King "The Fire of Ambrosia."
Our King further employs various skillful means to govern and guide sentient beings, resolving their disputes and litigation;
he comforts the orphaned and the weak, shows compassion for the widowed and the solitary, and brings their noble practices to fulfillment,
causing them all to forever sever the ten unwholesome karmas.
"Practicing the ten wholesome paths of action correctly is like the conduct of a Wheel-Turning King.
Sudhana spoke again,
"What is meant by 'endowing one with the seven factors and transforming through the Middle Way'?"
He replied: "Listen attentively!
I shall explain it for you."
As for the "seven branches":
first, there is the virtue of the sovereign, whom the world looks up to and supports, like the head of a person;
second, there are assisting ministers, loyal and virtuous at their left and right, like the arms of a person.
Third, there is the national territory, vast, wealthy, and all-encompassing, like the belly of a person;
fourth, there are the strategic defenses, which encircle and bind together the myriad regions, like the navel of a person;
fifth, there are the granaries and treasuries, filled with abundant wealth and provisions, so that wherever one goes there is no hardship, like the thighs of a person.
Sixth, possessing military might with a troop and cavalry that are sharp and elite, such that one controls movement according to one’s own will, it is like the lower legs of a person;
seventh, having neighboring territories that pay tribute at the proper times and facilitate the coming and going of royal commands, it is like the feet of a person.
"Furthermore, there are two qualities that can sustain the seven branches:
first, martial prowess;
second, strategic wisdom."
The two virtues support one another, like the eyes and feet of a person;
the seven branches provide a foundation upon which the True Teaching is implemented, so that all who encounter it follow it, and there is nowhere it does not spread.

Like mountains giving rise to clouds, like the earth supporting all things, and like moisture nourishing plants and trees, his virtue was spread upon the common people; thus, throughout the four seas, all followed his sagely transformation.
When wisdom and virtue are mutually deficient, it is like a cart with only one wheel or a bird with only one wing; such a being can certainly neither soar through the sky nor travel far.
Our King possesses a reputation that is universally renowned.
You should further know, O Benevolent One, that our Great King has accomplished nine qualities by which he is able to turn the wheel of sovereignty. What are these nine?
First, by virtue of his excellence he subdues the four neighboring states, causing them to personally perform their official tributes;
second, when tribute and taxes fail to arrive, he moves them with benevolence and trustworthiness;
third, when they are moved yet do not comply, he persuades their rulers and ministers to harbor mutual suspicion and obstruction.
4. Should they change their hearts, or if there be dissent between ruler and ministers, he shall preach to bring about harmony and cause them to return to the Sage’s transformation;
5. If his good exhortations are not heeded, the King’s army shall launch a punitive expedition;
6. He shall observe the leader of those people to determine whether they possess the virtue of a general or not.
Seventh, to examine their lack of virtue and deliberate upon the defense of the city;
eighth, to know the strength of their fortifications and estimate the relative strength of their troops;
ninth, to assess the internal harmony within one's own country and the sharpness of one's own troops.
Our Great King possesses these nine qualities; his eye of wisdom is ever clear, illuminating all things.
Therefore, the eight directions all submit to his righteous transformation, seeking to become his subjects and never turning back;
they are like the myriad streams that flow toward the sea, all becoming of one flavor, without any divergent intent.

Virtuous one, you should know that the Great King of our country has served many Buddhas; he is a great Bodhisattva endowed with great compassion who manifests in the human realm to nurture all classes of beings.
Knowing that sentient beings should be gradually tamed, he first proclaims the royal law to moisten and nourish their bodies, ultimately causing their minds to attain liberation.
Therefore, Your Majesty, you possess two kinds of noble virtue. What are these two?
The first is internal virtue:
First, the genuineness of lineage and the profundity of benevolence and wisdom;
second, external virtues:
as briefly clarified above, these shall be explained in detail later.
Sudhana said: "What are these internal virtues?
I pray that you will explain them to me."
He replied: "O Virtuous One!

The royal lineage of our Great King is noble and preeminent; it has been inherited by legitimate succession through successive generations. From the moment of his conception and throughout his gestation in the womb, he was protected and mindful of by the devas."
From the time he emerged from the womb until his accession to the throne, blessings and auspiciousness arrived in succession, and the ten thousand nations rejoiced.

His sagely virtue advanced daily; he was widely learned and possessed a powerful memory, and was endowed with benevolence, wisdom, filial piety, fraternal affection, reverence, compassion, kindness, and harmony.
Their hearing and sight are keen and clear, and they possess a sense of shame and remorse;
they are endowed with vigor, their bodies free from all ailments;
they harbor impurities with patience and endure insults, their minds free from sudden outbursts of violence.
He honors the worthy and values virtue, feeling compassion for all classes of beings;
regarding his own wealth and status, he always knows contentment;
and toward the perils and hardships of others, he constantly thinks of rescuing and protecting them.
He well-restrains the five sense faculties and does not indulge his passions;
his eloquence is unimpeded, and he can roar the lion’s roar;
his speech is truthful and sincere, free from all attachment and aversion.
He was adept at understanding worldly affairs, diverse languages, and various doctrines;
his deportment was solemn and dignified, such that all people stood in awe and reverence;
he comforted and exhorted his ministers, and nurtured and protected the common people.
He has compassion for sentient beings with an impartial mind free from duality;
he observes people’s words and countenances and fully knows their hearts;
even upon seeing the forms of elephants and horses, he likewise discerns their goodness or evil.
He repays those who have shown him kindness without weariness;
he skillfully protects those who are hostile and malicious;
when traveling through cities and towns, he sits upright within his carriage, examining his own mind with discernment, without looking back or forth toward either side.

Entering and exiting at the proper times, he shall comfort the people of the realm. Should there be those who are disobedient, who rebel against the royal commands, who cruelly harm the king’s subjects, or who act contrary to the Dharma, the king shall first address them with kind words and instruct them according to the Dharma. If they abandon their rebellion and follow what is compliant, the king will surely treat them with compassion and forgiveness; regarding the lands they occupy, he shall neither diminish nor seize them, nor shall he banish them.
"Having heard my command yet failing to reform, you must be subjected to punishment; in subduing the enemy and securing victory, the primary concern must be the peace of the people.
For this reason, the excellent reputation of our King spreads far and wide.
'O Benevolent One!'"
It should be known that for those living in the secular world, the day and night are divided into eight periods;

during the daytime and the evening, there are four distinct periods each, and within each individual period, there are further four divisions. Calculating them all together, there are thirty-two divisions throughout the day and night, which are determined by means of water clocks.
Regarding the four periods of the day:
from after the cock crow until before the hour of the Dragon (辰) is the first period;
from after the initial portion of the hour of the Dragon until the beginning of the hour of the Horse (午) is the second period.
The period from after the midday division until before the hour of Shen (15:00–18:00) constitutes the third watch;
the period from after the initial division of Shen until before sunset constitutes the fourth watch.
Within the first watch, the time before sunrise constitutes the first two divisions.
From after sunrise until the end of the morning constitutes the latter two parts; these four periods together are called the "initial time of the day.

My King is diligent and does not cling to sleep; during the four periods of the night, he remains tranquil for two periods, rises during the third period to settle his mind in right concentration and enjoy the bliss of the Dharma, and during the fourth period, he contemplates all classes of beings externally, without conceiving thoughts of greed or hatred.
From the first period of the day, beginning with the chewing of *dantakāṣṭha* (tooth-sticks) and ending with the performance of sacrificial offerings, there are ten stages in total.

What are these ten? First, chewing the tooth-stick; second, bathing for purification; third, putting on new garments; fourth, anointing with exquisite perfumes; fifth, adorning with pearl garlands; sixth, oiling the feet; seventh, donning leather sandals; eighth, holding a parasol; ninth, arranging the retinue; and tenth, performing the sacrificial offerings.
Sudhana asked, "Why is it, Great King,
that every morning you must first chew tooth-sticks and perform sacrificial offerings before attending to the affairs of state? He replied:
"O Benevolent One!
The flourishing of the world depends upon the king;
if the king wishes to govern others, he must first discipline himself."

Because the body is at ease, the mind and spirit are harmonious; the faculties are clear and the physical frame is tranquil, such that the dissemination of transformative influence is never faltering.
For this reason, our King first chews the *yāshā* twig before proceeding even to the sacrificial offerings.
Furthermore, each of these ten matters can individually produce ten kinds of merit.
Regarding the first—chewing a willow twig (*dantakāṣṭha*)—it possesses ten virtues:

first, it digests food consumed the previous day; second, it removes phlegm and mucus; third, it neutralizes various poisons; fourth, it eliminates dental plaque; fifth, it brings forth a fragrant breath; sixth, it clarifies the eyes; seventh, it moistens and lubricates the throat; eighth, it prevents the lips from becoming chapped and cracked; ninth, it enhances the voice and vitality; and tenth, it ensures that food does not lose its flavor.
In the morning after breakfast, one should always chew on a willow branch.
Using various bitter and pungent substances as tooth-sticks, one should employ them with careful attention; thus does one possess such virtues.
"Furthermore, when my King bathes with fragrant water, it possesses ten merits:

first, it can dispel wind disorders; second, it removes malevolent spirits; third, it fills one with vital essence; fourth, it increases longevity; fifth, it relieves all fatigue and exhaustion; sixth, it makes the body supple and soft; seventh, it thoroughly cleanses impurities; eighth, it nurtures physical strength; ninth, it inspires courage and valor; tenth, it effectively removes feverish distress."
"Furthermore, when our King wears new, clean garments, he possesses ten merits:

first, the increase of auspiciousness; second, ease and pleasure in his gait; third, the love and respect of his retinue; fourth, fearlessness in the midst of assemblies; fifth, peace and happiness of body and mind; sixth, the ability to benefit his lifespan; seventh, purity free from dust and grime; eighth, the far-reaching renown of his fame; ninth, the protective mindfulness of the worthy and holy ones; and tenth, universal praise."
"Furthermore, my King, there are ten merits in applying exquisite fragrant unguents: first, it increases vital energy; second, it makes the body fragrant and pure;

third, it regulates temperature to ensure comfort; fourth, it prolongs one's lifespan; fifth, it causes the complexion to be radiant and flourishing; sixth, it brings joy and pleasure to the mind and spirit; seventh, it clarifies the eyes and ears; eighth, it makes one strong and vigorous; ninth, it inspires love and respect in those who behold one; and tenth, it endows one with great majesty and virtue."
"Furthermore, my King, the wondrous pearl garland upon your crown possesses ten merits: first, supreme merit increases daily; second, rare treasures arrive spontaneously;

third, your countenance is full and joyful; fourth, your eloquence is clear and fluent; fifth, you are endowed with auspiciousness; sixth, your body and mind are free from affliction; seventh, blessings and celebrations constantly gather; eighth, your lifespan is increased; ninth, you possess great courage and valor; tenth, you receive joy when attending upon [the Buddha]."
"Furthermore, my King, there are ten merits in anointing the feet with fragrant oil:

first, it can eliminate wind-related ailments; second, it makes the body and mind light and agile; third, it clarifies the ears and eyes; fourth, it increases vital energy; fifth, it ensures that mindfulness is never lost; sixth, it diminishes drowsiness and sleep; seventh, it makes dreams auspicious; eighth, it prolongs one's lifespan; ninth, it removes all impurities; and tenth, it prevents the arising of various diseases."
"Furthermore, there are ten merits for our King when he wears exquisite leather sandals:

first, his feet become soft and supple; second, his body experiences lightness and ease; third, his gait becomes powerful; fourth, his vital energy is enhanced; fifth, his deportment is serene and dignified; sixth, his lifespan is increased; seventh, his majestic demeanor is orderly and solemn; eighth, those around him rejoice; ninth, his physical appearance is upright and magnificent; tenth, all the devas stand in awe and respect."
"Furthermore, my King, the attendant who holds the parasol possesses ten merits:

first, majestic dignity; second, a radiant complexion; third, protection from the heat while traveling in the open air; fourth, avoidance of wind and dust; fifth, the ability to shield against rain and moisture; sixth, not looking upon those lacking merit; seventh, inspiring awe and respect in all people; eighth, attaining physical tranquility; ninth, prolonging life and increasing vital energy; and tenth, pure and brilliant splendor."
"Furthermore, my King’s majestic retinue possesses ten merits: first, their deportment is dignified and orderly;

second, they inspire awe and respect in others; third, they increase the king’s courage; fourth, they augment the king’s majesty and power; fifth, they subdue wicked men; sixth, celestial deities provide them with protection; seventh, they ward off violent beasts; eighth, they bring comfort and clarity to the king’s mind; ninth, malevolent spirits cannot invade them; and tenth, they carry out the king’s commands."

Thus adorned and surrounded by his retinue, our Great King is like a team of four horses; he inspects what precedes and follows, harmonizing himself with others, balancing leniency and severity according to measure, and ensuring that firmness and gentleness are perfectly suited.
Like a great captain who commands a fleet of ships and promptly patches any leaks as they appear, he attends upon those within the inner palace—

the court ladies, the elderly and the infirm, the guardians of the royal chambers, and those of beautiful countenance and youthful vigor— commanding them to serve as attendants or to lead the way, burning incense, scattering flowers, blowing conchs, beating drums, and singing praises with all manner of adornments.

Some attendants accompany the king on his travels, holding fans and fly-whisks, and providing sandalwood paste, garments, and various exquisite requisites for his seasonal use; nothing is lacking, and such an entourage follows him to anticipate the king’s every wish.
