At the time of entering the "Chapter on the Vow of Samantabhadra’s Conduct" within the realm of inconceivable liberation, the Brahmin again addressed Sudhana, saying:

"My King has perfected the various ritual methods and pure dignified conduct described above; he first enters the maṇḍala to pay homage to the worthies and sages, praying for blessings and protection to nourish all living beings."
Some perform sacrifices to their ancestors, intending to repay their kindness and virtue, teaching people filial piety and reverence to bring spiritual benefit to all quarters.
Others go forth on tours of inspection to soothe the customs and examine the conditions of the regions; upon returning with their armies, they offer thanks for the completion of their tasks.

During times of drought, flood, calamity, or auspiciousness, they reflect upon themselves to receive blessings. At the time of such sacrifices, they focus their minds single-mindedly, reverent and without indolence, as if facing them before their eyes. They contemplate their features and recall their instructions, shedding tears of emotion as they present offerings. Exhausting their resolve without private motives, they honor the ministers of the realm who possess merit and virtue, those of excellent character and conduct—whether lay or ordained—who are of great virtue and advanced age, and whom the people revere. Once these individuals have passed away, their likenesses are depicted in paintings, and stupas and temples are erected according to their respective deeds.

Thus, within each day, our King exhausts his sincere heart internally and externally refines his service by providing food, drink, wealth, treasures, and the most exquisite rarities; he performs sacrifices, honors, and prostrations without ever falling into negligence or idleness.
These ten items, beginning with chewing the tooth-stick and ending with the sacrificial offerings, are completed during the first two parts of the morning.
When the sun first rises, he first summons a skilled physician to inquire after his well-being.
Throughout the divisions of day and night, they take food in appropriate measure.

Next, they summon those skilled in calendrical calculation, prognostication, yin-yang theory, wind and rain, solar and lunar dates, and the movements and degrees of the stars and moon; regarding discrepancies and correctness, concealment and manifestation, calamities and portents, or blessings and celebrations, there is nothing for which they do not offer sincere reports on how to perform rites of averting and removal.
Matters concerning both domestic and foreign affairs may be reported in confidence; during this time, he listens to all reports.

Once these tasks are completed, he sits upright to preside over the court, surrounded before and behind by ten thousand ministers who collectively manage the affairs of state and handle the king’s pronouncements. When the audience concludes, they depart at the end of the first period of the day, leaving the remaining two periods for other duties.
At the second period, she served the king’s meals, performed exquisite music, and provided various forms of entertainment to please the king’s mind.

At the third period, while he bathed and enjoyed his leisure, ten billion court ladies performed music within the palace; their deportment was exceptionally beautiful as they surrounded him on all sides, serving his every wish with gentle hearts and constantly giving rise to thoughts of compassion. The pure gardens were adorned everywhere, such that upon hearing or seeing them, one’s afflictions were eliminated.

When the fourth period had ended, he arranged various jewels in the king’s main hall to adorn the seat for debate. Throughout the kingdom, he sought out those of great wisdom—śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who had attained the fruits of the path—to expound the True Dharma. Having heard its meaning, he joined his palms in reverence, paid homage, and inquired after their well-being. With a heart of complete devotion and a heart of profound respect, he invited them to sit comfortably;
thereafter, he inquired:
"What are the wholesome dharmas?"
What are unwholesome dharmas?
What is correct?
What is deviant?
"What loss is there? What gain?
If it can be practiced, then practice; if it should be ceased, then cease.

Furthermore, one should frequently assemble veteran ministers of wisdom and recluses of lofty virtue to consult upon one's deficiencies, thereby sharpening one's intelligence; one should inquire about the affairs of state and evaluate their merits and faults.
By virtue of this king’s merit, his reign gradually flourished and reached full maturity.
The sentient beings within the realm experienced ever-increasing peace and happiness.
He was able to transform the world so that it became a cause for liberation.
Why is this so? Because all the deeds performed by Bodhisattvas are none other than the work of the Buddha.
It is like the white moon when it first rises and gradually brightens until, on the fifteenth day, its radiance is perfectly full, illuminating the ten directions.
It is also like the ocean tide: as the moon begins to wax, the tides gradually rise until the fifteenth day, when the waves surge greatly, swirling for ten thousand *li*.

The governance and transformation of the Dharma King are likewise so: as the King’s virtue increases, were there no king, wise ministers and elders would be like a ship without a master, circling in eddies and sinking.

Furthermore, it is like sentient beings who, when suffering from thirst and drought, pray to Śakra, Lord of the Devas; if Śakra protects them with his mindfulness, even if no rain falls for ten years, these sentient beings will not necessarily die.
If there were no king, within a single day the myriad people would fall into chaos and ruin, slaughtering one another until none remained.
From this one should know that, in protecting sentient beings, the king surpasses even Śakra.
"Furthermore, our King, having heard the sublime Dharma, constantly reflects upon and admonishes himself in order to transform all living beings.
Whenever he ascends the throne, his power is fierce and majestic; his royal virtue increases, and his majesty subdues his powerful neighbors."

Outside, the court ceremonies were established with various kinds of solemn guards and the playing of exquisite music; all attended the King with reverent gravity. Surrounded by his inner palace retinue, the King took his place upon the lion throne.

His body and mind were free from fear, like the sun emerging from the clouds, its radiance manifest and sovereign; he was like Śakra, Lord of the Devas, amidst the assembly of gods. Four great men, clad in golden armor like the Four Heavenly Kings, stood as attendants at the four corners of the hall, wielding various weapons to display the towering majesty and virtue of our King. The King’s will was one of forbearance and his heart humble toward the myriad people; he did not listen to nor look upon [petty matters], but constantly contemplated acting in accordance with righteousness.
Like the ocean swallowing rivers, like a mountain concealing treasures, the sounds of music fell silent, and his inner and outer minds became one.

At that time, my King surveyed the various dignified postures and exquisite ornaments of the high ministers; knowing them to be like illusions and transformations, he strengthened his resolve and spoke these verses in a voice of compassionate gentleness:
"Union must momentarily disperse; glory and nobility are all impermanent."
Human life is like a flash of lightning; even those with great strength must all return to death.
The demon of death diminishes what is full and flourishing; impermanence destroys the mountain of jewels.
Only the supreme Dharma is eternally firm and secure; one should therefore practice it with heedfulness.

After the King had spoken these verses, he issued a decree to his ministers, commanding them each to return to their respective posts to manage the affairs of state and benefit all sentient beings, never allowing their minds to become weary or negligent.
"O Benevolent One, you should know that this is called the internal virtue of my king.
Sudhana said, "What, then,
is called the external transformation through the king's virtue?"
He replied: "O virtuous one!

The establishment and protection of all sentient beings and the physical world (bhājanaloka) are both due to the karmic retribution of the beings themselves and are sustained by the power and virtue of the various sovereigns."

At the time when the kalpa was first formed, this receptacle world consisted entirely of beings born by transformation; their limbs were complete, they had no need for food or clothing, and their physical forms were full and radiant with light. There was no distinction between day and night. As their latent afflictions increased, the "taste of the earth" (pṛthivī-rasa) appeared accordingly, eventually leading to the gradual emergence of naturally fragrant rice.

Later, he established the system of landowners; far and near alike turned to him for refuge. He provided impartial protection and sustenance, becoming a Kṣatriya. From that time until the present, the royal transformation has continued without interruption.
Among those with desires, there is chaos without a ruler; when a state has a sovereign, all obtain peace. Therefore, it is said that the power of the king can protect sentient beings.
O Benevolent One, you should know that there are four castes among humans:
first, the Brahmin caste, who cultivate oral karma to a great extent;
Second, those of the kṣatriya caste mostly cultivate manual labor;
third, those of the vaiśya caste mostly cultivate agricultural enterprises;
fourth, those of the śūdra caste cultivate the occupation of running and chasing.
As for the other various classes, such as the Caṇḍālas and so forth, most practice the karma of evil vows (duḥśīla).

Nevertheless, these four castes and the other various classes differ in their habitual karma and their dwellings; though their pursuits from youth until old age vary, they all revere the four necessities.

What are the four? First, the cultivation of arts and crafts; second, the accumulation of wealth and resources; third, the shared enjoyment of sensual pleasures; and fourth, the individual pursuit of liberation.
Regarding the arts and crafts, from childhood until adulthood, each person within their respective class studies and practices their specific vocation.
For instance, the Brahmin profession involves cultivating wisdom and studying maps, charts, seals, portents, yin-yang theory, physiognomy, auspiciousness and misfortune, and the Vedic scriptures.

Of the Kṣatriya caste, they further cultivate archery and charioteering; their governance lies in nourishing the people, and their merit resides in prohibiting violence. They delight the multitude with music and song, and they mete out punishment to those who do not submit to the court.
The Vaiśyas engage in agricultural pursuits, sowing and plowing, gathering grain and storing it in granaries; they are the foundation of the realms of humans and devas.
The Śūdras conduct commerce by exchanging goods for what is lacking, engaging in trade and travel to increase their wealth and property.
Regarding those who pursue wealth: once their crafts and skills are perfected, they all devote themselves to their own affairs.
Within their respective factions, they compete to construct the means for their livelihood.

Regarding those who enjoy pleasure: having acquired abundant wealth and profit, they select and settle their residences; they engage in marriage, feasting, and excursions, indulging freely in the delights of sound and color.
Regarding those who speak of liberation, they may be briefly categorized into two groups:
first, those of the Brahmin and Kṣatriya royal castes;

when their hair has turned gray and their years exceed fifty, their strength fails and their appearance declines, they grow weary of the world and seek the Way, their resolve for transcendence being profound. All claim to practice true cultivation, yet as their training differs, their lineages of teachers vary accordingly. Among these ninety-six types, each adheres to its own fundamental doctrine; some seek rebirth in heaven, while others calculate this to be liberation.
Second, there are the disciples of the Tathāgata of the Śākya clan;
third, the practitioners of the Three Vehicles who partake of the flavor of the nectar of immortality, cultivating loving-kindness and compassion to benefit all classes of beings.
Such various heterodox and orthodox schools, whether lay or ordained, who maintain their minds with spiritual discipline, all rely upon the kingdom for their sustenance and preservation.

Furthermore, because our King has propagated and disseminated the teachings, those who study them are like the wheel and cord of a potter, and the arts and practices they cultivate are like gathered clay.

The King’s administration of righteous transformation is like a craftsman molding clay; his skillful benefit to himself and others is like the completion of various vessels. Without the power of the King, meritorious deeds would not be accomplished, and the Dharma would perish without remainder—how then could there be any capacity for salvation and relief?
Furthermore, one-sixth of all the merits cultivated by those subjects shall always belong to the king.

The mountain of the king’s merit is lofty and firm, difficult to destroy; yet as for the rest of the external realm, if righteous governance is not practiced, the people within the country will indulge their passions and accumulate evil, leaving those who cultivate goodness with no means of even momentary peace.
Thus, one-sixth of all sinful karma resulting from obstructing spiritual practice and committing unwholesome deeds falls upon that king.
Although the mountain of the king’s own sins is steep and difficult to destroy, for this reason, our king’s merit and wisdom are preeminent.
At that time, the brahmin spoke again to Sudhana:
"Do you not hear the words of the Earth Deity?
The Earth Deity constantly says:..."

"I could carry the entire earth with all its contents and Mount Sumeru upon my back without considering it heavy, nor would I ever grow weary; yet there are three kinds of people whom I constantly find exhausting and from whom I have no desire to bear the burden."
What are the three?
First, harboring thoughts of rebellion and plotting to harm the king;
second, contemplating the abandonment of kind relatives and being unfilial toward one's parents.

Third, those who deny cause and effect, slander the Triple Gem, disrupt the Sangha that upholds the Dharma Wheel, and obstruct those practicing virtue—these three types of persons I detest most deeply; I would not wish to support them for even a single thought-moment.
"Furthermore, as our King proclaims and spreads the true transformation, all Buddhas protect and mind him; how much more so the dragons and spirits?

By means of this upright mind, he is able to restrain all evils, just like holding a hook or a whip; thus, false teachings do not arise, and those in the world who act to his disadvantage are moved and subdued to practice with right view.
He is also like a bull-king: when the King walks, all the other cattle follow him."
The king is likewise: as his righteous transformation spreads, all sentient beings follow it in harmony.
Furthermore, just as an iron hook can restrain a mad elephant, the king’s righteous governance can subdue wicked people, ultimately leading them all to return to liberation.
"Furthermore, when our king establishes a state and governs the people, he constantly attends to three matters:
first, to be mindful of eliminating the five fears; second, to carefully select the three types of ministers; and third, to diligently refine the royal cuisine."
Why is this so? As the sovereign of the trees nourishes the people, his foremost priority is to eliminate their fears.
Your virtue as a minister is fully perfected, sufficient to assist and harmonize the state.
"The imperial cuisine consists of exquisite delicacies; he loves himself and all things, teaches people loyalty and filial piety, and honors his elders and superiors.
Sudhana asked, "What are the five fears that this country alone does not have?"
He replied: "Virtuous one!
First, the King’s virtue is characterized by frugality, and his revenues and expenditures are equitable."
First, there is no fear of being greedily seized by the king;
second, the royal lineage is chaste and virtuous, regarding non-greed as their treasure;
and there is no fear of being oppressed or suppressed by courtiers.
Third, officials attend to their duties with benevolence and forgiveness in their hearts;
there are no cruel magistrates who inflict injury or terrorize the people.
Fourth, all people are righteous and yielding, and the state is free from deceit and injustice.
There is no fear of thieves or bandits plundering;
fifth, neighboring regions are harmonious and peaceful, submitting to one's influence and converting to its teachings;
there is no fear of external border incursions or calamities.
"In other lands, there are five fears, and people are inevitably unsettled.
Therefore, O King, your sacred transformation extends everywhere. Sudhana said:
“What are the three ministers whom the king carefully selects? He replied,
“O virtuous one!”

Just as the Sun Deity King dwells high in his solar palace, forty-two thousand yojanas above the earth, the people of the four continents cannot perceive his physical form, yet they receive his illumination; gazing up at the solar disc, they all know its location.

The sacred virtue of our King is like that of the solar orb; he governs the realm with great brilliance, illuminating all things without exception. He opens the way for beings and accomplishes all affairs, discerning and dispelling the darkness.

Ten thousand ministers and one hundred million fierce generals are all enlightened and directed by the King’s radiance, serving as the glory of the state. He carefully selects his three high ministers to preside over these hundreds of officials.
What are the three? First are the ministers of counsel; second are the generals and commanders; third are the envoys and ministers of mission. Regarding the ministers of counsel:

they assist and harmonize the King’s transformation of the people, administer the government on his behalf, aid the King’s virtue above and show compassion to the King’s subjects below. They advance the worthy and employ the capable, purifying their hearts as they fulfill their duties, like the sun shining to distinguish all things according to their kind.

As for the two generals, they are the chief ministers of the military; they must be loyal and sincere, possessing profound benevolence and substantial righteousness, with both virtuous conduct and wisdom flourishing, and their courage and strategy unimpaired. For the sake of protecting sentient beings, they eliminate evil by attending to its root, like the sun shining forth, washing away darkness and dispelling gloom.

From the beginning of the seventh month until the tenth, concluding with the drum-signaling precepts, the military shall follow Heaven with solemnity; they must exert themselves to pursue opportunities as they arise, and it is appropriate to establish camps and examine the terrain.
In this way, when a commander-in-chief receives his mandate to face the enemy, he may attack or defend according to the proper timing, ensuring that no battle is unfavorable.
Furthermore, O Benevolent One, you should know that my kingdom has five cities. What are these five?
The first is the Mountain City, which relies upon high ground and occupies precipices, surrounded by sheer cliffs.
Second are water-fortresses, moated by rivers that encircle them on all four sides;
third are sand-fortresses, situated in vast, remote deserts where there is no water or grass outside;
fourth are earth-fortresses, with solid walls and high ramparts, their interiors stocked with military supplies.
Fifth is the city of humans, where the ruler is sagacious and the ministers are virtuous, possessing profound counsel and far-reaching strategy.
When these five types of cities are compared according to their respective merits, the city of humans is the most excellent; it is that which my country honors.
Therefore, Your Majesty dwells in the wondrous transformations of inconceivable supernormal powers.
As for the three types of envoys, they are as follows:

the traveling envoy who receives missions from all quarters, going back and forth with the King’s commands; he is like the envoy of the sun, whose flowing light reaches the plains and marshes, leaving no valley in darkness.

Why is this so? Because the King’s virtue is subtle and profound, and his dwelling is deep and secret; thus, the myriad regions cannot behold him, and the four seas know nothing of him. It is entirely due to the ministers who proclaim the King’s bounty that those from distant lands come to the frontier with sincere devotion, and all within the eight directions respectfully submit. Those who were not yet at peace find peace, and those already at peace do not regress.
Therefore, Your Majesty, together with the elders, ministers, and high officials, has carefully selected those of excellent ability and prudently chosen their duties;
it is said that a royal envoy must possess ten virtues to be deemed fit.

1. Providing resources with loyalty and devotion; 2. Loving and respecting one's sovereign and parents; 3. Possessing a powerful memory and extensive learning; 4. Having a vast and profound capacity for discernment; 5. Possessing eloquence and rhetorical skill that range freely; 6. Being proficient and well-versed in both internal (Buddhist) and external (secular) studies; 7. Being humble, benevolent, and yielding; 8. Being upright and incorruptible; 9. Having a dignified bearing that stands out from the crowd; 10. Comprehending the king’s secret intentions.

Possessing these ten virtues and receiving the mandate to proclaim his majesty, wherever he traveled, he maintained purity of body and solitude; he did not become muddled by wine or lust, nor did he sleep in communal dwellings, lest the secrets of state be leaked during intoxication or slumber.

When serving as an envoy to a neighboring state, one must deliver the King’s words without being swayed by personal gain or altered by intimidation. Whether in action or withdrawal, whether advancing or retreating, all movements must accord with the timing of the moment. Regarding local customs and the suitability of the land, one should adapt to the nature of things to bring about transformation. One must thoroughly understand the King’s strategic maneuvers without hesitation, striving to manifest capable skill so as to comfort those of a different culture.

By means of these three ministers, the King’s virtuous transformation was perfected; evil was transformed and goodness was made manifest, his majesty extending to the ten thousand regions like the flowing light of the sun, which illuminates objects and dispels darkness, so that both near and far were made bright.

Therefore, our country, having received the sagely transformation of the King, possesses many virtuous people whose movements and stillness are appropriate to their station. Wherever they dwell or travel, they do not associate with evil persons.

These include those who deny cause and effect, those who abandon or oppose their sovereign and parents, those who lack compassion by nature, those who delight in seeing the faults of others, those who are vulgar, base, and lowly, those who do not fear sin or transgression, those with excessive desire and anger, those without shame or remorse, those who are stubborn-minded and timid-natured, and those who envy the superior and are jealous of the capable. People such as these are never approached; nor are we ever ridden by those who are headstrong and unruly, nor are we made to manage various wicked elephants and horses.
Nor shall he tame or raise useless birds or beasts;
nor shall he travel through deep mountains, vast marshes, deserted villages, burial grounds, wildernesses, mountain precipices, or the haunts of fierce beasts and non-human beings;
nor shall he gaze directly at taverns, slaughterhouses, or places of lewdness and impurity.
If one encounters an exceptionally auspicious event, one should circumambulate it clockwise to pay homage.
To protect one's merit, one must never step upon the shadows or the walking tracks of the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, one’s parents, teachers, elders, or persons of high station.
Toward those who are worthy of veneration and possess virtuous qualities, one should pay respectful homage with a mind free from contempt.

Upon seeing Buddhist stūpas, sacred shrines, monasteries, the dwellings of sages and saints, or the residences of superior persons, one should exhort both oneself and others to honor, maintain, and repair them so that they may be brought to completion.
Because of this, the devas and nāgas all gave rise to joy; wind and rain fell in their proper seasons, the five grains ripened in abundance, and the myriad subjects lived in peace and happiness.
Those the king employed at his side were loyal and virtuous; the sycophantic, the fawning, and the cruel could not draw near him.
It was like a sandalwood grove surrounded by sandalwood trees, unmixed with *eranda* weeds.
Just as the Anavatapta Lake has fragrant currents of virtuous water free from any salty taste,
so too does the King distance himself from evil people.
He is not like a sweet fruit hidden by a fierce beast.
Sudhana spoke again:
"What kind of person is fit to preside over the royal kitchen? He replied:
“O virtuous one!
A master of the kitchen should possess ten qualities. What are these ten?

1. Purity of lineage; 2. Refinement and flexibility of the three karmas (body, speech, and mind); 3. Full possession of loyalty and filial piety; 4. Faith, yielding, humility, and harmony; 5. Knowledge of the king’s dietary preferences; 6. Skillful mastery of dietary prohibitions; 7. Expertise in tempering flavors; 8. Knowledge of the proper time for the king’s meals; 9. Ability to discern whether food is sweet or poisonous and skill in neutralizing them; 10. Knowledge of the appropriate foods for various times of day, night, month, and season.
"One who possesses these ten virtues may be appointed to oversee the royal kitchen.
One must measure the number of attendants and the location for preparing food, ensuring it is pure, fragrant, and clean, and that the supervisors maintain vigilance without fail. The brāhmaṇa said:

"O Benevolent One, you should further know that I constantly reflect upon all the superior qualities—whether heard of or seen—among the realms of gods and humans; when I observe my noble king, there is not one that he does not fully possess."
What is the meaning of this?
"Virtuous one, you should know that the lion, king of beasts, possesses one supreme virtue: namely, the absence of a dual mind.
For example, when he kills a great elephant, he exerts his full power; [he does not spare it]."
When killing other small beasts, he likewise exerts his full strength.
My King is also like this: he fears neither great matters nor treats small matters with negligence; he exhausts the power of his compassion and wisdom, reaching the ultimate end without omission.
"Virtuous one, you should know that all the kings of aquatic birds possess two virtues:
first, they exercise profound discernment of mind; for instance, when seizing fish, they enter the water and stand poised, gazing with single-minded focus, remaining as immovable as a mountain."
Second, when one contemplates the creatures of the water, they all obtain what they desire.
My King is likewise: dwelling on high, he looks down and hears the governance of the myriad regions;
silent and unmoving, his spiritual resonance is unimpeded; his words do not issue in vain, for everything is spontaneously accomplished.

The brahmin said: "Virtuous one, you should further know that my king possesses three virtues, and his holy transformation flows abroad like the golden wheel-turning monarch’s well-trained horse-king, who has three merits."
What are the three?
First, his mental nature is gentle and supple, and his strength enables him to travel great distances;
second, he does not fear cold or heat, and he remains composed when traversing dangerous terrain.
Third, he is skilled at reconciling enemies and finds it easy to manage affairs, never lacking for anything.
My King is likewise: first, his speech is invariably gentle and truthful; he benefits others through the Dharma, teaching and transforming sentient beings until they achieve ultimate perfection;
second, he is diligent in all government affairs, his mind free from partiality or bias; and he is able to relinquish precious wealth to provide for all.
Third, possessing great wisdom, courage, and vigor, he subdues all enemies; he levies taxes with appropriate moderation and always knows when to stop.
Endowed with these three virtues and fanning them with a gentle breeze, foreign lands stand in awe of his majesty while his own realm cherishes his benevolence.
The brahmin said, "Virtuous one,
you should further know that my king’s four virtues and holy transformation are spreading abroad, just as King Jīvañjīvaka of Magadha possessed four meritorious qualities."

What are the four? First, establishing trust to oversee the daily schedule; second, upholding righteousness to distribute food equitably; third, displaying valor when facing the enemy; and fourth, not following the lead of a hen.

My King is likewise: first, he bestows rewards and metes out punishments at the appropriate time; second, he provides impartial relief to all quarters; third, he subdues the violent and obstructive through righteousness; and fourth, he does not listen to private intrigues.
"Endowed with these four virtues, his transformation of others extends to the boundless. The brāhmaṇa said,

"Your Reverence should further know that my king possesses five virtues through which his holy transformation flows abroad, just as the noble goose-king Śītāntara in the Heaven of Desire possesses five meritorious qualities."

What are these five? First, mating with those who are impassioned; second, calling out without fear; third, seeking food with measured moderation; fourth, having no heedlessness of mind; and fifth, not accepting the sycophantic words of other birds.
My King is likewise:
first, he purifies his mind and curtails desire, never indulging the inner palace;
second, his speech is deliberate and precise, such that none outside disobey his commands.
Third, in giving and receiving, one must not err, striving instead to provide for food and clothing.
Fourth, one regulates the mind through the discipline of the Way, remaining diligent in distancing oneself from transgressions.
Fifth, one achieves a correct mind and does not associate with those who are sycophantic or deceitful.
"Endowed with these five virtues, his bounty extends to the eight quarters of the world. The brahmin said:
"Your Majesty should further know that our King’s sixfold virtuous transformation flows abroad, just as the noble dog-king of Magadha possesses six merits."

What are the six? First, eating whatever is obtained; second, being content with little; third, sleeping peacefully and easily; fourth, waking readily when the grass moves; fifth, maintaining a single-minded equanimity toward both poverty and wealth; and sixth, courageously guarding against thieves.
My King is likewise in three respects: first, tributes from the ten thousand regions are received according to the local produce without fail;
second, during times of scarcity, he offers little yet always harbors a sense of shame and humility;
third, his undertakings are auspicious, and he easily attains peaceful sleep.
Fourth, maintaining right view within one's heart, one becomes aware of every movement of thought;
fifth, honoring virtue and respecting one's kin, one feels compassion for the poor and lowly;
sixth, cherishing all living beings and constantly mindful of protecting them, one possesses majestic courage and sovereignty, free from all bandits and calamities.
Possessing these six virtues, billions upon billions share one heart.
Reflecting thus, I see that every category of being achieves virtue; looking up, I praise our King, whose fame is lofty and far-reaching.
He skillfully gathers in sentient beings and is diligent and tireless.
My King is able to practice these twenty-one kinds of increasingly superior merits;
thus, all enemies will naturally disperse and perish.
No foreign invaders will be able to enter the kingdom.
Furthermore, you should know that even if one lacks these twenty-one virtues and possesses only three, one may still govern and transform the people well.
First, one is able to distribute precious wealth to provide for all;
second, one would rather sacrifice body and life than utter false or deceptive speech;
third, one possesses great courage and valor, capable of subduing enemies.
Even if these three were absent and he possessed only a single virtue, he would still be able to govern and transform others—namely, that he possesses great merit and virtue.
Such a benevolent king is the most supreme.

Just as the eighty-four thousand Dharma gates ultimately converge upon the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), so it is with the king: his various wondrous stratagems ultimately converge upon merit (*puṇya*).
If the king possesses merit, the king’s realm will be prosperous, peaceful, and harmonious, free from turmoil and affairs of state.
The wealth and happiness of sentient beings extend through the myriad regions;
they benefit body and mind in the near term, and lead equally to liberation in the distant future.
This is accomplished through the King’s compassionate merit and benevolent kindness; thus, I shall extensively expound upon the inexhaustible wondrous conduct of our Sovereign.

At that time, the brahmin, having thus extolled King Amṛtāgni’s internal and external virtues to the youth Sudhana and inspired in him joy and reverence, wishing to further proclaim this meaning, praised him in verse:
"When sentient beings in this world Are buffeted by the winds of the three poisons And are on the verge of falling into the evil realms, None but the King can restrain them."
Sentient beings are attached to the five desires, and from this, greed and violence arise;
when a king upholds the True Dharma, he leads them toward the path of eternal truth,
whereas the plundering of wealth and beauty occurs because they lack the support of the royal law.
Just as fish in a river or pond, large and small, devour one another, so too do kings maintain themselves and others through law;
yet neither in the present nor the future is there ever peace or happiness.
When the True Teaching is widely disseminated, it becomes for all the cause of liberation.
People take the king as their life; the king takes the Dharma as his body.
Once the ways of the world are peaceful and harmonious, the Buddha-Dharma begins from this point.
When governance is tyrannical, people long for chaos; when punishments are lax, the law is not enforced.
When grace and majesty are never faltering, the myriad nations are ever at peace and prosperous.
Through many lifetimes serving many Buddhas, one’s merit and virtue surpass those of a king;
with profound compassion and deep benefit, billions of beings share in universal well-being and joy.
Our King was born into a flourishing lineage, his majestic radiance equal to the sun;
forgetting himself to save all living beings, throughout the land there is no poverty or want.
Knowing that the body is fundamentally impure and is beset by impermanence, he remains steadfast.
The Great Being who disciplines his mind, Upholds what is right and nothing else.
Like parched grass in a drought, the people long for relief; His benevolent transformation is like a rain-bearing cloud.
With a compassionate heart he sends down virtuous teachings, Moistening and nourishing all sentient beings.
The ruler follows the hearts of the people, showing love and compassion so they may find rest;
he exercises his majesty to suppress greed and violence, ensuring rewards and punishments accord with what is appropriate.
Yet there may be those with exquisite forms and voices who harbor poison, whom people do not love.
Some possess great wisdom, yet their minds are obscured by defiled desire;
our Lord is supremely dignified and handsome, subduing anger and admonishing all cravings.
His mind is like a pure, bright mirror, reflecting all things without ever partiality.
A bright mirror reflects only physical forms and does not discern the thoughts of the mind;
yet the King’s mind-mirror is pure, penetratingly seeing the very source of the mind.
His attendants are free from flattery and depravity; his ears and eyes perceive only the good and virtuous.
Flattery and cruelty were things he could never tolerate;
yet there were those who harbored malicious intent, wishing to harm the king’s subjects.
With his mind perceiving their hidden designs before they were manifest, he caused them all to return to loyalty and rectitude.
Fragrant forests harbor fierce beasts; The salt sea poisons clear streams.
Corrupt governance harms the virtuous; The wicked ruin the sovereign’s virtue.
The fragrant river flows with water of virtue; Sweet fruits flourish in the sweet forest.
The eight directions share in universal joy; Ministers are virtuous because the sovereign is sagacious.
May the King maintain the precepts that prevent calamity, And rescue the masses by purifying their source.
Bringing wealth, longevity, and benefit to all living beings, He shall pull them out from the ocean of greed and hatred.
Since compassion is so deep and vast, the True Dharma is likewise proclaimed far and wide;
the aged, the young, and the orphaned or destitute are protected and nurtured to dwell in peace and happiness.
The worthy and virtuous are honored, and the elderly are revered for their kinship.
Her kinsmen and the palace ladies, both within and without, were all harmonious and serene.
With gentle speech she regulated the myriad people; with a peaceful countenance she served her teachers and elders.
In her ancestral rites and acts of reverence, she never displayed a weary expression; thus may her blessings flow for ten million generations.
Ancient rulers who lacked the Way were arrogant and extravagant, showing contempt for their own kin;
they pursued their own interests without concern for others, and their ill repute spread far and wide.
Our King, however, understands that all phenomena are like illusions; he benefits all beings while forgetting his own self.
There is a Way that protects all sentient beings, Possessing auspicious renown.
Greed, anger, stinginess, and envy— These are all causes of suffering;
The deluded and ignorant do not always know this, Yet their retributions follow like shadows and echoes.
The King takes the people as his foundation; though they number in the billions, they are as one body.
He employs them like his own limbs, ensuring their toil and rest are never beyond measure.
Our King reflects upon the footsteps of those who came before, establishing a model that serves as a guiding standard for all.
His actions accord with the hearts of the people; he abandons evil and follows what is good.
He loves others as he loves himself, leading himself to follow the way of others.
Once the nine clans have followed his influence, the hundred officials will observe the King’s governance.
The eight directions submit to the Sage’s transformation; with hands folded in dignity, he acts through non-action (*wuwei*).
He attributes merit to the cultivation of the mind; when the mind is still, there is truly nothing to do.
Loyal ministers assist my sovereign, moving in harmony like limbs and arms.
The myriad nations attained clarity and wisdom; throughout the four seas, his sovereign virtue was extolled.
Truly inheriting the teachings of all Buddhas, he awakened sentient beings through the Dharma, causing them to realize their own minds, like lotus flowers blooming under the sun’s rays.
The people protect their lord, just as the king protects his people;
as the forest guards the king of beasts, so do the beasts guard the forest.
In other lands there are many fivefold fears: the greed of kings and the favoritism of courtiers.
Cruel magistrates entrap the innocent, and thieves openly commit theft and robbery;
when these four calamities exist within one's own borders, external invaders will surely come to invade.
When our King maintains purity both within and without, the people of the land shall have no five fears.
In this world there are four types of accomplishments: first, wisdom; second, precious wealth;
third, the enjoyment of the five sensory pleasures; and fourth, the pursuit of liberation.
Most kings lack many of these; when they pass away, no one praises them.
Just as the bellows are held by the wind, when the wind ceases, life is cut short.
Our King is endowed with these four dharmas; his wisdom and virtue polish his person.
Possessing abundant and wondrous treasures, he provides relief to the poor and destitute.
The five desires have no equal, yet he remains unstained like a lotus;
it is only to lead sentient beings that he subsequently causes them to enter the Buddha-wisdom.
Abiding in the liberation of illusion, he manifests as dwelling amidst greed and hatred.
Transforming and subduing evil people, you cause them all to turn toward the Buddha-way.
Before long, you shall see various gates of skillful means;
ultimately benefiting sentient beings, for this reason your fame resounds afar.
Subtle wisdom is regarded as the wind; its life-force is eternally inexhaustible.
You should quickly go to behold it, and do not give rise to a mind of indolence or pride.
To see once a person of supreme wisdom is better than dwelling for hundreds of thousands of years.
Some may live for a thousand years, yet constantly eat what others have discarded;
they know nothing of the three periods of time and possess little of the wealth of Dharma.
Satiated only in their bellies, they nourish their desires; though possessing human form, they are no different from beasts.
Those who have studied little may be haughty at heart; they are easily satisfied like water in a cow’s footprint, or like a mouse holding a morsel in its paws, claiming their own ability to be great.
When the ocean of wisdom is vast and immeasurable, those unable to fathom it instead increase their slander.
When oxen drink water, it becomes milk; when snakes drink water, it becomes poison.
When the wise study, they achieve Bodhi; when the foolish study, it results in birth and death.
Not understanding this is due to the fault of insufficient learning.
Therefore, the people of my country are learned and never weary;
my king has many supportive ministers, and the capital city is likewise secure.
Abounding in wealth and rich in men and horses, neighboring states are all friendly and harmonious.
Thus endowed with these seven branches, the courageous and wise one constantly abides therein.
Among humans and in the heavens, through various supreme merits,
he benefits all sentient beings, as has been proclaimed above.
When the wise hear a single principle, they touch upon its manifold applications boundlessly;
as kings of the Dharma through essential words, they discipline themselves and bring peace to all people.
Worldly glory never recedes from them, and the supramundane subtlety is beyond thought.
"Just as the ocean receives the flow of rivers, its capacity becomes ever more deep and vast.
At that time, having praised the king with these verses, the brahmin addressed Sudhana, saying:

"Virtuous one, you should know that while the body hairs and pores of all sentient beings number three koṭis each, our Great King now possesses three koṭis of internal meritorious practices and likewise three koṭis of external meritorious practices."
By means of this virtuous transformation, you have compassionately nurtured all living beings.

Although I have just now spoken of but a single hair’s worth of the Great King’s merit for the sake of benevolence, the remainder of the King’s virtues are so profound and vast that they are difficult to describe; my wisdom is shallow and limited—how could I possibly conceive of or express them?

Moreover, as I am occupied with official duties, I have no leisure for prolonged discourse. Your Majesty is currently bestowing his transformative influence from the main hall; you should go there and behold him with single-minded devotion.
At that time, having heard these words spoken by the brahmin, Sudhana paid homage at his feet with deep reverence and took his leave to proceed to the royal palace.
From afar he beheld the king seated upon a lion throne of great lotus-womb made of the wondrous jewels of Nārāyaṇa-vajra, situated within the central hall of the palace.
It has a dais made of incalculable multitudes of maṇi jewels;
it has feet made of incalculable sun-light radiance jewels;
and it is adorned with incalculable exquisite jewel images.
A net made of golden cords covered it from above;
incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) clusters of maṇi jewels radiated brilliant light;
and incalculable celestial garments of exquisite jewels were spread upon it.
Various celestial fragrances were used to permeate the air everywhere, and diverse precious flowers were strewn across the ground;

countless jeweled banners were arranged in rows on all four sides, and innumerable jeweled pennants hung down all around. Canopies made of *maṇi* jewels—radiant with various colors like the plumage of peacocks—were spread above to cover it.
At that time, the Great King was in the prime of his youth and possessed a magnificent countenance; he was dignified and awe-inspiring.
He was endowed with all the marks and signs of excellence, adorned with exquisite beauty.
A wish-fulfilling maṇi served as his jeweled crown, adorning his head.
He used Jāmbūnada gold to form crescent moons that adorned his forehead;
he used the stainless king of jewels, the Indra-nīla mani, to form ear-rings that adorned his ears;
and he used priceless wish-fulfilling mani-kings to form necklaces that adorned his neck.
His arms were adorned with armlets made of the king of wish-fulfilling jewels, the wondrous *maṇi* that radiates stainless light;
he possessed a parasol made of Jāmbūnada gold,
and its spokes were fashioned from various interspersed precious gems.
Its navel is made of *maṇi* jewels of radiant flavor, adorned and interlaced with hundreds of thousands of jeweled nets;
its bells are made of pure-treasury jewels, constantly emitting wondrous sounds that proclaim the inexhaustible Dharma;
and *maṇi* jewels of nocturnal radiance emit great light, pervading the ten directions to provide illumination.
It was perfectly complete, with a shaft made of lapis lazuli, which a man constantly held to cover its top.

King Amṛtāgni, whose royal virtue was preeminent, possessed great power and authority; he subdued distant regions, and there were none among the kings of neighboring states who did not revere and serve him.

A stainless silken cloth was tied upon his crown, and ten thousand ministers surrounded him before and behind, while a hundred thousand fierce soldiers stood in ranks to his left and right. Their appearance was terrifying, like the messengers of Yama; with arms bared and eyes glaring, their teeth gnashing and brows knitted, they brandished weapons, so that all who saw them were struck with awe and fear.
Among the people within the realm, there are those who violate the king’s law;

whether they have taken another’s life, stolen another’s property, violated another’s wife, engaged in false and divisive speech, harsh and meaningless speech, or harbored greed, hatred, and wrong views—having committed such various evil deeds, their bodies are bound with the five fetters and led before the king to be punished according to their crimes.
Some are burned with fire;
some are boiled in hot water;
some are cast into glowing embers.
Some were doused with boiling oil and subjected to various forms of burning and cauterization until their flesh was reduced to a pulp;
some were driven up high mountains and pushed over to fall;
and some had their heads severed.
Some had their waists severed;
some had their ears and noses cut off;
some had their hands and feet amputated.
Some have both eyes gouged out;
some have their skin flayed;
others have their bodies dismembered with limbs and joints severed, such that their bones are piled into mountains and their flowing blood forms lakes.
Furthermore, he saw human heads, hands, feet, and skeletons filling the blood everywhere.

There were also countless pigs, dogs, jackals, crows, and vultures, all vying to rush into the pool to drink the blood and devour the flesh, letting out a great, hideous clamor that terrified those who heard it.

Within the pool were corpses of various forms and colors; some were livid blue-black, while others had pus flowing from them. Foul odors and filth lay scattered everywhere, as they swelled and rotted away, with their intestines, stomachs, and internal organs all exposed.
Nails, hair, sinews, and veins were scattered throughout the pool.

Some suffered from the torments of minor offenses, undergoing various forms of punishment and mutilation such as flogging, lashing, amputation, and dismemberment; they groaned and wailed, uttering cries of great terror.
Some call out for their parents;
others call out for their kinsmen, their voices thundering like a clap of lightning, piercing the hearts of men with bitter anguish.
Such immeasurable torments as these exist there, comparable to those in the Saṃghāta Great Hell.
Having seen this, Sudhana thought to himself:

"For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, I have resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, cultivating the path of a bodhisattva and seeking the practices of a bodhisattva. I have questioned spiritual friends regarding how to cultivate the roots of virtue for enlightenment and how to distance oneself from all unwholesome roots.

Yet now I see this king abandoning the dharma of the roots of virtue and committing great evil deeds, oppressing and harming sentient beings even unto taking their lives; he feels no fear for the future suffering of the evil realms that is now manifest before him, as he stands on the verge of falling into ruin."

How can one, while seeking to inquire into this, practice the bodhisattva conduct and train in the bodhisattva path so as to give rise to a fully developed, vast, and great compassion that protects and saves all sentient beings?
With such a mind, he contemplated in various ways.
While he was reflecting thus, a deity in the sky addressed him, saying:
"O son of good family!

Do you not remember the instructions of the spiritual friend, the Elder Universal Eye, as well as the various subtle and wondrous dharmas of this king’s manifold merits that were praised by all the brahmins whom you recently encountered?
Sudhana looked up and said to them,
"I remember it deeply and have never forgotten it.
The devas spoke again:
“Good son! If you constantly maintain mindfulness, do not give rise to doubt. Good son!”
Do not feel weary of or abandon the words of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
A spiritual friend constantly guides you with the True Dharma; how could they ever cause you to fall into a perilous and evil place?
Good son! The bodhisattva’s skillful practice of the wisdom of expedient means is inconceivable;
the wisdom that gathers and sustains sentient beings is inconceivable.
The wisdom that protects and mindful of sentient beings is inconceivable;
the wisdom that brings benefit and happiness to sentient beings is inconceivable;
the wisdom that disciplines and punishes sentient beings is inconceivable.
The wisdom that purifies sentient beings is inconceivable;
the wisdom that brings sentient beings to maturity is inconceivable;
the wisdom that penetrates deeply into sentient beings is inconceivable.
The wisdom that liberates sentient beings is inconceivable;
the wisdom that knows the timing for sentient beings is inconceivable;
the wisdom that knows the faculties of sentient beings is inconceivable.
The wisdom that compassionately regards and tames all sentient beings is inconceivable.
Son of good family!
Go to the king’s presence and, with a profound mind, inquire about learning the bodhisattva conduct and practicing the bodhisattva path.
At that time, having heard the words of the goddess, Sudhana went before the king, prostrated at his feet, and circumambulated him countless times.
With palms joined, he said: "Noble One!
I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
"I have heard that the Holy One is skilled at providing instruction; I pray that you will speak for me.
At that time, King Amṛtāgni, having finished attending to his royal affairs, took Sudhana by the hand, led him into the inner palace, seated him beside him, and addressed him, saying:
"O son of good family!
"You should observe the palace where I dwell and all its furnishings.
As he was told, Sudhana immediately surveyed them everywhere.
He saw that the palace was incomparably vast and expansive, composed entirely of various mani jewels.
A pavilion was formed from hundreds of thousands of various jewels;
pillars were made of vermilion-colored precious gems,
inlaid and set with an array of diverse colored jewels.
Inconceivable maṇi jewels radiated light that shone everywhere;
various kinds of maṇi jewels adorned every place;
and with exquisite musāragalva jewels, they formed carpets to adorn the ground.
The lion throne was adorned with hundreds of thousands of various kinds of precious gems;
a canopy made of Vairocana-maṇi-rāja jewels covered the seat,
while nets of various colors made of cintāmaṇi-rāja jewels hung down all around it.
Subtle jewel banners, radiant with the light and flavor of lion kings, were erected all around.
Furthermore, there were various wonderful jeweled ponds, their waters pure and endowed with the eight meritorious qualities.
Its banks were paved with agate, the king of jewels;
it was adorned with railings made of various colored gems;
and everywhere, rows of jewel-trees stood in solemn array.
Each was surrounded on all sides by jeweled walls.
There were ten billion attendant maidens, possessing exquisite complexions and dignified beauty that brought joy to those who beheld them;
their deportment was graceful and their mien was worthy of admiration.
In all her actions, there was nothing that was not skillful; she served others with a gentle mind and always gave rise to a heart of compassion.
Upon seeing this, Sudhana conceived a sense of wonder.
The King then addressed him, saying: "Good son,
what do you think?"

These various desirable fruits that you see—such as these physical forms, such retinues, such prosperity and joy, such abundance, and such sovereignty—how could they possibly be produced by evil karma?
He replied, “No,
[World-Honored One]. “Good son!”
I have attained the bodhisattva liberation of being like an illusion. Good son!
All the sentient beings currently in my land mostly practice evil deeds, like outcastes (caṇḍāla).
Regarding these evil sentient beings who do not accept wholesome instruction, I employ various other immeasurable and manifold skillful means;
yet I am unable to cause them to abandon their evil karma and turn toward the path of goodness.

"Good son! In order to subdue those sentient beings and bring them to maturity, I am preceded by great compassion and manifest as an evil person. Before these evil people, I demonstrate the commission of various evils and manifest as one who is patient yet harmful, oppressing, harassing, punishing, and subjecting them to various forms of suffering. When the sentient beings within my realm who commit evil see this, their hearts are filled with trepidation and their minds are struck with terror."

Regarding all sensual pleasures, when the mind gives rise to weary detachment and the mind gives rise to trepidation, one is then able to forever sever all evil karma, resolve upon bodhicitta, and attain non-retrogression.

“Good son! By this you should know that those evil-doing sentient beings whom you just saw undergoing various sufferings, as well as those who were able to subdue those violent and wicked beings, were all transformations.”

"Good son! By means of such various skillful expedients, I cause all sentient beings to sever the ten unwholesome karmas they have committed, and to fully cultivate and abide in the ten paths of wholesome action."
Ultimate benefit and happiness, ultimate peace and security, and ultimate perfection; having forever severed all suffering, they abide in the ground of the Tathāgata’s omniscience. Good son!
In my body, speech, and mind, I have never, even in thought, brought harm or affliction to a single sentient being. Good son!

According to my intention, I would rather endure the sufferings of the Avīci hell for all of future time than ever give rise to a single thought of anger, or harbor a notion of harming even a minute creature such as a mosquito or an ant; how much less would I commit such evil karma?
"Good son! I recall that even in my dreams I have never for a single thought-moment given rise to negligence, much less having killed a human being while awake."
Why is this so? Because a person is a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), capable of producing all manner of wholesome fruits.
It is like the sixteen great nations here, and even all beings dwelling upon the earth, who depend upon the great earth for their establishment, growth, and sustenance.
All such fruits of the path of the worthy and the noble are cultivated and realized by relying upon persons. "Good son!

I have attained only this liberation of illusory transformation; yet the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), knowing that all realms of existence are entirely like illusions, that all bodhisattva practices are entirely like transformations, that all worlds are entirely like shadows, and that all phenomena are entirely like dreams."

They enter the dharma-gate of non-attachment to the true mark, practicing all sublime deeds in accordance with the dharma-realm, like the net of Indra. With non-attached wisdom, they move within their spheres of experience without obstruction, entering universally and equally into the dharma-gate of samādhi. Having attained mastery in the *svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī*, they abide in the realm of the Buddhas, following it like a shadow follows a form.
How could I possibly know or describe the merit of the wisdom and conduct of those bodhisattvas? Good son,
to the south of here there is a city named *Prabhāsa* and a king named *Mahāprabha*.
"Go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
Then, the youth Sudhana prostrated at the king's feet, circumambulated him countless times, gazed up at him with deep reverence, and took his leave to depart.

The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Thirteen.
