Whether there is renunciation or lack of renunciation, right determination, wrong determination, or no fixed determination; whether there are roots of goodness coexisting with afflictions, or roots of goodness not coexisting with afflictions; whether one possesses complete roots of goodness or incomplete roots of goodness;

whether there are roots of goodness subsumed by unwholesome roots, or unwholesome roots subsumed by roots of goodness—I thoroughly know all such accumulated wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, without any doubt.
Furthermore, regarding all the Buddhas who appeared in the world during those eons, with their various names and in their continuous succession, I know them all.

Moreover, for each and every one of those Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, I know without obstruction all the oceans of great vows they made from their first aspiration seeking omniscience; all the oceans of spiritual friends they served; all the oceans of offerings they made to all Buddhas; all the oceans of bodhisattva practices they performed; all the oceans of adornments of Buddha-lands; all the oceans of perfections of Buddha-qualities; all the oceans of appearances as they attained perfect enlightenment; all the oceans of manifestations of great supernormal powers; all the oceans of skillful means in turning the wheel of Dharma; and all the oceans of taming and transforming all sentient beings. I know them all without any hindrance.

I also know the distinctions among the assemblies of those Buddhas; within those assemblies, there are sentient beings who attain liberation by relying on the Śrāvaka vehicle. I fully understand all the roots of goodness practiced by those Śrāvakas in the past, as well as all the Śrāvaka vehicles they have upheld and the various kinds of wisdom they have attained.

Within this assembly, there are sentient beings who attain liberation by relying on the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; all the roots of goodness cultivated by those Pratyekabuddhas, all the fruits of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle they have realized, the supreme liberation in which they abide, the samādhis they enter, the supernormal powers they manifest, the sentient beings they transform, and even their entry into parinirvāṇa—I know them all.

I also know that the assemblies of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are perfectly complete, all-pervading, and without limit; that those Bodhisattvas, from the time they first resolved their minds and planted roots of goodness, gave rise to immeasurable varieties of great vows and practiced various difficult ascetic deeds; that they fully accomplished the various *pāramitās* and adorned the path of a Bodhisattva with manifold ornaments; and that by means of their power of mastery, they entered the various stages of a Bodhisattva.
That is to say:
the various factors conducive to enlightenment of the bodhisattva stages; the various modes of sovereign conduct of the bodhisattva stages;
the various entries into and exits from samādhis of the bodhisattva stages; the various sovereign supernormal powers of the bodhisattva stages; and the bodhisattva stages themselves.
The various manifestations of mastery, the various establishments of the bodhisattva stages,
the various observations of the bodhisattva stages, the various purifications of the bodhisattva stages, the various bases of the bodhisattva stages,
the various characteristics of the bodhisattva stages, the various essences of the bodhisattva stages, and the various wisdoms of the bodhisattva stages.
The bodhisattva’s gathering of wisdom, the bodhisattva’s accomplishment of wisdom, the bodhisattva’s dwelling place, the bodhisattva’s vast sphere of conduct,
the bodhisattva’s great supernormal powers, the bodhisattva’s ocean of samādhis, the bodhisattva’s ocean of skillful means for liberation,
the ocean of distinctions among the samādhis entered by the bodhisattva, and all the wisdom of the teachings thus attained.
The light of illumination; the clouds of lightning-flash wisdom of all-knowledge that have been attained;
all the patiences (kṣānti) that have been acquired; all the courageous wisdoms; the realization of the ocean of all dharmas;
the entry into the ocean of all Buddha-fields; the deliverance of the ocean of all sentient beings; and all the skillful means displayed.
"O Sea! All the oceans of supernormal powers that have been initiated, and all the oceans of profound and vast great vows—I know them all. 'O Noble Son!'"

From the beginningless past until the present, throughout unspeakably unspeakable numbers of kalpas as numerous as the atoms in an inconceivable number of Buddha-fields, I fully know all the various and distinct oceans of kalpas, as well as all sentient beings, Buddhas, and their assemblies; and throughout all the oceans of kalpas extending to the end of the future, in their continuous succession and uninterrupted progression, I know them all.
"Good son! Just as you know this Sahā world, so too do you know the succession of all worlds, numbering as many as the atoms within all worlds, arising within the Sahā world;
and you also know the succession of all worlds within the Sahā world."
They also know the sequential order of all worlds within every single atom of the Sahā world;
they also know the continuous succession of the ten directions outside the Sahā world;
and they know the sequential order of the establishment and abiding of the worlds therein.

He also knows the sequential order of all worlds contained within the world-system called "Blazing Jewel Light Universally Illuminating the Ten Directions," which serves as the basis for the Sahā world;

he also knows the sequential order of the worlds contained within the infinite world-systems of the ten directions as gathered within this Flower Bank Adorned World-Ocean of Vairocana, the World-Honored One;
and he also knows the sequential order of all worlds existing within every single atom of all worlds in the Flower Bank World-Ocean.

Furthermore, I also know all those worlds—their various establishments, their various shapes, their various dimensions, their various foundations, their various boundaries, their various adornments, their various accomplishments, and their various destructions; I fully comprehend all their retinues, all their rims, all their rotations, all their lotuses, all their Mount Sumerus, all their rivers and oceans, all their grasses and trees, and all their various names.

He also knows that, in the past, this Flower Treasury World-Ocean was entirely produced through the power of the original vows of Vairocana Tathāgata, giving rise to such various worlds and all their various oceans of causes and conditions.

He also knows all worlds within the oceans of worlds throughout the infinite reaches of the ten directions, across the entirety of the Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, beyond the outer seas of the Flower Treasury World System.

He also knows the ocean of immeasurable eons through which the World-Honored One Vairocana has passed; the ocean of all his past fundamental deeds; the ocean of the vast vows he made in the past; the ocean of the teachings of all vehicles he gathered in the past; the ocean of bodhisattva practices he cultivated in the past; the ocean of Buddha-lands he purified in the past; the ocean of all Buddhas he served in the past; the ocean of all sentient beings he transformed in the past; the ocean of all spiritual powers he manifested in the past; the ocean of all skillful means he entered in the past; the ocean of all Buddha-dharmas he received in the past; the ocean of all samādhis he entered in the past; the ocean of all masteries he attained in the past; and the ocean of all merits he accomplished in the past.

The perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) consisting of all requisites bestowed in the past; the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) consisting of various pure conducts maintained in the past;
the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*) regarding various objects experienced in the past;
the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*) consisting of fierce, courageous, and heroic exertion cultivated in the past; and the various samādhis entered in the past.
The *dhyāna-pāramitā*; the various pure *prajñā-pāramitās* accomplished in the past;
the *upāya-pāramitās* manifested in the past as bodies of pervasive entry into all worldly reflections;
the *praṇidhāna-pāramitās* of the ocean of Samantabhadra’s conduct, pure and perfect, generated in the past; and all that was attained in the past by the Tathāgatas...

The perfection of power of the ocean of various sovereign spiritual powers; the perfection of wisdom of the ocean of sovereign wisdom that illuminates the world with the light of the knowledge of all Tathāgatas realized in the past;

universally encompassing the bodhi of all Buddhas, universally attaining the great wisdom-light of all Buddhas, realizing the nature of the all-knowledge of all Buddhas, attaining equal and perfect enlightenment in all places, and turning the wheel of Dharma through the play of spiritual powers.

In all the assemblies at every site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), within those assemblies, there were all the bodhisattvas who had planted all manner of roots of goodness in the past; from their first resolve, they had practiced the bodhisattva path, accumulated skillful means to mature sentient beings, and served the Buddhas and spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

In every thought-moment, they increased their attainment of various samādhis; in every thought-moment, they entered the gates of dhāraṇī; in every thought-moment, they attained an ocean of eloquence; in every thought-moment, they gave rise to sovereign supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); in every thought-moment, they cultivated the web of bodhisattva practices; in every thought-moment, they gathered the gates of various skillful means; in every thought-moment, they knew the web of the faculties of sentient beings; in every thought-moment, they accumulated the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*); and in every thought-moment, they realized and entered the ocean of doors of meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), attainments (*samāpatti*), and supernormal powers.

All of these are the oceans of practice cultivated by the Tathāgata Vairocana throughout the oceans of immeasurable eons within all dharma-realms throughout the ten directions; I fully understand them all.

I also fully know all that has been cultivated by all Tathāgatas throughout the ocean of eons, pervading the ten directions, the entire Dharma-realm, and the limits of space, as well as the realm of illusory wisdom sustained by their spiritual powers until the end of the future; all such things I completely understand.

Why is this? When I enter this liberation door of the ocean-like realm of the samādhis of all bodhisattvas, within a single thought-moment, I am able to fully comprehend the various mental activities of all sentient beings— their defilements, their purity, their transmigration, and their cessation—
as well as the various samādhis of all śrāvakas.
Because they have fully realized the peaceful liberation, samādhis, and supernormal powers of all pratyekabuddhas;

and because they have thoroughly understood the various samādhis, various stages, various dharma-gates, and various modes of entry of all bodhisattvas, as well as the ocean of the supernormal powers of the light of liberation of all Tathāgatas.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Volume Twenty-seven and Volume Twenty-eight,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā of Kaśmīra by Imperial Decree.
In the "Chapter on the Vows and Practices of Samantabhadra for Entering the Realm of Inconceivable Liberation," at that time, Sudhana said to Gopā: "Noble One!"
"How long has it been since you attained this liberation? Gopa replied, "Noble son!"
In a past age, beyond as many eons as there are atoms in a hundred Buddha-fields, there was an eon named Supreme Conduct and a world named Victorious Fearlessness.
Within that world was a continent of four quarters named Jambudvīpa, Constantly Endowed with All Pleasures;
therein was a royal capital named Great Tree Wondrous High Auspiciousness, which was the foremost among eighty-four thousand billion royal capitals.
At that time, this royal capital had eighty-four thousand *koṭis* of cities as its retinue; each of these cities was magnificently adorned and entirely pure.

Their ground was made of lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*), surrounded on all sides by sevenfold walls of precious materials. Each wall was covered above by a net of various-colored, radiant jewel-reflecting gems.

Each of these precious walls was further encircled by moats filled with fragrant water and sand of golden dust spread upon the bottom; blue lotuses (*utpala*), red lotuses (*padma*), yellow lotuses (*kumuda*), and white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*) were spread thickly across the surface of the water.
Each of these rivers is adorned with natural railings made of various jewels and networks of precious gems along their banks;
between each river, there are jeweled *tāla* trees arranged in seven concentric rows.
Furthermore, there are naturally occurring trees of jewel-adornments, from which hang necklaces, garments, garlands, and sashes, while nets of pure gold cover them above.

On all the roads leading to and from those cities and towns, for a width of eight paces on both sides, the ground was adorned with various exquisite and diverse jewels interspersed together, emitting brilliance and radiating light that illuminated everything.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable vidyādhara-mantra-siddhas who, having purified their bodies like the god Īśvara, walked to and fro, protecting all sentient beings.

Moreover, within each of those cities and towns, there were immeasurable parks and pleasure gardens where flowers, fruits, and groves of trees were fully provided; various kinds of birds sang with harmonious and elegant notes as they gathered there, sporting in joy without fear.
There always dwell immeasurable, pure, subtle, and lovely men and women within it, whose bodies emit a wondrous fragrance that perfumes all things;
throughout day and night, the devas constantly rain down exquisite flowers of hundreds of thousands of varieties, falling in profusion and confusion.
In each of those cities and towns, there were hundreds of thousands of earth-deities who provided protection.

Within and without those cities and towns, all the groves of jewel-trees, necklaces, garlands, sashes, and networks of precious bells—these various ornaments—were stirred by a gentle breeze, producing the sounds of manifold sublime Dharmas.

Upon hearing them, all were filled with joy; their afflictions were eliminated, their bodies and minds became cool and refreshed, and they were suffused with the bliss of the Dharma. Thus, they attained non-retrogression from Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and became fully endowed with the merits of the wondrous practices constantly praised by Samantabhadra.

"At that time, there was a king named Dhanapati, who constantly transformed the entire realm through the True Dharma. He had eighty-four thousand queens, concubines, and handmaidens, and five hundred ministers and high officials.
He had five hundred princes, all endowed with physical strength and vitality, possessing dignified and handsome features, brave and fearless, capable of subduing enemies."
The king had a queen named Padmaśrīgarbha, whose majesty was preeminent and whose countenance was unsurpassed;

she gave birth to a crown prince named Tejodhipati, who was exceptionally handsome and wonderful, a sight that all people delighted to behold, and was fully endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
That is to say:
the soles of his feet are level and full, like the bottom of a cosmetic box;
they are endowed with the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel, complete and perfect.
His hands and feet are soft and supple like *tūla* cotton;
his fingers are slender and long, and his webbed membranes are perfectly formed;
his heels are even and rounded, and his insteps are full and elevated.
Each part is in perfect proportion, radiant, pure, and exquisite;
his calves are smooth and rounded like those of the king of celestial deer;
his arms hang down past his knees, resembling the trunks of elephants.
The horse-king’s private parts are concealed within a sheath, their peak and form being hidden and secret;
each and every pore grows a single hair;
his deep blue hair curls to the right, its spiral patterns never disordered.
The skin of his body is golden in color, fine, thin, and smooth, such that no dust or impurities can adhere to it;
seven parts of his body—the two hands, two feet, shoulders, and nape—are flat and full;
his arms and shoulders are rounded and muscular, his spinal vertebrae do not protrude, and he is perfectly proportioned and symmetrical like a nyagrodha tree.
His jaw and chest were like those of a lion;
his neck was like a deep-blue lotus stalk, marked with three graceful folds;
his constant radiance shone in the four directions, extending one fathom from his face.
He has forty teeth, which are brilliant white, even, and closely set;
his tongue is crimson, long and broad, covering his entire face;
his Brahma-voice is pure and beautiful, a delight for all who hear it.
The eyelashes are blue-green and lustrous, even and orderly without disarray;
the upper and lower lashes blink like those of a bull-king, with the blue and white clearly distinguished;
the face is perfectly round, like the pure moon.
His eyebrows are slender and curved like the bow of Śakra;
his white hair-tuft is brilliant and pure, its markings curling to the right;
and upon his crown is a fleshy protuberance, resembling a celestial canopy.
With these various marks, his body was thus adorned. "Good son, at one time the Prince,

having received the instructions of his father the King, went forth from the palace city surrounded before and behind by twenty thousand handmaidens and attendants, as well as his kinsmen, to visit the Great Fragrant Sprout Garden on the Peak of Radiant Clouds to wander, observe, and enjoy himself."
At that time, the Prince mounted a most exquisite chariot made of Jambūnada gold, its adornments unsurpassed in the world.

Great flaming vajras formed its wheels, celestial exquisite vajras formed its hubs, and fragrant maṇi jewels formed its body. It was inlaid and adorned with the finest sandalwood, covered above by a network of various jeweled flowers, and featured a lion throne made of the great treasury-adorned king of maṇi jewels.
Five hundred court ladies each held precious ropes to guide and lead the horse, proceeding neither too slowly nor too quickly, advancing and halting with perfect measure.
A thousand precious horses drew a golden chariot, escorted by attendants before and behind.

A canopy was fashioned from the sovereign *maṇi* jewel of white lapis lazuli, adorned with sovereign *maṇi* jewels that emitted inconceivable and wondrous rays of light in all colors; its pole was made of exquisite *maṇi* jewels of sovereign dark-blue lapis lazuli reflecting all images, held by attendants who followed and covered it above.

Hundreds of thousands of millions of people held various precious parasols; hundreds of thousands of millions of people held various precious banners; hundreds of thousands of millions of people held various precious pennants; hundreds of thousands of millions of people played various musical instruments; hundreds of thousands of millions of people scattered various precious flowers; and hundreds of thousands of millions of people held various incense burners, burning all kinds of famous incenses, surrounding him before and behind as an escort.
The road was broad and level, with eight thoroughfares aligned in even rows;
it was bordered by various jewels and strewn with golden sand, upon which diverse precious flowers were scattered.
Rows of trees made of various jewels and jeweled railings were set out in succession between the eight thoroughfares.
It was covered with nets of various exquisite jewel bells and silken streamers, suspended and spread among the trees as an adornment.

Along both sides of the road, at every turn, were established halls of righteousness and houses of merit, as well as multi-storied pavilions made of various jewels and storehouses, all interconnected and extending far and wide, filled to capacity with precious gems and wealth.

Within some of these, rare treasures, necklaces, and ornaments were piled up; in others, silken fabrics and exquisite garments; in some, sweet and delicious food and drink were prepared; in others, incense, flowers, and personal requisites were stored. Furthermore, there were kept elephants, horses, and various jeweled carriages. There were also stationed beautiful women and male and female servants, all of whom were well-versed in every worldly etiquette and ritual, and had mastered every art and skill.
"Whenever sentient beings came to him seeking food, he gave it all away to them, ensuring that their wishes were never left unfulfilled.

At that time, within the royal capital of Great Tree Wondrous High Auspiciousness, there was a woman named Suprabhā, who had a young girl named Samantaprabhāśrī. The girl’s countenance was upright and her physical features were pure and majestic;
her proportions were perfectly balanced, and her height and stature were in exact measure."
His various marks were perfectly complete, with eyes and hair of deep blue;
his speech was like the Brahma-voice, pure, penetrating, and exquisite;
he possessed wisdom and sagacity, and was revered by all people.
He is proficient in skills and masterful in debate;
he is respectful, diligent, and tireless; he is upright, honest, and gentle;
he has few desires and little anxiety; and he is compassionate and non-harming.
Endowed with a sense of shame and dread of blame, free from guile and arrogance, his resolve and capacity were vast and profound, such that no one could equal him.

Together with his mother, he mounted a magnificent jeweled chariot and was surrounded by his retinue and countless female attendants before and behind; leading the way ahead of the Prince, they departed from the royal capital, singing and sporting as they traveled along the road.
Seeing the crown prince performing various musical entertainments and chanting with eloquent verses, his heart was filled with attachment, and he said to his mother:
"How wonderful! O compassionate mother, my heart’s desire is to serve this man with reverence; if my wish is not fulfilled, I shall surely perish."
Then, the mother Suprabhā said to her daughter:
"You should not harbor such a thought now. Why is this?

This noble person here is a prince who possesses the complete and perfect marks of a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin). Before long, he shall succeed to the rank of a Wheel-Turning King, at which time a Woman-Jewel (strī-ratna) will naturally appear, traveling through the air by flight and endowed with great majesty and virtue."
"I am now of a lowly and base lineage; you are not my equal. This is extremely difficult to obtain, so do not harbor such thoughts.
At that time, the young woman’s mind was resolved, firm and unyielding.
At that time, beside the Fragrant Sprout Cloud Peak Garden, there was a site of enlightenment named Dharma-Cloud Radiance;
at that time, a Tathāgata named Victorious Sun Body had attained perfect awakening at this site of enlightenment seven days prior.
At that time, the young woman, exhausted from wandering and sightseeing, dozed for a short while;
then, the Tathāgata manifested a supernatural transformation within her dream.
Upon awakening from the dream, a celestial messenger—a friend who had protected her as a bodhisattva in a previous life—spoke to her from the midst of the sky:

“O maiden! That which you have just dreamed is the Tathāgata Sūryagarbha, who, beside the Fragrant Sprout Cloud-Peak Garden, has attained perfect enlightenment within the Bodhimaṇḍa of Dharma-Cloud Radiance, and it has been but seven days since that occurrence. All the bodhisattvas...
Surrounded before and behind by the assembly of bodhisattvas, as well as by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas,
asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, the kings of the Brahma worlds,
the Śuddhāvāsa devas, and all the lords of rivers, lords of oceans, and lords of the earth;
The presiding deities of water, wind, fire, mountains, cities, gardens, medicinal herbs,
forests, crops, directions, space, day, and night; the spirits of the body, the feet, and the place of enlightenment,
together with their male and female retinues, all came desiring to see the Buddha and hear his teaching.
"Because they have heard the Dharma, they have all come together;
you too should now approach them with reverence and pay them homage.

At that time, the maiden Pūrṇacandrāśrī, having witnessed the Buddha’s supernatural transformations in her dream and being sustained by the empowerment of the Buddha’s merits, felt no fear and was peaceful and joyful. Since her heart had long admired the Prince, she immediately spoke these verses before him:
"My body is upright and peerless; my wisdom and physical marks are all perfected.
My speech and etiquette are thoroughly mastered, and my merit and fame pervade the ten directions."
Countless sentient beings in the world who behold my body all become attached;
yet toward those multitudes, I am ever pure, never giving rise to a mind of defiled attachment.
In my mind, there is no hatred or attachment toward anything; I am likewise free from delusion and resentment.
Relying solely on pure great compassion, I ultimately bring benefit to all sentient beings.
Now that I behold the Prince, adorned with the marks of supreme merit, my heart is filled with great joy pervading my entire body; my senses are delighted, and I long to draw near to him.
His complexion is like a pure and wondrous luminous jewel; his hair is deep blue-black and curls to the right.
His nose is high, long, and straight, most exquisitely dignified; his forehead is broad and level, and his eyebrows are fine and arched.
His body is like a mass of exquisite, pure gold; his marks and signs and radiant light are peerless.
His wondrous eyes are long and wide like blue lotuses; his teeth are white, even, and closely set, surpassing conch and snow.

With a face as bright and full as the moon and cheeks like those of a lion, a square mouth and lips red as vermilion, you never utter a word that is not in accordance with the Dharma; may the Most Victorious Honored One compassionately accept me.
The tongue is long, broad, and exceedingly supple; its color is like that of red copper with the luster of myriad jewels.
Its voice is like the resonance of Brahmā or the *kiṃnara*; all sentient beings who hear it are filled with joy.
His speech is eloquent and his smile is revealed with exquisite grace; his majestic radiance eclipses all others and his virtue is immeasurable.
With a joyful countenance and beautiful features, he is naturally adorned, such that those who behold him can never tire of the sight.
With a mind free from defilement and a body pure, adorned with the thirty-two marks, you will surely become a Wheel-Turning King in this realm; I pray only that you will compassionately accept me.

At that time, Prince Tejodhipati, in order to demonstrate to the world that women possess many faults and afflictions—obstructing both worldly and world-transcending happiness, and even being able to obstruct unsurpassed enlightenment—spoke these verses for the sake of the young girl amidst the great assembly:
"In this world, people falsely reckon upon various clans; It is only women who are objects of love, respect, and delight."
Supremely excellent and beyond compare, she is able to establish and sustain all virtuous companions.
A woman is the foremost jewel among humanity; she is also the cause for the liberation of devas and humans.
She continues the lineage of the noble family and the body of merit; thus the sages of the world declare that the woman is supreme.
All the burning afflictions scorching the heart, and the body oppressed by various anxieties and grievances—
his wife consoled him so that he attained coolness, like encountering sweet rain during a scorching summer heat.
The minds of ordinary beings are submerged in various sorrows and afflictions, as if entangled by a grave illness;
yet, because of the pleasures derived from a wife’s artful charms, they falsely claim that she is the supreme medicine for removing their grief.
Sentient beings with false views give rise to this thought: "A woman can act as the cause of the world;
She gives birth, nurtures, and raises [beings], adorned with merit; In the transformations of heaven and earth, none can surpass her."

The diligent pursuit of worldly affairs depends solely upon women; they exhort their husbands to perform all manner of virtuous deeds and are able to turn men according to their will—such women harbor no defiled thoughts toward others' hearts.
The sages have declared that all afflictions and every transgression of karma arise from women;
how much more so when one takes a woman of low birth as a wife—nothing in this world is more utterly evil than this.
Women are stubbornly attached to their own nature, as firm and immovable as the earth;
yet they follow only wealth, pleasure, and noble status, utterly abandoning the poor, the lowly, the decrepit, and the weak.
The great majestic power of the rishis with five supernormal faculties was lost because of a woman;
she who could ride upon their necks at will now caused the King’s daughter to turn toward tranquility.
Yama, the King of Death, and fierce winds, The Voca Sea beneath the earth,
Blazing fires, black serpents, swords, and poisons— A woman’s harm exceeds all these.
With a respectful heart, she provides all manner of wealth and treasures; with sincerity, she serves him without any thought of opposition.
Whether through wisdom and skillful means, or through firmness and gentleness, no one is able to know the mind of a woman.
Seeing people weep or laugh, she surpasses them all; with various illusions and delusions, she entices their hearts.
Her appearance is respectful and she feigns coquettish charm toward men, yet within her heart she harbors cruelty—none realize it.
Utterly deceptive speech is shown as truth, while utterly truthful words are all deemed false;
like venomous beasts that constantly harm sentient beings—alas, O man, how could one dwell with such a person?
Having served him with reverence for a long time, her arrogance only increased; when encountering even a moment of adverse circumstance, her wickedness grew even more.
Whether he was at home or abroad, at all times she would treat her husband with insolence and transgression, devoid of any sense of shame.
As fire consumes fuel and is never satisfied, as the ocean swallows rivers and knows no time of fullness, so too is the mind of a woman toward men; King Yama never tires of killing sentient beings.
Women do not consider lineage, nor age, status, or beauty;
they pursue every man without restraint, their insatiable passion being thus.
A woman’s desires are never satiated; she has not the slightest attachment to her husband’s heart.
Like a wild buffalo roaming at will, she constantly thinks only of gradually grazing upon fresh grass.
In youth, one’s mind flows with the passions of flourishing beauty; though wealthy and noble, one is bound to another as a dependent.
Amidst abundant jade delicacies, necklaces, and fine robes, she constantly wishes for poverty so that she may follow her own will.
All manner of services and offerings were fully provided—scented unguents, bathing, and exquisite adornments—yet she never felt shame for the kindness of her husband;
instead, her mind was unrestrained by perverse thoughts that never ceased.
Whether speaking with lustful passion or with words of compassion, it is as if nectar were produced upon her tongue;
yet within her heart, fierce evil gives rise to poison. Therefore, the words of women are difficult to trust.
A woman can cause estrangement within her husband’s clan; she prevents them from dwelling together in harmony for even a moment.
Her parents and brothers become bitter enemies, and all her relatives by marriage are cast aside.
Outwardly displaying a beautiful appearance while harboring flattery within, with every transgression and fault filling their bellies—
one should not look upon them for even a moment, much less long endure their coarse and evil speech.
A woman must at all times guard against all faults and suspicions;
if even a single aspect of her conduct falters, she will be held in contempt by the multitude, and if she harms the wind of custom and ruins social mores, she will be abandoned by all.
Whether women are young children, middle-aged, or even in old age past a hundred years,
and whether their internal or external clans are all honorable and noble, their every movement and posture must always be guarded by others.
While a maiden resides at home, she follows her parents; upon reaching the age for the hair-pin ceremony, she marries and follows her husband.
When her husband dies, she follows her son to avoid suspicion; thus, she is always said to lack self-mastery.
Having left the household life to renounce desire and cultivate tranquility, yet the mind dwells upon the realm of women rather than that of the noble ones—
like saffron dye staining a soiled garment, such a person is constantly ridiculed by the wise.
Like a prisoner released who longs to re-enter his cell, like a madman recovered from delirium wishing to relapse,
or like one cured of leprosy yearning for the days of sickness— the longing for a woman exceeds even these.
Just as dragons dwell in clear, still waters, Or as fierce beasts reside in golden caves,
So too does the wise person regard women, Even while practicing the precepts and meditative concentration.
A wise person would rather swallow hot iron than allow the sight of female beauty to disturb their mind;
for it turns the qualities of morality, concentration, and wisdom into universal enemies, causing one to abandon all the necessary conditions for tranquility.
A woman does not consider noble lineage, auspiciousness, wealth, status, wisdom, or fame;
she seeks only carnal desire with no other intent. How could she be one whom a wise person would draw near?
There are those who dwell in various dhyānas and possess great power, capable of slaying even the valiant and the royal sages;
yet at times, they may have their minds defiled by female beauty, thereby falling away from the virtues of self-mastery.
They engage in strife amidst elephants, horses, and military arrays; they sacrifice their lives to cross the sea to gather precious treasures;
noble lineages become beggars and slaves—all such deviations from the True Dharma arise because of women.
A woman’s moods of joy and anger are difficult to perceive; her defiled mind and perverse schemes are boundless.
Among all the wise men renowned in the world, there is none who can truly know a woman’s heart.
The celestial lords among the rishis of the five supernatural powers may know the exact volume of the waters of the great ocean,
yet even if they were to calculate for their entire lives, they could never know the individual thoughts of each woman.
Deceitful words are pleasing to the ear, as sweet as honey; yet the heart is like a sharp sword that harms others.
A disordered mind is skillful at seizing the hearts of men, harboring evil and devising schemes to spread all manner of poison.
Whether women are exquisitely adorned or unadorned, whether they walk, stand, sit, or lie down, they are all viewed with suspicion and aversion;
the foolish and the wise alike harbor ill will toward all women, feeling loathing even upon seeing their painted images.
The foolish child delights in climbing the branches of a poisonous tree; the deluded and distracted one wishes to dwell in the lair of a venomous serpent;
the madman grasps at glowing red-hot iron—to draw near to the color of women exceeds even these.
Stained by attachment to female beauty, the mind becomes clouded and intoxicated; when it goes against one's will, it brings forth the poison of anger that harms the body.
Fearing the times of joy and wrath in women, how could a wise person draw near and dwell with them?
The foul nature of women fills their hearts, like deep waters in a river where crocodiles and dragons dwell;
they disregard valor, strength, beauty, or lineage, indulging their desires according to their whims, heedless of right or wrong.
A woman’s mind is unstable like a swift wind, And as fleeting as a cloud or a flash of lightning;
Though served for a hundred years with all her desires provided, She never possesses even a slight thought of gratitude toward her husband.
They show no respect for the virtuous and treat the meritless with contempt; they loathe the poor and delight in the wealthy, pursuing their greedy desires.
They respond to sweet words with honor and sustenance, increasing their arrogance and pride, while having no heart to regard those who lack material resources.
A venomous snake, a withered desert, and the *vatsanābha* poison flower—dwelling with or wearing these may cause injury for a single lifetime;
yet approaching the colors of women surpasses even those, for it eternally destroys the body of merit in the future.
Women are treacherous and artful, constantly engaging in slander; they create estrangement between the six types of kin and among friends.
They conceal their own faults while broadcasting the failings of others; all manner of calamities and afflictions arise from women.
A woman’s mind is as unstable as a monkey; she constantly dwells on minor transgressions while forgetting great kindness.
A foolish man serves her with the reverence due to a teacher or a sovereign, yet like a slave serving his master, his devotion never finds satisfaction.
Women are like rivers that overflow their banks, sweeping away all sublime dharmas and destroying many bodies;
like turbulent currents that cause both banks to collapse, the harm women inflict upon virtue exceeds even this.
The woman’s net of desire is exceedingly firm and dense; she gazes about and walks slowly without a trace of shame.
She laughs, speaks, and quarrels with joy, her mind never wavering; she ensnares all who possess wealth and honor as if they were intoxicated by darkness.
A woman’s染愛 (tainted passion) arises from delusion; like a tree without roots, desire is extinguished like a lamp.
When physical beauty fades, love ceases in an instant, and all feelings of affection are utterly extinguished.
A woman’s love and desire last but a moment; her defiled mind and perverse speech are difficult to trust.
At times she values one as more precious than rare jewels, yet at other times she casts them aside with loathing like blades of straw.
The elephant king possesses the sovereign power to uproot trees; his color is like a great white cloud floating in the sky.
Yet, because his mind was intoxicated by a female elephant, he was entirely subdued according to the will of others.
When a bodhisattva gathers women for the sake of the Dharma, though he constantly instructs them with a detached mind,
if at times he becomes excessive and grows intimate with them, he is like a bird whose wings are broken and cannot fly.
The inclinations of women are ever base and low; like a river whose banks crumble and collapse, wherever they go they cause wholesome dharmas to decline;
the destruction of lineages and the extinction of clans all stem from this.
Women can spread the net of craving and desire, To ensnare and capture all foolish men;
The sentient beings of this world, stained by lust, Are like fish that swallow the hook and become their prey.
The wise observe and know that it is fundamentally impure, with the nine apertures constantly flowing day and night;
thus one should feel weary detachment toward the female body—how could one give rise to craving and attachment for it?
The female body is illusory like a floating bubble, a locus for the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death;
it is a heap of impurities exceeding a mountain in magnitude—how could one give rise to craving and attachment toward such a thing?
All sorrows, afflictions, and terrors arise from female form;
if one can contemplate this and remain free from attachment, one will be liberated, without sorrow or fear.

Therefore, the wise do not gaze upon women; if they should observe them at times, they do so with a mind of loving-kindness, perceiving them as mothers, daughters, or sisters, and accordingly teach them the Dharma of non-attachment.
One can discern that within and without a woman’s body, various impurities arise;
how then can the objects of the senses stir the fire of desire, burning away the roots of goodness accumulated over countless eons?
At that time, after Prince Subhāṣitarāja had spoken these verses, he addressed the maiden Prabhūtavarṇaśrī, saying:
"Whose daughter are you?"
To whom did you previously belong?
By whom were you protected?
If you already belong to someone else, I should not take you back into my care.
At that time, the Prince questioned him with these verses:
“You possess a body endowed with pure merit; Your physical marks are upright, majestic, and most subtle.
I now ask you; you should answer truthfully: From where were you originally born, and where do you dwell?”
Who are your parents and kinsmen?
Upon whom do you now depend for your dwelling?
If you have already become attached to another, I should not take you back into my care.
You do not take pleasure in stealing the wealth of others; you do not harm sentient beings out of a lack of compassion;
you do not defile your mind with sexual misconduct—ultimately, upon what teaching do you abide?
Do you not cause estrangement between others and their kin? Do you utter all manner of coarse and evil speech, which is false, meaningless, and distressing to living beings?
Do you greedily pursue sensory objects while harboring envy?
Do you not give rise to anger toward others? Are you not entangled by a mind bound to false and perilous views?
Do you not practice flattery, deceit, or delusion to mislead the world? And do you not commit various grave karmas that lead to contradiction and ruin?
Do you respect your parents, teachers, and elders? Do you honor all virtuous friends?
Upon seeing those who are distressed, impoverished, or destitute, are you able to give rise to a heart of compassion and benefit them?
If there are any spiritual friends who instruct you in the true Dharma,
are you able, with a mind of firm faith and joy, to respectfully and diligently practice their teachings and make offerings to them?
Can you take delight in all the Buddhas? Can you hold the Bodhisattvas in high esteem?
Can you give rise to reverence for the Sangha of the most excellent Dharma and its qualities?
Are you able to abide securely in the True Dharma? Are you able to remain far removed from what is not the Dharma?
Upon hearing praise of the boundless ocean of merit, are you able to give rise to love, joy, and reverence?
Do you see those who are solitary and without refuge, and can you give rise to a compassionate mind to rescue and protect them?
Do you see the sentient beings in the evil realms, and can you generate a vast mind of great compassion?
Can you give rise to the utmost joy regarding the prosperity and happiness of others?
Can you abide in a mind of equanimity toward all beings who are oppressed by suffering?
For the sake of sentient beings shrouded in the darkness of ignorance, do you seek great bodhi to bring them awakening?
Having cultivated all practices through an ocean of boundless eons, do you never give rise to weariness of body or mind?

At that time, having been thus questioned by the Prince, the girl’s mother, Suprabhā, stood before him and spoke of all the auspicious marks of merit pertaining to the girl, from her initial birth until her full growth, speaking in verse:
“O Benevolent Prince, you should now listen well To the various causes and conditions concerning this girl as asked:
Her gradual development from birth until her maturity, And her endowment with virtues and adornments, I shall now describe.”
In the past, on the very day the Prince was first born, this girl was likewise born from a lotus;
her faculties were pure and her features perfectly radiant, her limbs and joints adorned and fully complete.
At that time, during the spring months, I went for a stroll and entered that most excellent Śāla grove;
I beheld the various plants and trees beginning to flower, and the hundred grains and medicinal herbs all flourishing and thriving.
Exquisite trees and famous flowers bloom in myriad colors; They emit brilliance and radiate light like auspicious clouds.
Black bees swarm about and birds sing in harmony; Those who hear them forget their sorrows and indulge in joy.
Accompanying him were eight hundred court ladies; their countenances and deportment were so upright they captivated the hearts of men.
Dressed in exquisite and beautiful garments, they were fully adorned; their speech and songs were all exceptionally sublime.
In the garden was a bathing pool adorned with jewels, named Various Lotus Banners;
taking my court ladies with me, I went to the edge of the pool, scattering flowers upon the ground to arrange my seat.
Within that pure and fragrant pond, a thousand-petaled jewel lotus suddenly sprang forth;
its pedestal was made of Jāmbūnada gold, its stem of lapis lazuli, and its petals of maṇi jewels.
With exquisite fragrances and myriad jewels as its stamens, it universally radiates all manner of great light;
when sentient beings behold this sign, they are all struck with doubt: "How is it that the sun's light shines in the middle of the night?"
When the night has ended and the sun first rises, its radiance shines upon this lotus flower as it blooms;
the lotus emits light and utters wondrous sounds, manifesting the signs of this maiden’s initial birth.
At that time, I beheld this jewel among men, born from that lotus flower;
having cultivated pure deeds in the past without fail, he has now attained the perfect and luminous fruits of all wonders.
With hair like deep blue lapis lazuli and eyes like blue lotuses, his countenance is dignified and adorned with golden radiance;
he is fully graced with flower garlands and a jeweled topknot, possessing the auspicious and stainless hue of a lotus.
His body and limbs are all perfectly complete, With marks and signs and radiance beyond compare;
He sits solemnly and upright amidst jeweled flowers, Like a statue of pure and exquisite refined gold.
From every single pore across his entire body, The fragrance of all kinds of sandalwood issues forth;
From his mouth, the scent of blue lotuses constantly emanates, And all his speech and sounds are like the resonance of Brahma.
At times she smiles and speaks with a voice as wondrous as celestial music;
this jewel among women is a rarity in the world, and one such as she is not a match for those who are base or inferior.
I observe that in this world there is no one capable of being this woman’s lord, save for you, O Benevolent One, adorned with the marks of merit;
I pray that you will grant us great compassion and graciously accept her.
This woman is neither tall nor short; she is neither coarse nor slender.
All parts of her body are perfectly graceful, and she is fully endowed with all the marks of excellence, free from any blemish or ugliness.
Whatever arts exist in the world—writing, calculation, seals, and the methods of craftsmanship;
whether it be speech, recitation, or all that is pure and subtle—I pray only that the Benevolent Honored One will compassionately accept them.
He was also able to comprehend all military tactics; there were no skills in archery or swordsmanship that he did not master.
With a compassionate heart, he skillfully reconciled disputes and litigation; those who heard his name or looked up to his virtue were all brought to submission.
With past causes and supreme practices all perfected, Adorned naturally with every merit, Those who behold you rejoice, never wearying;
I pray only that the Benevolent Honored One will compassionately accept me.
Regarding all the various illnesses of sentient beings, Knowing their causes, their arising, and their increase or decrease,
One provides the appropriate medicine according to the ailment without error, Able to cause all sufferings to be completely extinguished.
All the linguistic conventions of Jambudvīpa, with their infinite varieties of shifting sounds,
and their diverse terminologies and etymological explanations— all such things he thoroughly masters.
All the musical instruments in the world, Dancing, singing, play, and hymns of praise,
Speech and debate that delight the human heart— These can cause all who see them to rejoice.
In every movement and posture, there is a standard; in choosing and rejecting, advancing and retreating, all accord with what is appropriate.
Toward all sentient beings, whether stained or unstained, one acts solely with a compassionate heart, free from attachment.
Walking slowly and observing with a mind undisturbed, The sense faculties are tranquil and mindfulness remains unimpaired;
Body and speech always follow the practice of wisdom, And all the faults of women are entirely abandoned.
All the virtues possessed by women, this maiden has fully cultivated and maintained;
you should know her to be a jewel among women of the world, so I pray that you will swiftly show compassion and accept her.
His mind is neither stingy nor envious; he is free from sensual desire, greed, and hatred.
His nature is upright, supple, and harmonious; his speech is exquisite and free from coarseness.
I pay respectful homage to all my elders and superiors; Single-mindedly seeking merit, my resolve remains unshakable;
I steadfastly uphold all the holy life (brahmacarya); I only pray that you will compassionately accept me with pity.
Seeing those who are aged and infirm, or afflicted by grave illness, Those beset by various calamities and living in poverty,
Without a master, without kin, and with no one to rely upon— One should constantly give rise to a mind of loving-kindness to rescue and protect them.
Not dwelling on the peace and happiness of one's own self, one always delights in benefiting all sentient beings;
adorning the mind with these merits, one ultimately contemplates the truth of reality.
In walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, the mind is never dissipated; Whether moving or still, speaking or silent, one always acts in accordance with the occasion.
Never for a single thought-moment has one abandoned sentient beings, Enabling all who behold them to feel deep respect.
Although toward all sentient beings, one does not give rise to the defiled minds of ordinary folk,
upon seeing those endowed with compassion and virtue, one always delights in drawing near to them without ever feeling satiated.
One is able to universally honor spiritual friends and remain far removed from all evil associates;
with a mind free from agitation or rivalry, one always acts in accordance with the Dharma, first reflecting upon every deed to avoid error or failure.
Universally free from resentment toward all, she constantly cultivates manifold merits to adorn her person;
her wisdom is peerless among men—this maiden is worthy to be wedded to the Crown Prince.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha’s Great Vaipulya, Scroll Twenty-Eight;
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha’s Great Vaipulya, Scroll Twenty-Nine.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā of Kaśmīra by Imperial Decree.
From the "Chapter on the Vows and Practices of Samantabhadra for Entering the Realm of Inconceivable Liberation":
At that time, within the garden of the Fragrant Tooth Cloud Peak, Prince Tejodhipati addressed the assembly and the venerable Subhūti, speaking to the young girl:
"O virtuous daughter!..."
For the sake of seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I vow to practice the bodhisattva path throughout the future,
to accumulate all factors conducive to enlightenment, to purely cultivate all the pāramitās,
to serve and attend upon all Buddhas of the future, to protect and uphold all the Buddha-teachings, and to adorn and purify...
One shall succeed to the lineage of all Tathāgatas in all Buddha-fields; one shall vow to bring all sentient beings to maturity;
one shall sever the suffering and affliction of all sentient beings; one shall establish all beings in a state of peace and security;
one shall purify the eye of wisdom of all sentient beings; and one shall cultivate all the sublime practices of a Bodhisattva.

When I enter the equal nature of the Bodhisattvas, when I abide in all the stages of the Bodhisattvas, when I cause those of the two vehicles to fulfill the fruit of Buddhahood, and when I cause all sentient beings to rejoice;

and when, for the sake of fulfilling the *dāna-pāramitā*, I ultimately achieve unsurpassed bodhi by relinquishing all internal and external wealth—even my head, eyes, and everything else—without any lingering attachment; at that time, you might create obstacles for me so that my practice cannot be perfected: when giving away material wealth, your mind becomes stingy; when giving away my children or wife, your heart is pained and distressed; when cutting off my limbs, your heart is filled with grief and despondency; or when I renounce you to leave the household life, your heart is filled with regret and resentment.
At that time, having questioned her thus, the Prince further spoke these verses for the sake of the young girl:
"Out of compassion for all sentient beings, I have resolved upon the vast mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta).
Throughout immeasurable billions of eons, I shall accumulate and perfect the wisdom of awakening."
Throughout immeasurable and boundless oceans of great eons, They purely cultivate all vows as vast as space;
Entering the stages, they remedy hindrances and perfect their practice, Until finally they shall attain the stage of the Tathāgata.
I vow before the Buddhas of the three periods of time, To fully study all the pāramitās,
To perfect skillful means and practice correctly, And to accomplish the path of supreme bodhi.
All defiled lands throughout the ten directions, I shall universally purify and adorn;
And within all evil realms and states of suffering, I shall provide rescue and protection so that all may emerge.
All sentient beings dwell in the ocean of existence, Constantly entangled and shrouded by afflictions, ignorance, and delusion.
I shall eradicate [all afflictions] until none remain, Causing all to dwell securely in the path of the Tathāgata.
I shall make offerings to all Buddhas, And I shall universally cultivate the stages of a Bodhisattva.
Constantly giving rise to vast compassion, I shall grant whatever is needed without greed or stinginess.
"When you see any who come to beg, even if you feel stinginess toward wealth, my heart always delights in giving to all living beings; you should follow me without opposition."
When I shall give my head to him, you must take care not to let your heart give rise to grief or distress;
I speak to you first so that you may know, and so that your mind may remain firm and forever unshakable.
Even if your limbs, hands, and feet are severed, and even regarding your wife and children, let there be no stinginess in your heart;
do not harbor hatred or disdain for those who beg, but reflect with clarity so that you do not turn back.
To fulfill the desires of all sentient beings, I am able to relinquish everything both internal and external;
Since you can accord with my bodhicitta, I shall likewise follow your will.
At that time, having heard these words, the maiden Samantābhijñāśrī addressed Prince Tejodhipati, saying:
"Excellent, O noble man!"

Regarding the bodhisattva practices you have asked about—those difficult deeds that can be performed and those hardships that can be endured—I shall follow them all with diligent cultivation, intimacy, and non-abandonment, like a shadow following a form, so that all your aspirations may be fully realized.
At that time, the young woman spoke these verses to the Prince:
"Even if for immeasurable and boundless eons, my body were consumed by the fires of all the hells,
if you, O Benevolent Honored One, would deign to accept me, I would gladly endure it and have no words for such suffering."
Even if throughout immeasurable births my body were ground to powder like fine dust,
O Benevolent Honored One, if you would graciously accept me, I shall endure with firm resolve, unshakable.
Even if for immeasurable and boundless eons I were to carry upon my head all the mountains of adamant,
O Benevolent Honored One, if you would graciously accept me, I would willingly endure this division of labor without weariness.
Throughout the ocean of kalpas of birth and death, you have given your own body and flesh as alms to sentient beings;
you have attained a secure station within the royal house of Dharma—may I, like your honor, likewise obtain this.
I only pray that the Prince will deign to show compassion and accept me, becoming my master so that we may practice together;
throughout the oceans of kalpas to come when I practice giving, may I always offer my own body for the sake of all beings.
Out of compassion for all sentient beings, you have given rise to the vast bodhicitta;
having already universally gathered all living creatures, I pray that you will likewise receive me with your loving-kindness and compassion.
My mind originally sought neither wealth nor nobility, nor did it crave the pleasures of the five desires;
it was solely for the sake of practicing together with those of like dharma that I made this vow to take benevolence as my guide.
With deep blue, long, and wide eyes of compassion, You universally observe all sentient beings;
Without giving rise to the defiled minds of ordinary folk, You will surely attain the fruit of tranquil enlightenment.
Wherever the Crown Prince passes and walks, the earth spirits cause precious lotus flowers to spring forth;
adorned with radiant and wondrous marks, he will surely become a Wheel-Turning King and deign to accept me.
I once saw this in a dream: the light of the Dharma-clouds illuminates the site of enlightenment;
the Buddha, having attained perfect awakening, radiates brilliant light, surrounded by immeasurable bodhisattvas.
In a dream, I beheld that Tathāgata of the Victorious Sun-body, resplendent like the radiance of a mountain of purple gold;
he immediately stroked the crown of my head with his hand, and upon waking, I leaped for joy with a heart full of delight.
In the sky there was a deity named Joyful Light, who had practiced with me in previous lives;
emitting a wondrous voice, he came to inform me that "that Tathāgata has now appeared in the world."
Because I previously gave rise to this thought—“I wish to see the body of the Prince’s meritorious virtues”—that deity spoke these words to me: “You shall surely behold him now.”
Having received the Buddha’s empowerment, I now behold you; all former aspirations are now fully realized.
I pray that we may go together to the Tathāgata and, with one mind, study the path to Bodhi.
At that time, having heard the name of the Tathāgata Sun-Victory-Body, the prince immediately attained a swift and pure mind called "Great Joy of Unobstructed Distinction upon Seeing the Buddha.

He then scattered five hundred mani-jewel flowers over the young woman, crowned her with a *maṇi*-jewel topknot of the Auspicious Treasury, and clothed her in a multicolored flame-patterned *maṇi*-jewel robe.

At that time, the young girl composed her mind in right mindfulness; she remained unshaken and showed no sign of excitement. With single-minded devotion, she joined her palms in reverence, gazing up at the Prince with right mindfulness present before her, her eyes never for a moment wavering.
Then, his mother, Sujātā, spoke these verses to the Prince:
"This maiden is a rare jewel among men, her body adorned with the marks of pure merit and sublime beauty.
Her heart has long been vowed to serve you, O Noble One; now all her aspirations and joys are fulfilled."
Firmly maintaining pure precepts, ever without flaw; Wisdom perfected, mindfulness never failing;
Replete with merit, her marks perfectly radiant— Among all women, none can equal her.
This maiden was originally born from a lotus; her lineage is pure and free from reproach or blemish.
She is entirely devoid of the faults of women and is worthy to follow the Prince in his joint practice.
His body is as fine and exquisite as silk floss; his hands and feet are as soft as *tūla* cotton.
Wherever they touch, all illnesses are dispelled, and body and mind abide in peace and happiness, free from all suffering.
The fragrance emitted from all the pores of his body is so exquisitely sweet that it surpasses the world without peer;
if one smells it even briefly, the mind becomes free from defilement, and by abiding in pure precepts, one attains physical peace.
The body is like the pure and wondrous color of true gold; unstained by dust or grime, it is like a lotus flower.
Sentient beings who behold it are freed from greed and anger; they all come to possess compassion and are devoid of wrath or harm.
The speech is exquisite and the voice is soft; all sentient beings delight in hearing it.
Passing through the mind and over the ears, it gladdens all the faculties; evil karma is eliminated and afflictions are extinguished.
With an inner mind pure and free from blemish, gentle and upright with no partiality, their speech is pleasing and appropriate;
all who hear it rejoice, and their minds are brought under discipline.
Endowed with shame and remorse, free from deceit and delusion, Without arrogance or flattery, possessing loving-kindness and compassion,
Seeking the True Dharma to deliver all sentient beings, They serve virtuous friends with reverence and diligence, never feeling weary or satiated.
Neither regarding physical appearance nor lineage, nor even becoming intoxicated by honor and pleasure,
but with humility and a mind free of self, he sought exclusively the path to unsurpassed bodhi.

At that time, Prince Tejodhipati, together with the maiden Sumatīśrī and twenty thousand court ladies, along with their retinues, each mounted a precious chariot and departed from the Fragrant Sprout Garden in order to approach, revere, and make offerings to the Tathāgata Sūryagātraprabhāsa. They proceeded to the Dharma-Cloud Radiance Bodhimanda.

Having arrived, he alighted from his carriage and proceeded on foot toward the Buddha’s dwelling. Beholding the Buddha’s physical marks—dignified, serene, and with faculties perfectly disciplined like those of an elephant king—and seeing that he was pure within and without, free from all defilement like a great dragon pool, he was filled with leaping joy and gave rise to pure faith.
His love and devotion increased as he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and circumambulated him countless times.

At that time, the prince and the young girl each took five hundred great mani-jewel, exquisite lotuses and scattered them as offerings over the Buddha; through the Buddha’s supernatural power, they spread throughout the void, covering the Tathāgata and the entire assembly.
"At that time, the Prince further constructed five hundred vihāras for that Buddha;
each was made entirely of fragrant wood, interspersed with five hundred mani-jewels, and adorned throughout with various kinds of miscellaneous gems."
At that time, the Tathāgata, knowing that the crown prince’s faculties were already mature, immediately expounded for him the Sūtra of the Universal Eye Lamp Gate.
Upon hearing this sūtra, the crown prince realized thirteen gates to the ocean of samādhis within all dharmas, namely:
he attained the gate of the samādhi of the manifestation of light from the ocean of vows of all Tathāgatas; he attained the gate of universally illuminating the three periods of time...
The samādhi-door of the treasury of light; the samādhi-door of attaining direct vision of the sites of enlightenment of all Buddhas;
the samādhi-door of attaining the universal illumination of light upon entering the realms of all sentient beings;

the samādhi-door of attaining the lamp of light that is the mass of wisdom universally illuminating all worlds; and the samādhi-door of universally illuminating the ocean of the faculties of all sentient beings.
The samādhi-door of the Lamp of Wisdom; the samādhi-door of attaining the Cloud of Wisdom-Light that Protects and Saves All Sentient Beings;
the samādhi-door of attaining the Great Wisdom-Light Lamp that Subdues and Brings to Maturity All Sentient Beings;

the samādhi-door of attaining the manifestation before one's eyes of the sounds of all Buddhas turning the wheel of Dharma through the power of hearing and retention; and the attainment of the perfection of Samantabhadra.
The Samādhi-door of the Ocean-Cloud of Pure Vows and Practices: because he has attained such a samādhi-door, there are no among all dharmas in which he does not attain profound samādhis.

At that time, because she had heard the Dharma, the maiden Kanyā Samantaprabhāśrī immediately attained a samādhi named Invincible Ocean-Treasury of Wisdom and became non-retrogressive in her progress toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

"At that time, the prince, together with the young woman and their retinue, heard the Dharma and attained benefit. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him countless times, took their leave, and returned to the palace to visit his father, the king."
Having arrived, he prostrated at the King’s feet and addressed him, saying:

“Great King, you should know that the Tathāgata Sūryagātra has appeared in the world. Not long ago, within the Bodhimaṇḍa of Dharma-Cloud Radiance, beside the Fragrant Sprout Cloud-Peak Garden in this kingdom, he attained equal and perfect enlightenment.”
At that time, King Dhanapati, suddenly hearing these words, asked the prince:
"Who told you such a thing? Was it a deva?"
"Is it a human being?
The Prince replied, "It was spoken by this maiden, Kanyāśrīsampadā."
When the king heard this, he was filled with immeasurable joy, like a poor man who has discovered a great hidden treasure. He thought to himself:

"The Buddha is the unsurpassed jewel; his appearance in the world is rare and difficult to encounter. If one is fortunate enough to behold him, they will surely sever all afflictions and evil karma, and shall not fall into the perilous paths of birth and death."
The Tathāgata appears in the world as the Great King of Physicians, able to cure the grave illnesses of the afflictions of sentient beings;
the Tathāgata appears in the world as the Great Bright Lamp, able to shatter the dark ignorance of sentient beings;
the Tathāgata appears in the world as the Great Guide, able to lead sentient beings to the secure abode of all-knowledge.

Having formed this thought, he beat the drums to proclaim his decree to the minor kings, the assembly of ministers, his retinue, as well as the kṣatriyas, brahmins, elders, and householders, and to all the people of the cities and villages, commanding them to assemble and addressing them thus:
"You should know that the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is rare and difficult to encounter; I now wish to go to approach, pay homage to, and revere him."

At that time, the king immediately abdicated the throne in favor of the crown prince; having completed the consecration ceremony, he went together with his retinue of ten thousand people to the site of enlightenment to visit the Tathāgata.
Having arrived, he prostrated himself, circumambulated [the Buddha] a hundred thousand times, and withdrew to sit at one side together with his retinue.

At that time, the Tathāgata surveyed the assembly in the place of enlightenment as well as the King Dhanapati and his retinue. From the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, he emitted a great radiance called "The Lamp Illuminating the Minds of All Sentient Beings. It shone universally throughout immeasurable worlds in the ten directions and stood before all the lords of the world, manifesting the various inconceivable buddha-activities of the Tathāgata and performing vast, divine transformations so that the minds of those sentient beings ready for conversion might attain purity.

At that time, the Tathāgata, by means of his inconceivable and sovereign spiritual power, manifested a body of supreme height and magnitude surpassing all worlds. With a perfect voice that universally accords with the ocean of all languages, he preached for the great assembly a gateway of dhāraṇī named "The Lamp Free from Obscuration that Enters the Meaning of All Dharmas," accompanied by a retinue of dhāraṇī gateways as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field.
At that time, having heard this, the king immediately attained the great light of wisdom regarding all dharmas.

Within that assembly, there were bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms of Jambudvīpa who simultaneously realized the *dhāraṇī* gate of the lamp that dispels obscurations and enters into the meaning of all dharmas; sixty nayutas of sentient beings exhausted all outflows and their minds attained liberation; ten thousand sentient beings became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye; and immeasurable sentient beings resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, the Tathāgata again, by means of his inconceivable power, universally manifested great spiritual transformations throughout all worlds in the ten directions, teaching and transforming sentient beings through the Dharma of the Three Vehicles.
At that time, because King Dhanapati’s mind was illuminated by the light of the Great Dharma, he had this thought:

"If I remain at home, I shall not be able to realize this profound flavor of the Dharma of merit; however, if the Buddha permits me to leave the household life and go forth, I shall surely achieve accomplishment in this Dharma."
Having formed this thought, he stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I now wish to draw near to the Tathāgata, to leave the household life, and to practice the Way.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"Follow your own inclination; you should know the time for yourself.

At that moment, King Dhanapati, together with his retinue of ten thousand people, simultaneously left the household life to study the Way under the Buddha. With diligent cultivation, before long, they all attained the *dhāraṇī* gate of the "Lamp Free from Obscuration Entering the Meaning of All Dharmas," as well as the various gates of samādhi mentioned above.
Furthermore, they attain the ten gates of bodhisattva supernormal powers;
furthermore, they enter the gate of the bodhisattvas' boundless eloquence;
furthermore, they attain the unimpeded and pure body of a bodhisattva.
They go everywhere to the abodes of all Tathāgatas of the ten directions;
they listen to the subtle and wondrous Wheel of Dharma turned by the Buddhas, being able to receive and uphold it all without any forgetfulness or loss;
furthermore, they act as great Dharma masters for the Buddhas, extensively expounding all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings.
Furthermore, by means of their spiritual powers, they manifest bodies throughout the lands of the ten directions in accordance with the minds of sentient beings;

they serve as great lamps of illumination for all worlds, extolling the appearance of the Buddhas in the world, extolling the original vows and practices of the Buddhas, extolling the merits accumulated by the Buddhas, extolling the causes and conditions of the Buddhas' past lives, extolling the sovereign spiritual powers of the Buddhas, and upholding all the teachings of the Buddhas.

"At that time, on the fifteenth day, the Prince ascended the main hall and sat upon the lion throne, surrounded by his court ladies; the seven treasures of the wheel-turning monarch arrived spontaneously."
First is the wheel-treasure, named Unobstructed Movement with Spokes and Rim, adorned with a hundred thousand exquisite jewels and radiating the light of Jāmbūnada gold;
second is the elephant-treasure, named Vajra Mountain, possessing vast and great majestic power;
third is the horse-treasure, named Swift Wind.
Fourth is the jewel-treasure, named Cloud of the Sunlight Treasury;
fifth is the woman-treasure, named Auspiciousness Endowed with Splendor;
sixth is the steward-treasure, named Great Wealth.
The seventh was the Treasure of the General, named Vimalanetra;
thus these seven treasures suddenly appeared, and he was fully accomplished as a Wheel-Turning King, ruling over the four continents.
Possessing sovereign majesty and power, he governed through the transformation of the True Dharma, subduing all and bringing joy to every person.

The king had a thousand sons who were handsome, brave, and robust; they possessed formidable power and prowess, and he had no enemies. His transformed realm was vast and wide, extending to the very limits of the great ocean; its ground was soft and supple, free from thorns and brambles, peaceful, prosperous, and free from all calamities and afflictions.

At that time, there were eighty-four thousand small royal capitals throughout Jambudvīpa; in each royal capital there was a monastic complex (*saṃghārāma*) numbering five hundred. Within each monastic complex, one hundred multi-storied pavilions (*kūṭāgāra*) were erected, surrounded on all four sides by circumambulatory corridors, amidst lush and verdant groves, where they observed the winter and summer retreats (*varṣā*).
The places for walking meditation were all adorned with various jewels, and every necessity for life was fully provided.

Furthermore, within each monastery, shrines (caityas) dedicated to the Buddha were established; they were all lofty, vast, and exquisitely adorned. Within those cities, everyone invited the Tathāgata to receive offerings of inconceivable flowers, incense, banners, canopies, and wonderful jeweled silks.
At that time, the Tathāgata accepted their invitation; by his power of mastery, his body entered all royal capitals, causing immeasurable sentient beings to plant various roots of goodness,
immeasurable sentient beings to attain purity of mind,
and immeasurable sentient beings to give rise to a heart of joy.
Innumerable sentient beings increase their love and respect;

innumerable sentient beings swiftly give rise to the mind of great enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), extensively benefiting all classes of beings through great compassion, diligently practicing all the true dharmas of the Buddhas, and being able to penetrate and enter every practice they cultivate as they dedicate it toward the path of the Buddhas' omniscience (*sarvajñatā*);
they thoroughly comprehend the profound ocean of the Buddhas' Dharma and universally enter the non-discriminative wisdom of the three periods of time.

Universally illuminating the realms of all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, they know the sequential order of the appearance of all Buddhas in the world; they attain the skillful means of the seed-intelligence (*jñāna*) of all Buddhas, and are adept at taming and transforming all sentient beings.

They initiate the vast practices and vows of Bodhisattvas, purify all Bodhisattva paths, abide in the nature of the Bodhisattvas' impartial wisdom, enter the great gate of the Buddhas' inexhaustible eloquence, and turn the pure, unobstructed wheel of Dharma of the Buddhas. They universally manifest their bodies throughout all lands, standing before all sentient beings, knowing the faculties, inclinations, and understandings of those beings, as well as the various oceans of their minds, and accordingly taming and bringing them all to maturity.

At that time, the Universal Monarch Mahātejas and all those within the royal capital city were able to behold the Tathāgata Sūryavarcas displaying various inconceivable great supernormal powers, thus bringing such sovereign, vast, and beneficial benefits.
“Good son, what do you think?

Was that prince Mahātejas, who at that time received the consecration from his father the king, ascended the throne as a wheel-turning monarch, and made offerings to the Buddha, anyone else? It was none other than myself.”
The World-Honored One, Vairocana Tathāgata, is he.
As for that father-king named Dhanapati at that time, could he be anyone else?
He is none other than the present Ratnakusuma-prabha Tathāgata.

That Buddha currently resides beyond world-oceans as numerous as the atoms within an ocean of worlds in the eastern direction. There is a world-ocean named Clouds of Reflected Images of the Dharmadhātu and Space, and within that ocean of worlds, there is a world-system named Mani King Universally Manifesting the Images of the Three Times.

Within that world-system, there is a world named Buddha-Perfect-Lamp. In that world, there is a site of enlightenment named Banner of the Reflected Bodies of All World-Leaders, where the Tathāgata Jewel-Flower-Radiance has attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

He is surrounded by an assembly of bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of buddha-fields; within this great assembly, he turns the wheel of the true Dharma, causing immeasurable sentient beings to reach full maturity.

When that Buddha was practicing as a bodhisattva in the past, he cultivated and adorned this ocean of worlds. All those Buddhas who have attained perfect enlightenment and appeared in the world throughout the past, future, and present within that ocean of lands were all transformed and delivered by that Buddha Ratnakusumaprabha; it was he who first caused them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and ultimately brought them to full maturity.
Good son! Was the first consort of King Dhanapati, the mother of Prince Mahāteja, named Padmaśrīgarbha, anyone other than this person?

This present Mother of Buddhas, Lady Māyā, has attained the unimpeded liberation of the light of illusory wisdom; she contains within her body the birth of all Buddhas of the past and future, and it is she who has now given birth here in this realm to the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Vairocana.
Was the mother of the girl Yaśovatī at that time, named Sujātā, anyone else?
She was none other than my own mother, the lady Sunetra of the Śākya clan, who now holds a staff.
"Good son! As for the retinue of that Universal Monarch Mahātejas at that time, could they have been anyone else?
They are none other than all the bodhisattvas currently present in the assembly of the Buddha, the World-Honored One."

In this way, these bodhisattvas have fully cultivated and gathered all the practices of Samantabhadra and have perfectly accomplished the great vows of Samantabhadra; though they constantly remain here in this Buddha-assembly’s site of enlightenment, they are able to manifest universally in all worlds, abide in the equanimous samādhi of all bodhisattvas, and always behold all Buddhas directly before them.

They are able to hear and retain all the wheels of Dharma turned by the oceans of sublime voices of all Tathāgatas, which are equal to the realm of empty space; they abide in the power of wisdom that masters all phenomena, and their fame is heard throughout all Buddha-lands.
