Furthermore, I recall a past kalpa named Anupalabdha, during which I encountered eighty hundred thousand koṭi-nayuta Buddhas, Tathāgatas, whom I served and made offerings to.
I further recall an eon named Sublime Light, during which I encountered as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in Jambudvīpa, whom I served and made offerings to.
Furthermore, I recall a past kalpa named Unsurpassed Light (*Anabhyudgata-prabhā*), in which I encountered twenty Ganges-sands of Tathāgatas, whom I served and made offerings to.
Again, I recall a past kalpa named Supreme Auspiciousness (*Parama-śrī*), in which I encountered one Ganges-sand of Tathāgatas, whom I served and made offerings to.
Furthermore, I recall a past kalpa named Appearance of the Sun, in which I encountered eighty Ganges-sands of Tathāgatas, whom I served and made offerings to.
Again, I recall a past kalpa named Wandering of Supreme Nature, in which I encountered sixty Ganges-sands of Tathāgatas, whom I served and made offerings to.
Furthermore, I recall an eon named *Sudharmacandra*, during which I encountered and served seventy Ganges-sands of Tathāgatas, making offerings to them. Noble son!

Thus, as I recall kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I have never been separated from the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas. With various skillful means, I have reverently made offerings to them; from all those Tathāgatas, I have heard this Bodhisattva liberation of "Unobstructed Mindfulness and Pure Adornment. Having heard it, I have received and upheld it, practicing according to the teaching without ever forgetting it.

Regarding all the deeds performed by all those Tathāgatas of the past kalpas—from their initial generation of the mind until the exhaustion of the Dharma—I have, through the power of this liberation of pure adornment, recollected them in accordance with reality, making them clearly manifest before me. Holding them fast, I have practiced accordingly, observing them in every thought-moment without ever becoming weary or negligent.
“Good son! I know only this bodhisattva liberation of the pure adornment of unimpeded mindfulness.

As for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, who have emerged from the night of birth and death, who are brilliantly clear and lucid, and who are forever free from the darkness of delusion—[I do not know their ways].”
Once, while in deep sleep, his mind was free from all hindrances and his body experienced lightness and ease;

he attained pure awakening regarding the nature of all phenomena, decisively discerning the profound treasury of the sūtras and all difficult points concerning the definitive and non-definitive meanings.
He skillfully protected himself and others, constantly and diligently practicing the pure precepts of a bodhisattva, whether in gain or loss.
With a mind ever-equal, they skillfully give rise to supernormal powers and wondrous wisdom;
they accord with the various expedient means of the world, increasing their merit and wisdom without satiety; they exert great diligence to zealously cultivate the factors conducive to enlightenment;
they accumulate compassion without weariness; and they accomplish the Tathāgata’s ten powers and fearlessnesses. Ten...

Regarding these eight unique qualities of all Buddha-dharmas, which accord with and awaken all sentient beings, [the Bodhisattvas] practice with diligent effort day and night, having no other thoughts; how then could I know or describe their meritorious conduct?
"Good son! In this city of Kapilavastu, there is a teacher of boys named Viśvāmitra. Go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path."

At that time, because he had heard the Dharma, the youth Sudhana was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; his inconceivable roots of goodness grew rapidly. He prostrated at her feet, circumambulated her countless times, gazed up at her with earnest devotion, and then took his leave and departed.

At that time, Sudhana descended from the celestial palace and proceeded toward the city of Kapilavastu. He went to the place where Samantabhadra was, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him to the right, and with palms joined in reverence, stood to one side and said: "Noble One!

"I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice, nor how a bodhisattva should cultivate the bodhisattva path.
I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction; I pray that you will explain this to me."
Viśvāmitra replied, “Noble son!
There is a youth named Śāriputra who practices and studies the bodhisattva dharma-gate of the knowledge of letters.”
"You may question him; he will explain it for you.
At that time, Sudhana went to his place, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him countless times, and with palms joined before him, said: "Noble One!
I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice, nor how they should cultivate the bodhisattva path.
Having heard that the Holy One is well able to provide instruction and guidance, I pray that you will explain this to me.
Then, that youth said to Sudhana: "Noble son!
I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called 'Endowed with Perfect Knowledge of All Arts.'"
I constantly chant and maintain these seed-syllables (*akṣara*), which are as follows:

when chanting the syllable *A*, one is able to enter deeply into the gate of the *prajñāpāramitā* called "Manifesting the Meaning that All Dharmas are Fundamentally Unborn through the Supreme Power and Virtue of the Bodhisattva."
When pronouncing the syllable *ra*, one is able to enter deeply into the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Universally Manifesting the Subtle Understanding of Boundless Limits.
When pronouncing the syllable *pa*, one is able to enter deeply into the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Subtle Wisdom Universally Illuminating the Equal Limit of the Dharma Realm."
When pronouncing the syllable *ca*, one is able to enter deeply into a gate of the Prajñāpāramitā called "The Universal Wheel that Can Sever Differentiated Form.
When pronouncing the nasalized syllable *na*, one is able to enter deeply into a gate of the Prajñāpāramitā called "Realizing the Limit of Non-reliance and Non-abiding."
When pronouncing the syllable *la*, one can deeply enter the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Stainlessness through Abiding Apart from Name and Form.
When pronouncing the syllable *na*, one can deeply enter the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Expedient Means of Non-retrogression."
When pronouncing the syllable *ba* (pronounced as in "bā-mu-wo-fan"), one is able to enter deeply into a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called the "Vajra-Circle Maṇḍala.
When pronouncing the syllable *na*, one is able to enter deeply into a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called the "Universally Perfect Circle."
When pronouncing the syllable *sa* (pronounced like *shǎi shǐ wǒ fǎn*), one is able to enter deeply into a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Oceanic Treasury.
When pronouncing the syllable *va* (pronounced like *wú kě fǎn*), one is able to enter deeply into a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Universal Diligent Seeking for Birth and Abiding."
When pronouncing the syllable *Ṭa*, one is able to enter deeply into the gate of the Prajñāpāramitā called "The Full Moonlight of the Constellations.
When pronouncing the syllable *Ya* (pronounced with the retroflex *ya*), one is able to enter deeply into the gate of the Prajñāpāramitā called "The Accumulation of Distinctions."
When pronouncing the syllable *ṣṭa*, one is able to enter deeply into the gate of the *prajñāpāramitā* called "Universally Illuminating Radiance that Quells and Eliminates Afflictions."
When pronouncing the syllable KA (upper tone), one can deeply enter the gate of Prajñāpāramitā named "Uninterrupted Universal Cloud.
When pronouncing the syllable SA (pronounced as *suo-wo* in reverse), one can deeply enter the gate of Prajñāpāramitā named "Pouring Down a Great Rain."
When pronouncing the syllable *maṅ*, one is able to enter deeply into the gate of Prajñāpāramitā named "The Great Swift Manifestation of Various Colors Like Myriad High Peaks.

When pronouncing the syllable *ga* (pronounced with the *ka* and *a* sounds as in the word *gaka*), one is able to enter deeply into the gate of Prajñāpāramitā named "The Universal Accumulation of Wheels."
When pronouncing the letter *ṭha*, one can deeply enter a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Treasury of Equality and Non-discrimination in True Thusness.
When pronouncing the letter *ja*, one can deeply enter a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Pure Wandering Throughout the Ocean of Worlds."
When pronouncing the syllable *svā*, one can deeply enter the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Universal Recollection of All Adornments of the Buddhas.
When pronouncing the syllable *ḍa*, one can deeply enter the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Subtle Observation of All Multitudes of Dharmas."

When chanting the syllable "Śa" (pronounced as "shi-wo-fan"), one is able to enter deeply into the gate of the *prajñāpāramitā* called "The Radiance that Follows the Wheels of the Teachings of All Buddhas."
When pronouncing the syllable *kha*, one is able to enter deeply into the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Treasury of Wisdom Manifesting from the Ground.
When pronouncing the syllable *kṣa*, one is able to enter deeply into the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Treasury of Wisdom Born from the Cessation of the Ocean of All Karmas."
When pronouncing the syllable *sata*, one is able to enter deeply into the gate of the *prajñāpāramitā* called "Opening Pure Radiance to Eliminate All Obscurations of Delusion."
When pronouncing the syllable *nyā*, one can deeply enter the gate of Prajñāpāramitā named "The Gate of Wisdom for Transcending the World.

When pronouncing the syllable *hṛta* (with the third tone), one can deeply enter the gate of Prajñāpāramitā named "The Lamp of Wisdom of Selflessness and Absence of Persons for Benefiting Sentient Beings."
When pronouncing the syllable *ba* (pronounced with the *puo* and *wo* finals), one is able to enter deeply into a gate of the Prajñāpāramitā called "The Perfectly Adorned Palace of All.

When pronouncing the syllable *cha* (pronounced with the *che* and *zhe* finals, both high tones), one is able to enter deeply into a gate of the Prajñāpāramitā called "The Wheel of Universal Coverage, the Treasury of Increasing Expedient Practices."

When pronouncing the syllable *samaḥ*, one is able to enter deeply into the gateway of the *prajñāpāramitā* called the "Rotating Treasury that Manifestly Beholds All Buddhas in Accordance with the Ten Directions."
When pronouncing the syllable *Hvaḥ*, one can deeply enter the gate of the *prajñāpāramitā* called "The Ocean-Treasury Born from the Power of Skillful Means for Observing All Subtle Sentient Beings."
When pronouncing the syllable *ṭsa*, one can deeply enter the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "Spontaneously Entering the Ocean of All Meritorious Qualities.
When pronouncing the syllable *ga*, one can deeply enter the gate of Prajñāpāramitā called "The Firm Oceanic Treasury that Universally Sustains All Dharma Clouds."

When pronouncing the syllable *cha*, one is able to enter deeply into the gate of the *prajñāpāramitā* called "The Manifestation of All Buddhas of the Ten Directions through the Power of Vows, Which is Like Space."
When pronouncing the syllable *ṇa*, one is able to enter deeply into a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called the "Inexhaustible Realm of Entering the Boundary of the Syllable Wheel.
When pronouncing the syllable *pha*, one is able to enter deeply into a gate of Prajñāpāramitā called the "Ultimate Perfection of Teaching and Transforming Sentient Beings."
When pronouncing the syllable *ska*, one is able to enter deeply into the gate of prajñāpāramitā named "The Radiant Wheel of Universal Illumination of Unimpeded Eloquence within the Vast Treasury."
When pronouncing the syllable *iṣa*, one is able to enter deeply into the gate of Prajñāpāramitā named "Expounding the Wisdom of All Buddha-Dharmas.

When pronouncing the syllable *śca*, one is able to enter deeply into the gate of Prajñāpāramitā named "The Great Roar Pervading the Thunder of the Dharma throughout the Space-like Realm of All Sentient Beings."
When pronouncing the syllable *cha* (upper tone), one can deeply enter the gate of the *prajñāpāramitā* called "Expounding the Dharma of Non-Self to Open the Buddha’s Realm and Enlighten All Beings."
When pronouncing the syllable *ṭa*, one can deeply enter a gate of the Prajñāpāramitā called "The Treasury of the Differentiation of All Dharma-Wheels.
O son of good family!

When I chant these syllables, with these forty-two gateways to the *prajñāpāramitā* as the foremost, all chapters and phrases follow along without obstruction, enabling one to enter deeply into immeasurable and innumerable gateways to the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Sudhana said: "Noble One! How should one practice to attain this liberation?"
He replied: "Good son!
If bodhisattvas diligently cultivate ten dharmas and bring them to full perfection, they will be able to attain this bodhisattva liberation of 'Skillfully Knowing All Arts.'"
What are these ten? They are: being endowed with wisdom;

diligently seeking virtuous friends; being courageous and diligent; remaining free from all hindrances and delusions; maintaining pure right conduct; honoring the true teachings; contemplating the emptiness of the nature of phenomena; eliminating false views; cultivating the right path; and possessing true knowledge.

If bodhisattvas are fully endowed with these ten dharmas, they will be able to swiftly attain this liberation. Why is this? Because bodhisattvas, being possessed of wisdom, diligently seek out virtuous friends;

having seen them, they draw near to them, regarding them with joy, love, and reverence, conceiving of them as Buddhas. By virtue of drawing near to them, they constantly receive their instructions; because they receive these instructions, they are able to practice difficult deeds with courageous and vigorous diligence.
Having attained diligence, one is able to eliminate all unwholesome states through wholesome dharmas.

Because of the extinction of unwholesome states, all wholesome dharmas are brought to full completion; once these are perfected, one is able to distance oneself from all hindrances and delusions. Being free from all hindrances, body, speech, and mind attain great purity, which accords with right practice. Through this purity, one develops a sense of reverence toward the teachings of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Because of this reverence for the teachings, one diligently seeks to observe the emptiness and quiescence of all phenomena. Having realized the emptiness of phenomena, wherever the mind is directed, there is no obstruction. One deeply penetrates dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), abandons the view of causelessness, extinguishes the mind of false views, and cultivates the Right Path. Having entered the Right Path, one attains true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*); because of attaining true wisdom, one attains this liberation and realizes the profound *dharmadhātu*.
Sudhana spoke again:
"What is the name of this reality? He replied:
“Good son! These very words are called the truth.
Sudhana spoke again:
“What kind of speech is called true? He replied, “Good son!
"Not speaking falsely is what is called truth.
He asked again, "What is meant by not speaking falsely?"
Saṅgīti replied: "Those words are true;
their essence is eternally unchanging because it is of a constant, singular nature.
He spoke again:
"What is the nature of non-alteration? He replied: "Good son!..."
"Because one realizes the nature of phenomena through one's own direct realization.
He asked again:
"What are the characteristics of the nature of phenomena?"
"Are the dharma of the subject that understands and the object that is understood one or two? He replied, "Good son!..."
In this way, the Dharma realized by the Bodhisattva himself is neither one nor two.

By the power of this, he is able to benefit himself and others equally, just as the great earth can produce all things without any thought of self or other, or of subject and object in the act of benefiting. Yet the nature of that Dharma is neither with marks nor without marks; its essence is like space, difficult to know and difficult to comprehend.
“Good son! This Dharma is subtle and wondrous, difficult to proclaim through written words or speech. Why is this so?

Because it transcends the sphere of all letters; because it transcends the sphere of all speech; because it transcends the spheres of all activities of verbal karma; because it transcends the spheres of all conceptual proliferation, discrimination, and deliberation; because it transcends the spheres of all investigation, reflection, and calculation; because it transcends the spheres known by all ignorant sentient beings; because it transcends the spheres of all demonic activities associated with afflictions; because it transcends the sphere of all mind and consciousness; because it is without "this" or "that," without marks and detached from marks, transcending all spheres of falsehood; and because it dwells in the non-abiding, tranquil sphere of the noble ones.

"Good son! The realm of self-realization of those noble ones is without form or characteristics, without defilement or purity, without grasping or abandoning, and without turbidity or confusion; it is supremely pure, and its nature is eternally indestructible."
Whether the Buddhas appear in the world or do not appear in the world, the nature of the *dharmadhātu* remains eternally one in its essence.

Good son! For the sake of this Dharma, Bodhisattvas practice countless difficult practices; having attained the essence of this Dharma, they are well able to benefit all sentient beings, causing them to dwell in ultimate peace within this Dharma.

"Good son! This is reality; this is the non-differentiated characteristic; this is the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); this is the essence of all-knowledge; this is the inconceivable dharma-realm; this is the non-dual dharma-realm; this is the bodhisattva liberation that is perfectly complete through skill in all arts."
"Good son! I know only this liberation.

As for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, they are able to master all mundane and supramundane skillful dharmas, extraordinary talents, arts, scripts, and mathematics, comprehending them all without omission."
Furthermore, he is well-versed in medical prescriptions and incantations;

for all sentient beings afflicted by malevolent spirits, cursed by enemies or haters, deluded by sorcery and illusions, pursued by corpses, suffering from epilepsy, emaciation, or various poisons and diverse maladies, he is able to rescue them all and restore them to full health.
Furthermore, he was skilled in discerning rare treasures and exotic wares;

regarding gold, jade, pearls, shells, coral, lapis lazuli, *maṇi* gems, *śaṅkha* shells, crystal, agate, copper, iron, lead, tin, *kāsāra*, and all other such mineral deposits, he knew their origins, their diverse classifications, and their respective values.

Villages, towns, and nations; large and small capital cities; palaces, gardens, and groves; rocky crags, springs, marshes, and wetlands—in short, all places where people dwell—the Bodhisattva is able to provide protection and guidance for them according to their respective circumstances.

Furthermore, he knows that his body possesses six hundred and sixty-three marks; among these marks, he evaluates their relative excellence, discerns their associated suffering or joy, determines their auspiciousness or inauspiciousness, and distinguishes their length.
Though one may possess all the various marks, they do not equal a beautiful voice;
though one may possess many beautiful voices, they are not as good as superior merit.
Furthermore, one should understand that regarding the karma cultivated through this merit, its retribution may be transformed or not, and whether it is fixed or unfixed.

Furthermore, he was skilled in observing celestial phenomena and terrestrial geography, the *chan* and *wei* texts on yin and yang, the auspiciousness or misfortune of human physiognomy, the portents of malevolent stars, the formations of clouds and mists, the cries of birds and beasts, the movements of creatures between water and land, the signs of good or bad fortune, the abundance or scarcity of the year's harvests, and the security or peril of nations.
Thus, regarding all the arts and skills existing in the world, there is none that he has not mastered, having exhausted their very source and foundation.
Furthermore, he is able to discern the supramundane dharmas;

he correctly defines their names and clarifies their meanings, observing their essential characteristics. Regarding those that are subtle and profound, he provides definitive analysis and exposition, practicing in accordance with them. His wisdom enters therein, free from doubt and hindrance, without ignorance or darkness, without dullness, without distress, without sinking, and without anything that is not directly realized.
How then could I possibly know or describe his meritorious conduct? Good son!
In this kingdom of Magadha, there is a village named Arthavān.
Within that realm there is a city named Vardhana.
There dwells an upāsikā named Varagomin; go to her and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
Then, the youth Sudhana prostrated at the feet of Viśvāmitra, circumambulated him countless times, gazed up at him with deep reverence, and departed with a heart full of longing and devotion.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Vast and Profound, Scroll Thirty-one;
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, Vast and Profound, Scroll Thirty-two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā of Kaśmīra by Imperial Decree.
The Chapter on Entering the Sphere of the Inconceivable Liberation and the Vows and Practices of Samantabhadra.

At that time, the youth Sudhana proceeded by stages until he reached the village of Arthavatī in the city of Potalaka. Arriving at the dwelling of the laywoman Bhadrottamā, he prostrated at her feet, circumambulated her countless times, and stood to one side with palms joined in reverence.
He addressed him, saying: "Noble One!

I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice, nor how a bodhisattva should cultivate the bodhisattva path. I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction; I pray that you will explain this to me."
Bhadrajyotis replied: "Good son!

I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called the 'Inexhaustible Wheel of Non-Abiding. Having realized it for myself, I further explain it to others. Abiding within this great samādhi, I give rise to all dharmas as inexhaustible and non-abiding."

That is to say: the inexhaustible and non-abiding eye of the nature of all-knowledge; the inexhaustible and non-abiding ear of the nature of all-knowledge; the inexhaustible and non-abiding nose of the nature of all-knowledge; the inexhaustible and non-abiding tongue of the nature of all-knowledge; the inexhaustible and non-abiding body of the nature of all-knowledge; the inexhaustible and non-abiding mind of the nature of all-knowledge; the inexhaustible and non-abiding waves of merit of the nature of all-knowledge; the inexhaustible and non-abiding lightning-light of wisdom of the nature of all-knowledge; the inexhaustible and non-abiding wisdom that illuminates sentient beings of the nature of all-knowledge; and the inexhaustible and non-abiding swift supernormal powers of the nature of all-knowledge.
"Good son! I know only this liberation door of the inexhaustible wheel of non-abiding.
As for the inexhaustible dharma doors of the meritorious wisdom-practices and all unattached qualities of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, how could I possibly know or speak of them?"
"Good son! To the south of here there is a great city named Kṣetra; therein dwells an elder named Dṛḍhavimukti, whose profession is the selling of gold."
“Go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
At that time, Sudhana prostrated at the feet of Bhadrasena, circumambulated him countless times, gazed up at him with earnest devotion, and departed with a mind full of longing.

At that time, the youth Sudhana traveled south by stages until he reached that city. He went to the householder’s dwelling, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him to the right, and stood to one side with palms joined in reverence. He addressed him, saying:
"Noble One!..."

I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice or how they should cultivate the bodhisattva path. Having heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction and guidance, I pray that you will explain this to me.
The elder said: "Good son!
I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called 'Pure Adornment of Unattached Mindfulness.'"
Since I first attained this liberation, I have diligently sought the True Dharma at the abodes of all Buddhas throughout the worlds of the ten directions without ceasing. Good son!
I know only this liberation door of the pure adornment of unattached mindfulness.

As for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have attained fearlessness and roar like lions, who dwell securely in the vast and superior accumulation of merit and wisdom, and who awaken all beings with their great voice—how could I possibly know or describe such meritorious conduct and wisdom of these bodhisattvas?
"Noble son! In this very city there is an elder named Candraprabha (Moonlight), whose residence is constantly filled with radiance.
Go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path."
Then, the youth Sudhana prostrated at the feet of the elder, circumambulated him countless times, gazed upon him with deep reverence, and took his leave.

At that time, Sudhana proceeded to the dwelling of the elder Candracchattra; he prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him to the right, joined his palms in respectful salutation, stood to one side, and said: "Noble One!

I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path. Having heard that the Holy One is well able to provide instruction and guidance, I pray that you will explain this to me.
The Moon of Wondrous Virtue replied,
"Good son! I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called 'Stainless Wisdom Radiance'."
Sudhana said, "Noble One! How does one practice so as to attain this liberation?"
The elder said: "Good son!
If bodhisattvas can practice ten dharmas, they will be able to fully attain this liberation."
What are these ten? They are:
never abandoning or distancing oneself from spiritual friends;
They never abandon the recollection and vision of the Buddhas;
they never abandon the delight in hearing the true Dharma;
and they never abandon the practice of first greeting with kind intent, reverently making offerings, and serving the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends.
They never abandon the wisdom of extensive learning, nor their virtuous friends, Dharma masters, and those capable of preaching the Dharma;
they never abandon hearing about all the practices of the perfections (pāramitās);
and they never abandon hearing about all the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas).
They never abandon the three gates of liberation;
they never abandon the dharmas of the four sublime abodes;
and they never abandon the essence of omniscience.
“Good son! If bodhisattvas never abandon these ten dharmas, they will be able to attain this liberation door of the stainless light of wisdom.
Sudhana spoke again:
“Noble One! How does this gate of liberation manifest so that it may be realized?
The householder replied:
“Good son! You should now manifest the mind of the prajñāpāramitā and bring it into perfect correspondence; then, whatever you see and know, you will be able to realize and enter into it.”
Sudhana spoke again: "Noble One!
Is it by hearing the words and phrases of the Prajñāpāramitā that one realizes it through direct manifestation?"
He replied, “No. Why is that?”
“Because the Prajñāpāramitā perceives the true essence of all phenomena and brings them to direct realization.
Sudhana said: “Is it not by means of the wisdom born of hearing and the nature of the wisdom born of reflection that one sees True Suchness and attains personal realization?”
The householder replied,
"No. It is impossible that one could attain self-realization through hearing and reflection."
"Good son! Regarding this matter, I shall provide a parable; you should listen attentively:
Suppose there is a vast desert without springs or wells. During the heat of spring or summer, a man traveling from west to east encounters another man coming from the east and asks him:"
"I am now parched with heat and thirst; where is there water, and where is the cool shade of a tree?
I wish to drink, bathe, and rest therein to dispel this heat and thirst."
That Great Man, who was skilled in knowledge and skilled in exposition, addressed him, saying:
"From here, travel eastward; there are two roads, one to the left and one to the right."
"You should proceed with diligence along the right path; you will certainly reach the place of sweet springs and find shelter in its cool shade.
"Noble son, what do you think?"

"Would those who are parched with heat and thirst, even upon hearing the names of such springs and trees, and by reflecting on them and proceeding toward them, be able to eliminate their heat and thirst and attain coolness? He replied: "No."
"Why is this? It is because one must rely on the path shown to reach that spring and pool; only by bathing and drinking there can the feverish thirst be removed, and one attain coolness. "Good son!"
The Bodhisattva is likewise; it is not by means of the wisdom derived from hearing and reflection alone that they are able to realize and enter all Dharma-gates.
Good son! What is called "sandy desert" refers to birth and death (saṃsāra).
Those who come from the West refer to all sentient beings; "heat" refers to their various delusions, and "thirst" refers to their craving and attachment.
Those great men who come from the East and know the Way are the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; they abide in omniscience and have attained the true nature of phenomena—the reality of equality.
Their obtaining of pure water and being free from heat and thirst signifies their own realization of the ultimate truth.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
I shall now speak another parable for you; you should listen attentively.
Son of good family!"

Suppose the Tathāgata were to remain for the duration of a kalpa, employing various skillful means and eloquent speech to describe to the people of Jambudvīpa how the celestial *sūda* possesses every excellence—its soft and wondrous texture, its color, fragrance, and exquisite flavor.
"What do you think?
When those sentient beings hear, receive, and contemplate this in such a manner, do they know the flavor of heaven? He replied:
"No," said Candrottara, "it is likewise here:
one can realize and enter the true nature of prajñā not merely through hearing and reflection."
Sudhana spoke again:
"How does a bodhisattva skillfully proclaim the teachings so that all sentient beings may truly realize them?
Candracchattra replied:
“Good son! The true nature of prajñā realized by bodhisattvas is the definitive correct cause for those verbal expressions;
because they have realized this liberation, they are able to skillfully proclaim it for the sake of sentient beings.”
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva is endowed with ten dharmas, they attain this liberation. What are these ten? First, distancing oneself from all unwholesome dharmas;

second, not contravening the precepts established by the Tathāgata; third, distancing oneself from all stinginess and envy; fourth, making offerings to all Tathāgatas; fifth, diligently cultivating all meritorious deeds; sixth, being fully endowed with wisdom; seventh, being fully endowed with skillful means; eighth, being fully endowed with great vows; ninth, being fully endowed with wearying detachment; and tenth, being fully endowed with diligence.
If bodhisattvas are endowed with ten dharmas, they realize this liberation.
Son of good family!

I know only this bodhisattva liberation door of the stainless light of wisdom; as for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who cultivate various gates of bodhisattva wisdom, constantly applying diligent attention, performing unsurpassed deeds, with minds that are upright, natures that are harmonious and supple, always delighting in tranquility, dwelling securely in great compassion, not departing from the world yet having no attachment in their hearts, never seeking recompense for whatever they do, always mindful of the vast realms of all Buddhas, always contemplating the true and wondrous Dharma of all Buddhas, always delighting in associating with the assembly of bodhisattvas, always practicing the various pāramitās of bodhisattvas, always abiding in the stages realized by bodhisattvas, and always observing the powers, fearlessnesses, and unique buddha-dharmas of the Tathāgatas.
Having entered the immeasurable ocean of great samādhis and attained the ultimate liberation through the gateway of the true Dharma, how could I possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct?
"Noble son! To the south of here there is a city named Mahānirghoṣa. There dwells an elder named Ajitasena.
Go to him and ask: 'How should a bodhisattva learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path?'"
At that time, Sudhana prostrated at the feet of Candracchattra, circumambulated him countless times, gazed up at him with earnest devotion, and departed with a heart full of longing.

At that time, the youth Sudhana, reflecting upon the liberation of the light of wisdom he had attained, traveled south by stages toward that great city. Arriving at the householder’s residence, he prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him to the right, and standing respectfully with palms joined, addressed him from one side, saying: "Noble One!"

I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice, nor how they should cultivate the bodhisattva path. Having heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction and guidance, I pray that you will explain this to me.
The elder replied, "Good son!
I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called 'Inexhaustible Aspect'."
"Because I have realized this gate of liberation, I see immeasurable Buddhas and have attained an inexhaustible treasury.
Sudhana spoke again:
"How does a bodhisattva attain this liberation?"
He replied: "Good son!
If a bodhisattva can diligently cultivate ten dharmas, they will be able to realize such liberation."
What are the ten? First, one should dwell in seclusion and quietude to deeply contemplate the five desires, for the purpose of cultivating various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*);
second, one should diligently apply skillful means to enter various *samādhis*, in order to universally manifest form-bodies to transform sentient beings.
Third, one should observe with wisdom that saṃsāra and nirvāṇa share the same single characteristic;
fourth, one should diligently cultivate firm power of mindfulness so as to know what is wholesome and unwholesome without forgetfulness;
fifth, one should diligently accumulate the merits of a bodhisattva, never feeling satiated with the path of the pāramitās.
Sixth, one should diligently plant the forest trees of pure precepts, so as to constantly sport within the garden of the Dharma;
seventh, one should diligently rescue and protect sentient beings with evil views, so that they may transcend deviant paths and abide in right view;
eighth, one should diligently bestow various medicinal herbs of the Dharma, so as to eliminate the diseases of affliction in sentient beings.
Ninth, one should diligently observe that all phenomena of the three periods of time are like dreams and illusions, so as to remain free from defiled attachment;
tenth, one should diligently refute the false doctrines of external paths, so that heterodox views do not harm sentient beings.
If bodhisattvas diligently seek and cultivate these ten dharmas, they will be able to realize such liberation;
furthermore, they will attain mastery in entering and emerging from countless hundreds of thousands of dharma-gates.
Furthermore, good son!
If a bodhisattva can distance himself from ten things, he will attain this liberation. What are these ten?
First, staying far away from all individuals who violate the various precepts;
second, staying far away from all individuals who violate right views;
third, staying far away from all individuals who violate proper deportment.
Fourth, they distance themselves from all individuals who live by wrong livelihood;
fifth, they distance themselves from all individuals who engage in miscellaneous worldly discourse;
sixth, they distance themselves from all individuals who are indolent and lazy.
Seventh, they distance themselves from all individuals who are attached to sensual pleasures;
eighth, they distance themselves from all individuals who constantly delight in associating with householders in white robes;
ninth, they distance themselves from all individuals, whether monastics or householders, who delight in cultivating false merit and do not abide in right practice.
Tenth, they distance themselves from those individuals who are far removed from all deep and heavy afflictions, whose bodies and minds are negligent, and who cannot be admonished or restrained.

If Bodhisattvas can always distance themselves from these ten kinds of unwholesome persons, yet do not harbor feelings of aversion or abandonment toward them, nor give rise to thoughts of inferiority regarding them, but instead regard them with compassion and accept them for the sake of their training and subduing.

The Bodhisattva further reflects that all sentient beings dwelling within the cycle of birth and death, by associating with such unwholesome persons, destroy their roots of goodness and fall into evil realms; therefore, they should always remain far removed from all evil people.
"Good son! This is how a bodhisattva, by remaining far removed from ten things, is able to realize such liberation. Good son!"

I know only this liberation door of the inexhaustible sign; as for the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, who take great compassion as their foremost priority, initiate all practices, and bring to manifestation all the power of their past vows; who resolutely and diligently seek the wisdom of all-knowledge; who accumulate and adorn various Buddha-lands; and who profoundly contemplate the essential nature of all phenomena—[I do not know their ways].

They constantly and joyfully strive to seek all the powers, fearlessnesses, and unique buddha-dharmas of all Tathāgatas, as well as their marks, secondary characteristics, and perfect voices, up to and including all supreme merits, realizing them all through direct manifestation. They are able to accord with and understand the profound liberation of all Tathāgatas, skillfully entering into all expedient means. Knowing that the nature of all sentient beings, self, person, life-span, individual, nourisher, and *pudgala*, as well as the aggregates, bases, and elements, is entirely empty and quiescent, they remain free from attachment.
They are always able to benefit and bring happiness to all the world, causing it to be peaceful and secure, free from all afflictions;
and they constantly and diligently delight in the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).
They constantly and diligently rescue and protect all sentient beings;

they constantly and diligently honor all true dharmas, delighting in hearing the Dharma and practicing in accordance with it. They are able to benefit sentient beings through correct teaching, causing them all to abide in peace and happiness and not enter the worldly realms. Abiding in supreme diligence that continues without interruption, they dwell in non-retrogression and undefiled conduct. Fully endowed with the path of vast and impartial wisdom, they vow to deliver sentient beings, remaining invincible to any who would seek to subdue them.
How could I possibly know or describe such meritorious wisdom-practices of a bodhisattva? Good son,
to the south of this city there is a village named Dharma;
“There is a brahmin named Most Tranquil.
Go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path.
Then, the youth Sudhana prostrated at the feet of Anābhibhū, circumambulated him countless times, gazed up at him with earnest devotion, and departed with deep longing.

At that time, the youth Sudhana, contemplating and recollecting the liberation door of the inexhaustible marks, proceeded by stages until he reached that village and approached the brahmin Most Tranquil.
Having seen him, he prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him, and stood with palms joined in reverence.
He addressed him, saying: "Noble One!

I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not yet know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva practice or how they should cultivate the bodhisattva path. Having heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction and guidance, I pray that you will explain this to me.
At that time, the brahmin said to Sudhana:
"Noble son! I have attained a bodhisattva liberation called 'Speech of Sincere Vows'."
By virtue of this sincere vow and truthful speech, all bodhisattvas shall never regress from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
there has been no regression in the past, there is no regression in the present, and there shall be no regression in the future.

"Good son! Because I abide by these words of truthful majesty and sincere aspiration, regarding all activities within both mundane and supramundane dharmas, there is nothing that is not accomplished; whatever is sought according to one's wishes, all shall be brought to fulfillment."
Sudhana said, "Noble One! What is the meaning of this liberation of true majesty called 'Speech of Sincere Vows'?"
The brahmin said: "O son of good family!

That which is truly the word of aspiration is the meaning of suchness, the meaning of non-alteration, the meaning of non-dual essence, the ultimate meaning, the meaning of truth, and the meaning of the dharma-body of the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time."
Sudhana spoke again:
"How do all bodhisattvas practice so as to attain this Dharma-body? He replied:
“Good son! If a bodhisattva can cultivate ten kinds of dharmas, they will fully and perfectly attain this Dharma-body. What are these ten?
That is to say:

the body of equality, the pure body, the inexhaustible body, the body of cultivated accumulation, the body of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the body free from applied and sustained thought, the inconceivable body, the tranquil body, the space-like body, and the body of wondrous wisdom.
"If Bodhisattvas are endowed with these ten bodies, they shall attain the Tathāgata’s pure Dharma-body.
Sudhana spoke again: "Noble One!"
"In what stage do the bodhisattvas, dwelling in this liberation, attain these ten bodies?
The brahmin replied, "Noble son!"
In the first stage of a bodhisattva, by abiding in this liberation, one attains an equal body.
Why is this? Because one penetrates the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), is free from all crookedness, and perceives the equality of all phenomena.
In the second stage of the bodhisattva, one dwells in this liberation and attains a purified body. Why is this?
Because, being free from the defilement of transgressing precepts, one’s nature of all precepts is eternally pure.
In the third stage of the bodhisattva, by abiding in this liberation, one attains an inexhaustible body. Why is this?
Because one has abandoned the unwholesome dharmas of desire, anger, stinginess, and envy, and dwells in various supreme concentrations.
In the fourth stage of the bodhisattva, one who abides in this liberation attains the cultivation and accumulation of the body. Why is this?
Because they constantly and diligently cultivate and accumulate all the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) of all Buddhas.
In the fifth stage of the bodhisattva, one dwells in this liberation and attains the dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*). Why is this?
Because by observing and awakening to the principles of all truths, one realizes the essential nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-svabhāva*).
The Bodhisattva in the sixth stage, abiding in this liberation, attains a body free from applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).
Why is this? Because the principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is difficult to understand and difficult to know; it is not within the domain of applied and sustained thought.
In the seventh stage of the bodhisattva, one dwells in this liberation and attains an inconceivable body. Why is this?
Because they have accumulated all the Buddha-dharmas, possess skillful means, and have fulfilled their practice of wisdom.
In the eighth stage of the bodhisattva, one dwells in this liberation and attains a body of tranquility. Why is this?
Because all afflictions no longer manifest, and one is free from all worldly conceptual proliferations and such activities.
In the ninth stage of the bodhisattva, one dwells in this liberation and attains a body of space. Why is this?
Because the characteristics of the body are boundless, pervading all things.
The ten stages of the bodhisattva: by abiding in this liberation, one attains the body of wondrous wisdom. Why is this?
Because the subtle and sublime realm of all-knowledge is universally gathered and perfected therein.
Sudhana spoke again:
"What is the difference between the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata and those ten kinds of Dharma-bodies of the bodhisattvas? He replied:
“Good son! You should know that while the essence and nature of the Dharma-body are without difference, there are distinctions in its merits and majestic power.
Sudhana spoke again:
"What is the meaning of this? He replied, "Good son!
This refers to the fact that the dharma-bodies of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are equal and without distinction.
Why is this? Because the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are equal, being of one and the same essence.

In this way, even such distinctions as ordinary beings and sages, delusion and awakening, defilement and purity, cause and effect, coming and going, and advancing and retreating, are all of one and the same characteristic.

As for what is called the difference in merit and power, it is that the body of the Tathāgata is perfected in merit and possesses supreme power, whereas the Bodhisattva is not so; for this reason, I shall now proclaim a parable for you to reveal its meaning.

Good son! It is like a wondrous maṇi jewel or a pearl that, before being carved, polished, and refined by a skilled artisan, lacks luster; those who see it do not conceive a sense of love or esteem for it. However, once it has been polished and refined, its luster becomes brilliant and intense, and it is held in high esteem as a treasure by humans and devas. Although the substance of the pearl remains unchanged, this is due to the difference in their respective characteristics.

Although all bodhisattvas share the same essential nature as the body of a Tathāgata and are both termed "Dharmakāya," it cannot be said that their inconceivable, pure jewels of merit and wisdom, nor their supernormal powers and majestic authority, are equal to those of a Tathāgata.

Why is this so? Because all Tathāgatas, throughout incalculable eons, have purely cultivated all subtle and wondrous merits until they are ultimately perfected, boundless and immeasurable like the great void, filling the worlds of the ten directions. These merits are wondrously good and pure, free from the defilements of delusion; they are vast and luminous, shining everywhere, and their supreme power universally delivers sentient beings. Although these Bodhisattvas possess the Dharma-body, their merits are not yet complete, for they still possess residual defilements.
For example, from the first day to the fifteenth day of the waxing moon, although their substance and essence remain the same, their radiant appearances differ.
Why is this? Because there is a distinction between the states of being full and not yet full.
Good son! The Dharma-body of a bodhisattva and the Dharma-body of a Buddha are likewise so, because there is a distinction between their states of being full or not full.

The body of a bodhisattva is like the moon from the first day until the fourteenth day; its radiance cannot shine in perfect fullness. The Dharma-body of a Tathāgata is like the white moon on the fifteenth day, when it is perfectly full; its radiance shines everywhere, without limit or obstruction.

Furthermore, those ten kinds of Dharma-bodies of the Bodhisattvas share the same essential nature as the body of the Tathāgata; they possess no dual characteristics. However, because the merits cultivated differ, they cannot be said to be identical.
Therefore, good son! If bodhisattvas abide in this liberation and are endowed with the ten bodies, they will be able to realize the Dharma-body of the Buddhas, in which all merits are perfected.
"Furthermore, by means of ten meanings, a bodhisattva attains a vajra-like indestructible body. What are these ten?
First, because it cannot be destroyed by any afflictions or the poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion."
Second, because it cannot be destroyed by pride, stinginess, envy, false views, or perversions;
third, because it cannot be destroyed by any evil destinies, sufferings, or oppressions;
fourth, because it cannot be destroyed by gain or loss, defamation or praise, fame or insignificance, or suffering or pleasure.
Fifth, because it cannot be destroyed by birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, or affliction;
sixth, because it cannot be destroyed by any heterodox views, external paths, or false doctrines;
seventh, because it cannot be destroyed by the various māras of afflictions, the māra of the aggregates, or the māra of death.
Eighth, because it cannot be destroyed by any celestial Māras or their retinues;
ninth, because it cannot be destroyed by any Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas;
tenth, because it cannot be destroyed by any desirable objects of the world.
If a bodhisattva can fulfill these ten meanings, they will attain a body like that of the Buddhas— indestructible like a vajra.
"Good son, furthermore,
there are ten kinds of skillful right paths through which one can correctly understand them, free from erroneous explanations."

What are the ten? First, if there are sentient beings who should be disciplined by means of the Mahāyāna, he teaches them the various paths of the Bodhisattvayāna, and does not expound the path of the Śrāvakayāna for them.

2. If there are sentient beings who are to be tamed by means of the Śrāvaka Vehicle, he teaches them the various paths of the Śrāvaka Vehicle, and does not expound the path of the Bodhisattva Vehicle.

Third, if there are sentient beings who should be disciplined by means of the Buddha-vehicle, he teaches them the path of the Tathāgata’s omniscience, and does not expound the path of the Pratyekabuddha-vehicle.

Fourth, if there are sentient beings who should be tamed by means of the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, he teaches them various paths of the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, but does not expound the path of omniscience for them.

Fifth, if there are sentient beings who cling to a self and to phenomena, one preaches for them non-self and the emptiness of all phenomena, and does not speak of a self, a person, a sentient being, a life-span, a soul, a nourisher, a *pudgala*, a provisional self, or the path of phenomena.

Sixth, if there are sentient beings who cling to existence and non-existence, one preaches for them the Dharma that abides in the middle and is free from extremes, rather than preaching the Dharma of existence and non-existence which falls into extremes.
Seventh, if there are sentient beings whose minds are distracted, one preaches for them the tranquility of various *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, rather than preaching various paths of distraction.
8. If there are sentient beings who delight in worldly dharmas, one preaches for them the path of supramundane suchness-wisdom (*tathatājñāna*), and does not preach the path of ignorant infants.

9. If there are sentient beings who take pleasure in dwelling within birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), one preaches for them the path of nirvāṇa that transcends birth-and-death, and does not preach the path of abiding in the world to transform sentient beings.

Tenth: If there are sentient beings who cling to the emptiness of phenomena and so forth, and do not practice the right path, he preaches for them the straightforward Dharma free of thorns, and does not speak of the thorny, false, and perilous paths.
"Good son! If bodhisattvas possess these ten dharmas, they will enter the right path, be well able to understand that there is no false or erroneous teaching, and their speech will be truthful."
"Good son! I know only this bodhisattva liberation of dwelling in truthful speech and inexhaustible majestic virtue.

As for those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who never deviate from their conduct in accordance with truthful speech, whose minds always follow it without regression, who don the firm armor of the power of their original vows, and whose great compassion does not abandon sentient beings; [how can I know their practice?]"

Increasing merit and wisdom without weariness, skillful means manifest continuously; diligently cultivating the wisdom of the Ground of Increasing Radiance, awakening in accordance with the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, entering deeply among sentient beings, and knowing the right path well;

the bodhisattva’s ground-wisdom abides in the equanimous and pure mind of the past Buddha-dharma, abides in the equanimous and pure mind of the future Buddha-dharma, and abides in the equanimous and pure mind of the present Buddha-dharma.
Abiding in the mind of the equality and purity of the nature of precepts; abiding in the mind of the equality and purity of the nature of the mind;
abiding in the mind of the equality and purity of the nature of views; abiding in the mind of the equality and purity of the nature that can sever the doubts of oneself and others;
and abiding in the mind of the equality and purity of the wisdom-nature regarding all right and wrong paths.
They abide in a mind that is equal and pure through the practice of the path of cultivation which extinguishes delusions;
they abide in a mind that is equal and pure through the superior cultivation of all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*);
they abide in a mind that is equal and pure through the vast compassionate transformation that subdues all sentient beings; and their speech is always sincere, never false.
"Delusion gives rise to immeasurable gates of merit and wisdom; how could I possibly know or explain them? Good son!"
To the south of here there is a city named Sumanāmukha; in it there is a boy named Guṇākara and also a girl named Guṇavatī.
"Go to him and ask how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct and cultivate the bodhisattva path.

At that time, the youth Sudhana conceived a heart of deep reverence for this great Dharma; he prostrated at the feet of the brahmin, circumambulated him countless times, gazed up at him with earnest devotion, and departed with single-minded longing.

At that time, the youth Sudhana, having received this great Dharma from the brahmin Paramaśānta and having perfumed his mind with it, traveled south by stages until he reached the city of Sumanāmukha. There he beheld the youth Guṇakara and the maiden Guṇavatī; he prostrated at their feet, circumambulated them countless times, and stood before them with palms joined.
He addressed him, saying: "Noble One!

I have already set my mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I do not know how a bodhisattva should learn the bodhisattva conduct or how one should cultivate the bodhisattva path. I have heard that the Noble One is well able to provide instruction; I only pray that you will, out of compassion, explain this for me."
Then the boy and girl said to Sudhana:
"Noble son! We have realized the bodhisattva liberation called 'Abiding as an Illusion'."

Having attained this liberation and brought it to full perfection, one uses this pure wisdom to universally observe all phenomena, seeing that there is nothing that is not an illusory dwelling, accomplished through illusion.
That is to say:
seeing that all worlds abide as illusions, because they are produced by causes and conditions;
seeing that all sentient beings abide as illusions, because they arise from karma and afflictions.
One sees that all worlds are like a magical illusion (*māyā-vihāra*), because they arise through the successive conditions of ignorance, craving, and so forth;
one sees that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are like a magical illusion, because they are produced by various illusory conditions such as the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*);
one sees that all three periods of time are like a magical illusion, because they are produced by inverted cognition such as the view of self.

He sees that all sentient beings—subject to birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and affliction—are dwelling in illusion; they were originally non-existent but now exist, being false and unsubstantial, produced by the conceptualization and discrimination of deluded thoughts.
He sees that all buddha-lands are dwelling in illusion, produced by the inversions of thought, mind, and view, and by ignorance.
He sees that all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are dwelling in illusion, accomplished through the discrimination of wisdom and abandonment.

One sees that all bodhisattvas dwell as illusions, for they are accomplished through the continuous manifestation of their own self-discipline, the ripening of sentient beings, and the dharmas of their various practices and vows;

one sees that all Buddhas and the assemblies of bodhisattvas, along with their transformations, supernormal powers, majestic authority, and all their activities, dwell as illusions, for they are accomplished through the habitual perfuming of various modes of understanding, practices, vast vows, and wisdom.

"Good son! The self-nature of illusory phenomena is inconceivable. We two can only know this liberation of dwelling in illusion; as for the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who skillfully enter the net of boundless illusory affairs and, in accordance with them, fully understand the wisdom produced by illusion—how could we possibly know or describe their meritorious conduct?"

At that time, after the youth Śrīsaṃbhava and the maiden Guṇavatī had spoken of their own liberation, through the power of inconceivable roots of goodness, they caused Sudhana’s body to grow rapidly, becoming supple and radiant, and addressed him, saying:
"O son of good family!
In this southern direction, near the gateway to the ocean, there is a land called Kṣetravatī;
in that land there is a garden named Mahāvyūha, and within it is a vast, lofty pavilion named Vairocanavyūhagarbha.

It arises from the various fruits of the Bodhisattva’s roots of goodness; it arises from the various powers of the Bodhisattva’s mindfulness, vows, mastery, and supernormal knowledges; it arises from the various skillful means of the Bodhisattva; and it arises from the various merits and wisdom of the Bodhisattva.

"Good son! A bodhisattva who dwells in the inconceivable liberation, out of great compassion, universally manifests such realms for the sake of all sentient beings and extensively brings forth such adornments."
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya dwells therein for the purpose of gathering and sustaining those born in his original realm—his parents, kinsmen, and all the people—to bring them to maturity;
furthermore, he desires that those beings of similar kind who share the same birth and the same practice may attain firm stability within the Mahāyāna;
and he further desires that all those sentient beings, according to their respective stages and their original roots of goodness, may all be brought to full maturity.
Furthermore, it is because I wish to reveal to you the liberation-gates of bodhisattvas;
to reveal how bodhisattvas pervade all places and possess mastery over taking birth according to the power of their original vows;
and to reveal how bodhisattvas manifest before all sentient beings in various bodies to provide instruction and awakening, constantly teaching and transforming them.
It demonstrates that Bodhisattvas, through the power of great compassion, universally gather all worldly resources to bestow them upon sentient beings without weariness;
it demonstrates that Bodhisattvas fully cultivate all practices, knowing that all practices are free from all signs;
it demonstrates that Bodhisattvas take birth in various places, understanding that all births are signless.

Go to him and ask: how does a bodhisattva practice the bodhisattva conduct? How does one cultivate the bodhisattva path? How does one study the bodhisattva precepts? How does one purify the bodhisattva mind? How does one generate the bodhisattva vows? How does one gather the requisites for the bodhisattva's aids to enlightenment? How does one enter the stage of the bodhisattva’s sovereign mastery? How does one fulfill the bodhisattva perfections? How does one attain the bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena? How does one become endowed with the qualities of a bodhisattva? And how does one serve the spiritual friends of the bodhisattvas?
Why is this? Good son!

Those Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have deeply entered all bodhisattva practices and vows; they accord with the mental natures of all sentient beings and constantly manifest before them in all places. Having taught and tamed those bodhisattvas, having fulfilled all pāramitās, having dwelled in all bodhisattva stages, having realized all bodhisattva patiences, having entered all bodhisattva positions, having received the bestowal of the complete prediction of enlightenment, having traversed all bodhisattva realms, having entered the gates of bodhisattva liberation, and having attained the spiritual powers of all Buddhas, they receive from all Tathāgatas of the ten directions the consecration upon their crowns with the ambrosial Dharma-water of omniscience.

“Good son! That spiritual friend can moisten all your roots of goodness; can increase your bodhicitta; can solidify your vast resolve; can initiate all your virtues; can grow your bodhisattva faculties; can instruct you in the unobstructed Dharma; can cause you to enter the stage of Samantabhadra; can cause you to abide in the vows of a bodhisattva; can cause you to practice the conduct of Samantabhadra; can explain for you the merits accomplished through the immeasurable practices and vows of all bodhisattvas; and can cause you to manifest the sovereign dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.”

"Good son! You should not now cultivate a single root of goodness, illuminate a single dharma-gate, make a single great vow, receive a single prediction of enlightenment, or abide in a single patience, thereby conceiving the thought that you have reached the ultimate;
nor should you practice the most supreme perfections with a limited mind."
One should not dwell in the perfection of the ten bodhisattva stages with a limited mind;
one should not purify all buddha-fields with a limited mind;
and one should not serve and make offerings to spiritual friends with a limited mind.
Why is this? Son of good family!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should plant immeasurable roots of goodness and should gather immeasurable aids to the path.
Endowed with these, one should cultivate immeasurable causes for enlightenment; one should study immeasurable skillful dedications; one should transform immeasurable realms of sentient beings;
one should illumine the minds of immeasurable sentient beings; one should know the faculties of immeasurable sentient beings;
one should recognize the inclinations of immeasurable sentient beings; one should awaken immeasurable sentient beings; and one should discipline [them].
One should subdue immeasurable sentient beings; one should sever immeasurable afflictions; one should purify immeasurable karmic habits;
one should extinguish immeasurable false views; one should eliminate immeasurable defiled minds; one should give rise to immeasurable pure minds;
one should extract immeasurable poisonous arrows of suffering; one should dry up immeasurable oceans of craving and desire; one should...
One should shatter the immeasurable darkness of ignorance; one should demolish the immeasurable mountains of self-conceit; one should untie the immeasurable bonds of birth and death;
one should cross over the immeasurable currents of existence; one should dry up the immeasurable ocean of rebirth;
one should cause immeasurable sentient beings to emerge from the mire of the five desires; and one should cause immeasurable sentient beings to depart from the three [poisons].
Within the prison of the realms, one should establish immeasurable sentient beings upon the Noble Path;
one should dissolve immeasurable courses of greedy desire, extinguish immeasurable courses of hatred, and crush immeasurable courses of delusion;
one should break through immeasurable snares of Māra, abandon immeasurable works of Māra, and purify the [vows] of the Bodhisattvas.
With a mind of measureless aspiration, one should cultivate the measureless skillful means of a bodhisattva; one should give rise to the measureless superior faculties of a bodhisattva;
one should arouse the measureless resolute understanding of a bodhisattva; one should realize the measureless essence of equality of a bodhisattva;
one should purify the measureless supreme merits of a bodhisattva; one should discipline the measureless... of a bodhisattva.
One should measure the ocean of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); one should fulfill the immeasurable pure practices of a bodhisattva;
one should manifest the immeasurable worldly activities of a bodhisattva; one should accord with the immeasurable skillful means of a bodhisattva;
one should give rise to immeasurable power of pure faith; one should abide in immeasurable power of diligence; one should purify immeasurable power of right mindfulness; one should...
One should fulfill the power of immeasurable samādhis; one should give rise to the power of immeasurable pure wisdom;
one should strengthen the power of immeasurable resolute conviction; one should accumulate the power of immeasurable merit; one should increase the power of immeasurable wisdom;
one should generate the power of immeasurable bodhisattvas; one should fulfill the power of immeasurable Tathāgatas; and one should discern the immeasurable.
Regarding the Dharma-gates: one should penetrate immeasurable Dharma-gates; one should purify immeasurable Dharma-gates; one should give rise to the light of immeasurable Dharmas;
one should perform the illumination of immeasurable Dharmas; one should illuminate the faculties of immeasurable categories of beings;
one should know the diseases of immeasurable afflictions; and one should collect the medicines of immeasurable sublime Dharmas. One should...
One should heal the illnesses of immeasurable sentient beings; one should prepare offerings of immeasurable ambrosia;
one should travel to immeasurable Buddha-lands; one should make offerings to immeasurable Tathāgatas; one should enter the assemblies of immeasurable Bodhisattvas;
one should receive the teachings of immeasurable Tathāgatas; one should endure the afflictions of immeasurable sentient beings; and one should cause immeasurable multitudes to...
One should be born free from the evil realms; one should bestow supreme peace and happiness upon immeasurable sentient beings;

one should gather immeasurable sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*); one should enter immeasurable gates of dhāraṇī; one should give rise to immeasurable gates of great vows;
one should cultivate immeasurable powers of compassion; one should seek immeasurable qualities of the Buddha-dharma; one should initiate immeasurable...
According to the power of their contemplation, they should manifest immeasurable supernatural feats, purify immeasurable light of wisdom,
proceed to the immeasurable realms of sentient beings, undergo immeasurable births, manifest immeasurable diverse bodies,
endure immeasurable sufferings and afflictions, and accord with the immeasurable ways of ordinary people.
One should know the suffering of immeasurable sentient beings; one should expound the immeasurable teachings of the Buddhas;
one should relinquish immeasurable internal and external wealth; one should bestow gifts upon immeasurable fields of merit;

one should protect immeasurable roots of goodness; one should draw near to immeasurable spiritual friends; one should discipline immeasurable members of one’s own kin; and one should cultivate immeasurable...

One should measure the Buddha-dharmas by teaching immeasurable Buddha-dharmas; one should praise immeasurable observance of the precepts; one should awaken others to immeasurable violations of the precepts;
one should dedicate oneself to immeasurable skillful dharmas; one should thoroughly understand immeasurable dream-like and illusion-like dharmas;
one should cause immeasurable sentient beings to abide in pure precepts; and one should bestow [benefits] upon immeasurable sentient beings.
Through the vajra-samādhi, one should cause immeasurable sentient beings to relinquish views of existence;
one should cause immeasurable sentient beings to swiftly transcend the triple world; one should cause immeasurable sentient beings to contemplate non-self;

one should cause immeasurable sentient beings to awaken to the three vehicles; one should enter into immeasurable varieties of mental states; and one should contemplate the great realm of the bodhisattvas.
One should dwell in the great palace of the bodhisattva; one should contemplate the profound dharma of the bodhisattva; one should know the realm of the bodhisattva that is difficult to know;
one should practice the conduct of the bodhisattva that is difficult to perform; one should adorn the venerable virtues of the bodhisattva;
one should tread upon the stages of the bodhisattva that are difficult to enter; one should know the various practices of the bodhisattva; one should manifest the [qualities] of the bodhisattva...
By means of his all-pervading spiritual power, he should cause [beings] to receive the equal Dharma-clouds of Bodhisattvas,
to expand the boundless web of Bodhisattva practices, to fulfill the boundless perfections of Bodhisattvas, to receive the immeasurable predictions of enlightenment for Bodhisattvas,
to enter the immeasurable gates of Bodhisattva patience, and to be endowed with the immeasurable wisdom and supernormal powers of Bodhisattvas.
One should enter into the immeasurable causal conditions of a bodhisattva; one should demonstrate the immeasurable difficult-to-understand teachings of a bodhisattva;
one should manifest the immeasurable activities performed by a bodhisattva; one should sever the immeasurable suffering of the three poisons of a bodhisattva;
one should exhaust the immeasurable roots of delusion of a bodhisattva; one should purify the immeasurable bodhisattva stages; and one should explain...
One should purify immeasurable Buddha-fields; one should don immeasurable bodhisattva armor;
one should serve immeasurable Tathāgatas; one should resolve upon inconceivable bodhisattva vows;
one should cultivate inconceivable bodhisattva practices; one should receive inconceivable bodhisattva instructions; and one should know.
One should know the inconceivable conduct of bodhisattvas in accordance with afflictions; one should know the inconceivable conduct of bodhisattvas free from afflictions;
one should purify the inconceivable faults of conditioned phenomena of bodhisattvas;
one should know the inconceivable praise of the profound benefits of nirvāṇa by bodhisattvas; and one should know the inconceivable qualities of the Tathāgata.
Thus, there is the inconceivable praise of the Tathāgata, the inconceivable renown of the Tathāgata, the inconceivable renown of Nirvāṇa,
the inconceivable various worldly dharmas, the inconceivable eradication of worldly dharmas,
the inconceivable sublime conduct, the inconceivable speech, and the inconceivable manifold afflictions.
The inconceivable practice that extinguishes afflictions; the inconceivable adamantine phrase of sublime conduct;
the inconceivable adamantine phrase of speech; the inconceivable adamantine phrase of manifold afflictions;
the inconceivable adamantine phrase of extinguishing afflictions; the inconceivable secret phrase of sublime conduct; the inconceivable...
One should study and practice all such secret phrases of language, secret phrases of inconceivable defilements,
and secret phrases of the inconceivable cessation of defilements.
Good son! To state the essentials:
one should universally cultivate all bodhisattva practices because of the realization that all phenomena are equal;
one should universally transform all realms of sentient beings through skillful means of subduing them.
One should universally enter all boundless eons, because the power of one’s vows is vast;
one should universally manifest birth in all realms of existence, because of the manifestation of taking birth;
one should universally know the wisdom of all three periods of time, because of awakening in accordance with reality.
One should universally practice all the dharmas of the Buddhas, because their ultimate essence is identical;
one should universally purify all Buddha-fields, because they are equally adorned;
one should universally fulfill all the vows of Bodhisattvas, because they are perfected as a single body.
One should universally make offerings to all Tathāgatas, because supreme vows have manifested before them;
one should universally accord with the vows of all Bodhisattvas, because their single nature is equal;
and one should universally serve all spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), seeking various bodhisattva practices with resolve, in order to cause those teachers' minds to rejoice.

The Chapter on the Vows and Practices of Samantabhadra for Entering the Realm of Inconceivable Liberation:
"Furthermore, son of good family!
For this reason, you should seek spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) without allowing weariness to arise in body or mind."
Upon seeing a spiritual friend, do not give rise to weariness or complacency;
when questioning a spiritual friend, do not shrink from toil or hardship;
in attending upon a spiritual friend, do not harbor thoughts of retreat.
One should make offerings to spiritual friends without allowing them to be interrupted;
one should comply with the instructions of spiritual friends and not oppose them;
and one should harbor no doubts regarding all the virtues possessed by spiritual friends.
Upon hearing the spiritual friend expound the gates of transcendence, one should give rise to certainty;
upon seeing the spiritual friend act in accordance with afflictions, one should not feel resentment or surprise;
and regarding the spiritual friend, one should give rise to profound faith that must never be altered.
Why is this? Good son! It is because through spiritual friends, a bodhisattva hears of all the practices of bodhisattvas.
Through spiritual friends, one accomplishes all the virtues of a bodhisattva;
through spiritual friends, one gives birth to all the great vows of a bodhisattva;
through spiritual friends, one brings forth all the roots of goodness of a bodhisattva.
Through spiritual friends, one accumulates all the factors conducive to the path of a bodhisattva;
through spiritual friends, one develops the light of all bodhisattva dharmas;
through spiritual friends, one accomplishes all gates of transcendence for a bodhisattva.
Through spiritual friends, one cultivates and studies all the pure precepts of bodhisattvas;
through spiritual friends, one dwells securely in all the meritorious dharmas of bodhisattvas;
through spiritual friends, one purifies the intrinsic nature of the minds of all bodhisattvas.
By means of spiritual friends, one illuminates the firm resolve of all bodhisattvas;
by means of spiritual friends, one becomes fully endowed with all bodhisattva dharanis and gates of eloquence;
by means of spiritual friends, one is able to give birth to the pure treasury of all bodhisattvas.
Through spiritual friends, the light of wisdom of all bodhisattvas appears;
through spiritual friends, one obtains the superior vows of all bodhisattvas;
through spiritual friends, one attains a single vow identical with that of all bodhisattvas.
By means of spiritual friends, one hears all the sublime teachings of the bodhisattvas;
by means of spiritual friends, one attains all the secret places of the bodhisattvas;
by means of spiritual friends, one reaches the island of the Dharma-treasures of all bodhisattvas.
By means of spiritual friends, one gains the increase of all bodhisattva roots of goodness;
by means of spiritual friends, one expands the ocean of all bodhisattva wisdom;
by means of spiritual friends, one guards the profound and secret treasury of all bodhisattvas.
Through spiritual friends, one sustains the entire mass of merit of all bodhisattvas;
through spiritual friends, one purifies the paths of rebirth for all bodhisattvas;
through spiritual friends, one receives the clouds of the true Dharma of all bodhisattvas.
By means of spiritual friends, one enters the supramundane path of all bodhisattvas;
by means of spiritual friends, one gives rise to the great joy of all bodhisattvas;
by means of spiritual friends, one attains the fruit of enlightenment of all Tathāgatas.
Through spiritual friends, one gathers all the sublime practices of bodhisattvas;
through spiritual friends, one causes all the merits of bodhisattvas to blossom;
through spiritual friends, one travels to all directions to hear and receive the sublime Dharma.
Through spiritual friends, one expounds all the bodhisattva minds;
through spiritual friends, one accomplishes all the power of the great loving-kindness of bodhisattvas;
through spiritual friends, one gives birth to all the power of the great compassion of bodhisattvas.
By means of spiritual friends, one masters all the sovereign powers of bodhisattvas;
by means of spiritual friends, one gives birth to all the factors of enlightenment of bodhisattvas;
by means of spiritual friends, one is able to perform all beneficial deeds for bodhisattvas.
