"Good son! All bodhisattvas, by being sustained by spiritual friends, do not fall into the evil realms;
by being perfected by spiritual friends, they attain mastery over their rebirths."
Through the guidance of spiritual friends, one attains the knowledge of past lives;
through the inspiration of spiritual friends, one understands all kalpas;
through the protection of spiritual friends, one does not regress from the Mahāyāna.
Through the observation of spiritual friends, one does not transgress the bodhisattva precepts;
through the protection of spiritual friends, one does not follow after evil associates;
through the nurturing of spiritual friends, one does not fall away from the bodhisattva teachings.
Through being embraced by spiritual friends, one transcends the stage of ordinary beings;
through the instructions of spiritual friends, one does not enter the stages of the two vehicles;
through being inspired by spiritual friends, one attains liberation from the world.
Through the protection of spiritual friends, one is able to remain unstained by worldly dharmas;
through the nurturing of spiritual friends, one cultivates all bodhisattva practices with an undistracted mind;
and through the inspiration of spiritual friends, one accomplishes all requisites for enlightenment without the mind ever becoming discouraged.
Through the power of spiritual friends, one is not shattered by karma and afflictions;
through the sustaining support of spiritual friends, one is not terrified by any demons;
and through the armor of patience donned by spiritual friends, one is able to endure all malicious speech and insults.
Through the consolation of spiritual friends, one remains free from sorrow or joy regarding the sufferings and pleasures of the world;
through being nurtured by spiritual friends, one is able to extinguish all pride and always delights in the Dharma;
through being protected by spiritual friends, one is able to bring the Bodhisattva’s pure precepts to perfection.
Through the power of spiritual friends, one can comprehend all phenomena while the mind remains without attainment;
through the consolation of spiritual friends, one can remain free from fear within the triple world;
through the instruction of spiritual friends, one can know skillful means and the path for exiting the triple world.
Through the exhortation of spiritual friends, one gains faith in the profound Dharma with a mind that knows no satiety;
through the instruction of spiritual friends, one is not oppressed by the pursuit of fame, profit, or pride;
through the discourse of spiritual friends, one attains the knowledge of past lives and understands the causes of the past.
Through the empowerment of spiritual friends, one attains skillfulness throughout the limits of the future;
through the ability of spiritual friends to give birth [to wisdom], one attains the wisdom of skillfulness and knows the equality of the three periods of time;
through the acceptance of spiritual friends, one is able to transform the sentient beings' reliance upon and their karmic retributions of both the environment and its inhabitants.
Through the universal protection of spiritual friends, one can inwardly harbor a sense of shame and remorse, becoming endowed with all manner of virtues;
through the power of compliance with spiritual friends, one can maintain a serene countenance and speak with gentle words to guide sentient beings;
through the power of practicing under spiritual friends, one can abandon all views of nihilism and eternalism.
Through being protected by spiritual friends in accordance with the Dharma, one is able to remain far removed from the phenomena of gain and loss, defamation and praise;
through spiritual friends revealing that one should not speak of one's own abilities but should instead praise the virtues of others;
and through spiritual friends skillfully demonstrating how to diligently cultivate the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma).
Through spiritual friends, one is able to discern and expound the profound principles of the sūtras;
through spiritual friends, one is encouraged to practice and thus comes to delight in accomplishing the dhūta virtues;
and through spiritual friends acting as guides, one attains skillfulness regarding all phenomena of emptiness.

“Good son! By relying upon and serving spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), one is able to increase all the immeasurable and boundless factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.”
Why is this? Good son! A spiritual friend is able to purify all unwholesome dharmas and is able to cause one to abandon and cast off all hindrances, entanglements, and obstructions.
It can disperse and extinguish the dark clouds of ignorance; it can unravel all fetters of various views;
it can lead one out of the great city of suffering in birth and death; it can cause one to abandon and depart from places of fixed attachment;
it can tear asunder the net of all evil Māras; it can extract all the poisonous arrows of suffering; and it can bring about deliverance from ignorance.
The deep forest can enable one to transcend the wilderness of false views, cross over the torrential flood of the various realms of existence,
pull oneself out from the mire of craving and desire, avoid entering the various evil paths,
reveal the path to enlightenment, establish one in heedfulness, lead one to the place of practice, and bring about purification.
The path of omniscience can cause the eye of wisdom to increase, can nourish the bodhicitta,
can give rise to the mind of great compassion, can explain all bodhisattva practices, can instruct in all perfections,
can establish one upon all bodhisattva stages, and can cause one to attain...
The various gates of patience can give birth to all roots of goodness, can accomplish all requisites for practice,
can bestow all great merits, can cause one to reach universally the abodes of all Tathāgatas and manifest all dharmas of merit,
can exhort the cultivation of all supreme benefits, and can spur [one forward].
It exerts all paths of cultivation, can manifest the gateway for eternal emergence from birth and death,
can block all false paths, can cause one to enter the true path, can universally illuminate with the light of the Dharma,
and can universally moisten with the rain of the Dharma;
It enables one to respect teachers and elders and to abandon all indolence;
it enables one to enter into pure and wholesome dharmas with a mind that knows no satiety. "Good son!
A spiritual friend is like a preceptor, for they are able to instruct and guide with virtuous speech;
a spiritual friend is like a companion, for they do not abandon one while dwelling in the araṇya;
a spiritual friend is like supreme supernatural power, for they can manifest various kinds of mastery.
A spiritual friend is like a vajra sword, for he can sever afflictions and their latent tendencies;
a spiritual friend is like a preceptor, for he can perform the confession and removal of the five categories of offenses;
a spiritual friend is like supreme meditative concentration, for he can extinguish all secondary afflictions.
A spiritual friend is like a mani-jewel mirror, for they cause one to realize the knowledge of past lives before one's eyes;
a spiritual friend is like a bridge, for they enable one to cross over the currents of all states of existence;
a spiritual friend can sever the net of doubt, for they provide skillful and decisive resolution regarding the maturation of karma.
A spiritual friend is one who can skillfully establish others, causing them to swiftly enter the stage of non-retrogression;
a spiritual friend is one who can cause others to have deep faith in the subtle workings of karma and its results, as if seeing them for themselves;
a spiritual friend is one who is skilled at exhorting practice by disparaging all unwholesome dharmas.
A spiritual friend is the eye of wisdom, for they do not cling to any phenomena;
a spiritual friend is a mind like a bright lamp, for they awaken through accordance with the nature of original enlightenment;
a spiritual friend is like a guide, for they speak within the assembly for the sake of great beings.
A spiritual friend is one who can abandon evil associates, for they do not enter the dwellings of wicked people;
a spiritual friend is one who abandons non-discipline, for they are able to cause virtuous discipline to increase;
a spiritual friend is one who can teach timely speech, for they speak according to the faculties of sentient beings.
A spiritual friend encourages one to practice in accordance with the teachings, causing one to relinquish concern for food and clothing in order to gather in sentient beings;
a spiritual friend acts as a guide from the outset, causing one to practice exactly as taught;
a spiritual friend causes one to enter deeply, so that one enters deeply into both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
A spiritual friend is like a skilled physician, for they know the proper measure of food and drink;
a spiritual friend is like a yoga master, for they can cause one to enter into corresponding practices;
a spiritual friend is able to provide instruction, enabling one to see the sublime realm of the bodhisattvas.
A spiritual friend is one who can bring about awakening, causing one to realize the fundamental nature of all phenomena;
a spiritual friend is one who can provide consolation, ensuring that all sentient beings are free from sorrow and affliction;
a spiritual friend is like a lasso, capable of gathering sentient beings and leading them into the wisdom of the Buddha.
A spiritual friend is like obtaining a royal seal, for they are without obstruction regarding all dharmas;
a spiritual friend is one who can inspire and lead, causing all sentient beings to advance toward the knowledge of all modes;
a spiritual friend is a garden of Dharma, for it is a place where all bodhisattvas find joy.
A spiritual friend is like a formidable general, for he subdues and overcomes all the armies of Māra;
a spiritual friend is a great vidyā-mantra, for he can eliminate all suffering and calamity;
a spiritual friend is like a great ship, for he carries one across the cycle of birth and death to the further shore.
A spiritual friend is like a wish-fulfilling jewel, for they can cause all aspirations to be perfectly fulfilled;
a spiritual friend is able to provide protection, for they rescue sentient beings from the various evil realms;
a spiritual friend serves as a guiding sign, for they cultivate the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
A spiritual friend is like an ornament, for they adorn the body of all pure dharmas;
a spiritual friend is like a wondrous necklace, for they adorn the sons of the Buddha who have resolved their minds on enlightenment;
a spiritual friend is like an eldest son, for they are able to succeed to the lineage of the Buddhas so that it remains unbroken.
A spiritual friend is like a vessel of noble virtue, for they are replete with the wisdom and merit of all Buddhas;
a spiritual friend is like a pure mani-jewel, for they can purify all turbidities of the mind;
a spiritual friend is like pure precepts, for they can cause the three karmas to be entirely purified.
A spiritual friend is like a key, for they can open all doors of liberation;
a spiritual friend is like a great highway, for it is the path traversed by those who practice the conduct of Buddha-wisdom;
a spiritual friend is the realm of the Buddhas, for it is not the domain or ground of the two vehicles.
A spiritual friend is like the teaching of right wisdom, for they are not an object of knowledge accessible to the three vehicles;
a spiritual friend is like a concordant fruit, for they arise from the same category as all-encompassing wisdom;
a spiritual friend is like a clear and pure eye, for they can show sentient beings the paths that are level and those that are treacherous.
A spiritual friend is like a *dhāraṇī*, for they are able to sustain the practice and learning of all sentient beings;
a spiritual friend is one who can initiate, for they initiate the light of all wisdom;
a spiritual friend is one who can sever and extinguish, for they sever and extinguish the darkness of all ignorance.
A spiritual friend is like the most supreme medicine, for they can eliminate the diseases of the various delusions of sentient beings;
a spiritual friend is like an inexhaustible treasury, for they fulfill the manifold aspirations of sentient beings;
a spiritual friend is like skillful means and ingenuity, for they enable the realization of the stages of all Buddhas.
A spiritual friend is like a gateway, for it is the path through which one practices few desires and contentment;
a spiritual friend is like a skilled laborer, for they enable one to diligently cultivate pure deeds;
a spiritual friend is like a guide, for they lead one away from the causes and conditions of perilous difficulties.
A spiritual friend is like śamatha and vipaśyanā, for they extinguish all dharmas of craving;
a spiritual friend is one who expounds wisdom, for they cause others to enter the profound meaning of non-arising;
a spiritual friend is able to provide illumination, for they enable one to see that cause and effect are never lost or destroyed.
A spiritual friend is like a secluded and tranquil place, for they can quiet the mind through the cultivation of the Path;
a spiritual friend is one who shows the Path, for they lead one to the assembly of the Tathāgata;
a spiritual friend is like the sun and moon, for they can illuminate the most profound Dharma.
A spiritual friend is like a preceptor, for they are able to discern subtle wisdom;
a spiritual friend is one who can awaken others, causing them to realize that all phenomena are like dreams and illusions;
a spiritual friend is a supreme model, for they accord with sentient beings and constantly protect others.
A spiritual friend is one who understands worldly wisdom, remaining undisturbed in mind whether coming or going, speaking or remaining silent;
a spiritual friend is one who detests unwholesome thoughts, being naturally awakened and far removed from folly and delusion;
a spiritual friend is one who serves elders and superiors, free from the notions of self and person, as well as indolence.
A spiritual friend eliminates all delusions, for they perceive that neither their own body nor the bodies of others can be apprehended;
a spiritual friend possesses the wisdom of awakening, for they accord with the realization of both the mundane and the supramundane;
a spiritual friend abandons what is unbeneficial, for they enable themselves and others to transcend all realms of existence.
A spiritual friend is true wisdom, for they universally know the essence of all arising and ceasing;
a spiritual friend is without attainment and without sorrow, for they observe the essence of their own past karma;
a spiritual friend dwells in the practice of *dhūta*, for they constantly wash themselves with the Dharma of Bodhisattvas.
A spiritual friend is one who attains unimpeded mastery of meaning, because they awaken to the true nature of distinctions;
a spiritual friend is one who does not seek praise nor display their own virtues, because they increase reverence;
a spiritual friend is one who possesses sublime patience and wisdom, because they have profound awakening to the fruits of their own karma.
A spiritual friend is one who stays far removed from household life, for they do not associate with others out of a desire for gain or offerings;
a spiritual friend is one who dwells in the practice of seclusion, abandoning meaningless speech and drawing near to reality;
a spiritual friend is one who cultivates the correct objective sphere, constantly and diligently practicing the four foundations of mindfulness.
A spiritual friend is one who is skillful in question and answer, for there is nothing among all questions and answers that they do not know;
a spiritual friend is one who can refute heterodox arguments and skillfully establish the truth, for they destroy false views;
a spiritual friend is one who does not weary of poverty, for they are able to give rise to a heart of compassion toward those in such circumstances.
A spiritual friend is one who can gather others through the Dharma, for they cause them to enter deeply into the true Dharma;
a spiritual friend is one who can gather others through material gifts, for they cause all sentient beings to cultivate virtuous conduct;
a spiritual friend is one who constantly cultivates contentment, for they feel weary of and renounce the guarding against all faults.
A spiritual friend praises pure ethical discipline because they are able to realize and understand the various profound fruits of such discipline;
a spiritual friend rebukes the breaking of discipline because they have deeply awakened to the various faults of violating discipline;
a spiritual friend is one who can fulfill ethical discipline because they accept and uphold it according to principle without flattery or deception, through right mindfulness and awareness.
A spiritual friend is one who is able to observe skillfully, for they diligently inquire about all phenomena, both wholesome and unwholesome;
a spiritual friend is one who can act as a guide, for they exhort all sentient beings to diligently cultivate the Bodhi of the Buddha;
a spiritual friend is one who dwells in non-retrogression, for they have abandoned the four inversions and understand the nature of inversion.
A spiritual friend dwells in the mark of reality, because they universally know that all phenomena are signless;
a spiritual friend dwells in true understanding, because they know that consciousness, name-and-form, and all such phenomena are non-arising;
a spiritual friend attains fearlessness, because they awaken to the essence, characteristics, and function of the profound Dharma-gates of all Buddhas.
A spiritual friend is the dwelling place of pure precepts, because they universally know the wisdom regarding the body of bodhisattva precepts and their characteristics;
a spiritual friend is one who has deeply entered the gates of meditative concentration, because they dwell in samādhi, having left behind the mire of desire;
a spiritual friend is one whose mind is free from defilement and turbidity, because they dwell in a pure mind, having abandoned the hindrances and entanglements.
A spiritual friend is one who has attained all dhāraṇīs, because they expound the teachings according to reality with a mind free from attachment;
a spiritual friend is one who knows the gateways of profound depth, because they are able to universally enter the fundamental nature of all phenomena;
a spiritual friend is the dwelling place of faith, because they abide in the root of all wholesome dharmas.
A spiritual friend dwells in the teaching of tranquility, because they universally eliminate all craving;
a spiritual friend dwells in the straight path, because they are able to universally know suffering and non-self;
a spiritual friend dwells in the bodhisattva stages, because they have a universal understanding of the ten stages.
A spiritual friend is the ground of wisdom, for they are undeluded regarding all phenomena;
a spiritual friend is the ground of all Buddhas, for they are able to give birth to the dharmas of Bodhisattvas;
a spiritual friend dwells on the path of reality, which cannot be known by any of the two vehicles.
A spiritual friend possesses inexhaustible eloquence, for they are able to explain the essence of knowing and seeing things as they truly are;
a spiritual friend is well-freed from sorrow and affliction, for they know that the root of the suffering of birth and death is fundamentally without self;
a spiritual friend is not within the realm of letters, for they know that the path of speech is unattainable.
A spiritual friend dwells in the dharma of non-arising, because the nature of knowledge is ungraspable;
a spiritual friend is capable of tranquility, because they can extinguish all afflictions;
a spiritual friend can eliminate false views, because they are able to abide securely within right view.
"Furthermore, good son! A spiritual friend is like a compassionate mother, for she gives birth to all the lineages of the Buddhas;
a spiritual friend is like a venerable father, for he provides vast benefit and personally entrusts [the teachings]."
A spiritual friend is like a wet nurse, for they protect one from committing unwholesome deeds;
a spiritual friend is like a teacher, for they show the bodhisattvas what should be studied;
a spiritual friend is like a skilled guide, for they can point out the profound pāramitās.
A spiritual friend is like a skilled physician, for they can cure the various diseases of affliction;
a spiritual friend is like the Snowy Mountains, for they increase the medicinal herbs of all-encompassing wisdom;
a spiritual friend is like a valiant general, for they utterly eliminate all fears.
A virtuous friend is like a boatman, for they enable one to cross the great torrent of birth and death;
a virtuous friend is like a merchant leader, for they cause one to reach the island of the jewels of omniscience.
"Good son! If you can now direct your attention in this way and contemplate with right mindfulness, you shall be able to draw near to all spiritual friends.
Furthermore, good son!"
In serving all spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), you should develop a mind like the great earth, because it impartially bears the burden of all without weariness;
you should develop a mind like a diamond toward spiritual friends, because your impartial resolve is indestructible;
you should give rise to a mind like the Iron Ring Mountains toward spiritual friends, because no suffering can move you.
You should regard the spiritual friend with a mind of service, because you must comply with all their instructions;
you should regard the spiritual friend with a mind of a disciple, because you must not oppose any of their teachings;
you should regard the spiritual friend with a mind like that of a servant, because you must never grow weary of any task they may assign.
You should regard the spiritual friend as being like a great fire, for he burns away all afflictions;
you should regard the spiritual friend as being like a hired laborer, for you must never disobey whatever instructions he gives;
you should regard the spiritual friend as being like a man clearing away filth, for he causes you to abandon all pride.
"You should regard the spiritual friend as being like a great body of water, for they wash away all the stains of affliction;
you should give rise to a mind toward the spiritual friend like a great wind, for they shatter the mountain of self-conceit in sentient beings;
you should give rise to a mind toward the spiritual friend like empty space, for they are without obstruction regarding the objects of the five desires."
You should conceive toward spiritual friends a mind like the great ocean, because all the jewels of merit are therein perfected;
you should conceive toward spiritual friends a mind like the full moon, because it causes the cool and pure dharmas to reach fulfillment;
you should conceive toward spiritual friends a mind like a lion, because wherever they roam or dwell, they seize and devour the various demons and evil beasts.
You should develop a mind like that of a fine horse toward spiritual friends, because you follow them wherever they go and remain free from a wicked nature;
you should develop a mind like that of a bull king toward spiritual friends, because you benefit sentient beings without weariness;
you should develop a mind like that of a śramaṇa toward spiritual friends, because you abide in right livelihood and remain free from crookedness and flattery.
You should develop a mind like a lotus flower toward spiritual friends, for their precepts and wisdom are pure and they are unstained by the mud of desire;
you should develop a mind like a caravan leader toward spiritual friends, for they guide others to reach the city of Buddha-wisdom;
you should develop a mind like a great vehicle toward spiritual friends, for they carry heavy burdens while forgetting any expectation of gratitude in return.
You should develop toward spiritual friends a mind like that of a well-trained elephant, always serving and following them without any sudden violence;
you should develop toward spiritual friends a mind like that of the king of mountains, sustaining all things without being shaken;
you should develop toward spiritual friends a mind like that of a good dog, never showing anger or malice toward its master.
You should develop a mind toward the spiritual friend like that of a caṇḍāla, constantly deprecating yourself because you are free from the notion of self and others;
you should develop a mind toward the spiritual friend like that of a castrated ox, always intending to act in accordance with them because you are free from arrogance and anger;
you should develop a mind toward the spiritual friend like that of one living in close attendance, following and complying with the teacher and elders because you always hold them in deep respect.
You should conceive toward spiritual friends a mind like that of a ship, for it carries you back and forth without weariness;
you should conceive toward spiritual friends a mind like that of a bridge, for it ferries sentient beings across to the other shore;
you should conceive toward spiritual friends a mind like that of a filial son, for it serves and makes offerings while following their countenance.
"You should develop toward spiritual friends a mind like that of a prince, obeying their instructions without transgression.
Furthermore, son of good family!"

One should conceive the thought of one's own body as being afflicted by illness, conceive the thought of the spiritual friend as being a king of physicians, conceive the thought of the Dharma taught as being excellent medicine, and conceive the thought of one's practice as being the removal of disease.
Furthermore, son of good family!

You should conceive of yourself as one who has traveled far; conceive of the spiritual friend as a guide; conceive of the Dharma taught as the true path; and conceive of the practice undertaken as reaching the distant goal.
Furthermore, good son!

You should conceive the thought of seeking deliverance regarding yourself; the thought of a boatman regarding the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra); the thought of a vessel regarding the Dharma taught; and the thought of reaching the shore regarding the practice cultivated.
Furthermore, son of good family!

You should conceive of yourself as a farmer; of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) as a dragon king; of the Dharma being taught as seasonal rain; and of the practice being cultivated as the ripening [of the harvest].
Furthermore, noble son!

You should conceive the thought of yourself as being poor; conceive the thought of the spiritual friend as Vaiśravaṇa; conceive the thought of the Dharma taught as being wealth and treasure; and conceive the thought of the practice undertaken as being abundance and prosperity.
Furthermore, son of good family!
You should conceive of yourself as a disciple, of the spiritual friend as a skilled teacher, of the Dharma taught as a craft, and of the practice undertaken as a thorough understanding.
Furthermore, noble son!

You should conceive the thought of fear toward yourself, the thought of a valiant warrior toward the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), the thought of weapons toward the Dharma being taught, and the thought of eliminating an enemy toward the practice you are cultivating.
Furthermore, son of good family!
You should conceive of yourself as a merchant, of the spiritual friend as a guide, of the Dharma taught as precious jewels, and of the practice cultivated as the acquisition of those jewels.
Furthermore, noble son!
You should conceive of yourself as a son, of the spiritual friend as your parents, of the Dharma taught as the family inheritance, and of the practice undertaken as the succession of that lineage.
Furthermore, son of good family!

You should conceive of yourself as a prince, of the spiritual friend as a minister, of the Dharma being taught as the king’s decree, and of your practice as wisdom, dwelling in the royal city, donning the royal crown, and binding the royal silken ribbon.
"Good son! You should give rise to such a mind and form such an intention as to approach and serve spiritual friends. Why is this?"
All Bodhisattvas, with such a mind, draw near to spiritual friends so that their aspirations may forever be purified.
"Furthermore, good son!
Because of spiritual friends, bodhisattvas are always able to increase all roots of goodness, just as medicinal herbs grow upon the Snowy Mountains;
because of spiritual friends, they become vessels for the Buddha-dharma, just as the great ocean receives all flowing streams;
because of spiritual friends, they become abodes of merit and virtue, just as the great ocean produces all manner of jewels.
Because of the spiritual friend, the bodhicitta is purified, just as a fierce fire can refine true gold;
because of the spiritual friend, one emerges from all worlds, like Mount Sumeru rising from the great ocean;
because of the spiritual friend, one is unstained by worldly dharmas, just as a lotus flower is not defiled by dust or water.
Because of spiritual friends, one does not accept any evils, just as the great ocean does not harbor corpses;
because of spiritual friends, pure dharmas increase, just as the waxing moon gradually becomes full;
because of spiritual friends, the dharma-realm is illuminated, just as the brilliant sun shines upon the four continents.
Through spiritual friends, one’s great vows increase, just as parents nourish an infant.
Son of good family!
I have now briefly explained that if a bodhisattva can diligently seek to accord with the instructions of spiritual friends, they will immediately achieve success.
Regarding ten unspeakably unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of merits,
purifying ten unspeakably unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of profound mentalities,
increasing ten unspeakably unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of bodhisattva faculties, and perfecting ten unspeakably...
With an unspeakable power of majestic virtue numbering hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas,
he eliminates ten unspeakably unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of asaṃkhyeyas of bodhisattva obstacles,
transcends ten unspeakably unspeakable hundreds of thousands of billions of asaṃkhyeyas of demonic realms, and deeply penetrates ten unspeakably unspeakable...
One hundred thousand koṭis of asaṃkhyeyas of dharma-gates; one fulfills ten unspeakably unspeakable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of asaṃkhyeyas of aids to the path;
one cultivates ten unspeakably unspeakable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of asaṃkhyeyas of sublime practices;
and one initiates ten unspeakably unspeakable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of asaṃkhyeyas.
Great Vow! Son of good family!

I shall further briefly explain that all bodhisattva practices, all bodhisattva perfections, all bodhisattva stages, all bodhisattva gates of patience, all bodhisattva gates of samādhi, all bodhisattva wisdoms of supernormal powers, all bodhisattva gates of dhāraṇī, all bodhisattva wisdoms of dedication, all bodhisattva four immeasurables, all bodhisattva vast vows, and all bodhisattvas’ universal accomplishment of all Buddha-dharmas—all these are brought to fulfillment solely through the power of spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).

The spiritual friend is the root; it comes from the spiritual friend, is born in dependence upon the spiritual friend, grows in dependence upon the spiritual friend, and abides in dependence upon the spiritual friend. The spiritual friend is the causal condition; the spiritual friend is able to initiate [the path].
At that time, the youth Sudhana said: "Noble One!
I now know that all wholesome dharmas arise from spiritual friends."
"How can one swiftly attain fulfillment, swiftly attain purity, and avoid falling away regarding all spiritual friends and wholesome dharmas?
At that time, the youth Śrīsaṃbhava and the maiden Guṇavatī said to Sudhana:
"There are two kinds of precepts; if one fully receives and maintains them, one will attain the dharma of spiritual friends in its fulfillment."
What are these two?
First, the bodhisattva precepts;
second, the prātimokṣa precepts.
By upholding these two precepts, one is able to fulfill the qualities of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

As the Buddha has said, it is impossible for one who does not uphold the precepts themselves to cause others to uphold them, or for one who is not themselves disciplined to cause others to become disciplined.
"If Bodhisattvas are fully endowed with the merits of the dhūta practices, these two types of precepts will both become pure,
and they shall not lose the wholesome dharmas. Sudhana said, "Noble One!"
"What is called the merit of *dhūta*?
The boys and girls replied to Sudhana, "Noble son!..."
Regarding the term "dhūta," it refers to the twelve dhūtas of the bodhisattvas.
What are these twelve? The first is the practice of wearing rag-robes (pāṃśukūlika).
"Good son! What is the patched robe?
If bodhisattvas possess ten kinds of dharmas, they will attain the perfect accomplishment of the patched robe."

What are the ten? First, to practice diligently so as to attain firmness; second, to cause the mind to always remain humble; third, to have no weariness or fatigue regarding body or mind; fourth, for the mind not to be stained by or attached to clothing; fifth, to always delight in firm seclusion; sixth, to accomplish firm merit; seventh, not to manifest one's own superior virtues; eighth, not to give rise to contempt for others; ninth, to maintain and uphold pure precepts to perfection; and tenth, to be capable of enduring all forms of intimacy.
Good son! This is the bodhisattva abiding in pure faith, fully perfected.

By virtue of this mind, when hearing the exposition of the Tathāgata’s pure teachings, he does not begrudge his own body or life, but diligently cultivates the Buddha-dharma without breaking or destroying it.
Because of diligent cultivation, body and mind remain unmoving, causing what has been attained to be firmly accomplished;
because the mind is firm, one is always naturally humble;
and because the mind is humble, one accomplishes non-self.
Having attained selflessness, the mind is free from arrogance; because one has attained a mind devoid of pride through the power of humility, one accepts whatever others discard.

Washing and dyeing these into robes, one remains far removed from afflictions, feeling neither aversion nor attachment. One takes them only for the sustenance of the body to ward off cold and heat, and for the practice of the path, regarding nothing else.

Regarding these rag-robes, one perceives no faults and does not dwell on their coarseness; rather, one sees only the merits inherent in the rag-robes. Only those who have abandoned desire wear such garments.
Those who wear these robes have no afflictions in their minds; they follow the lineage of the noble ones and the conduct of bodhisattvas, and are praised by all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
By virtue of this cause and condition, they do not become conceited;
because they are not conceited, they do not disparage others.
Because they are free from arrogance and aversion, their pure precepts are perfected;

because their precepts are perfected, they are worthy of being approached and are protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. All kings of devas and humans, as well as kṣatriyas, brahmins, and others from cities, towns, and villages—whosoever sees or hears them—are without exception filled with joy; they pay respectful homage, prostrate themselves, and together praise and extol their virtue, saying:
"We are fortunate that such a person has appeared and dwells in this land."
"All fellow practitioners of the holy life were filled with joy. Good son!
These are the ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva fulfills and perfectly accomplishes the merit of wearing rag-robes."
"Furthermore, son of good family,
there are ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva fully and perfectly accomplishes the three robes. What are these ten?

First, the accomplishment of contentment; second, the accomplishment of fewness of desires; third, freedom from excessive seeking; fourth, freedom from all accumulation; fifth, freedom from loss; sixth, freedom from physical suffering; seventh, freedom from mental anxiety; eighth, freedom from vexation; ninth, freedom from grasping and rejecting; tenth, the path toward the exhaustion of outflows.
"Good son! Because such a bodhisattva has few desires in mind, he accepts whatever three robes he obtains without making any distinctions, thereby achieving contentment;
having achieved contentment, he remains far removed from seeking much."
Because he is free from many desires, he has no accumulations;
because he is free from accumulations, he does not fear loss;
because there is no loss, his body attains freedom from suffering.
Because the body is free from suffering, the mind is also free from sorrow;
because the mind is free from sorrow, one is far removed from affliction;
because affliction does not arise, one is distant from grasping and rejecting.
Because they have distanced themselves from acceptance and rejection, they advance toward the path of the exhaustion of outflows. Good son,
these are the ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva is fully endowed with and perfectly accomplishes the merit of the three robes.
"Furthermore, good son!
There are ten dharmas which, when fully perfected and accomplished, enable a bodhisattva to remain unstained by the dyed robes. What are these ten?

First, not following the conduct of sensual desire; second, not following the conduct of malice; third, not following the conduct of delusion; fourth, not following the conduct of anger; fifth, not following the conduct of ferocity; sixth, not following the conduct of jealousy; seventh, not following the conduct of stinginess; eighth, not following the conduct of arrogance; ninth, not following the conduct of fame, praise, or retinue; tenth, not following the conduct of gain from intimacy and offerings.

"Good son! Because one does not follow the course of craving and the other afflictions, one is not overcome by the four māras. When encountering various insults and humiliations, the mind does not become timid or weak; even when meeting those who are honored, one does not become arrogant. For this reason, it is called 'the mind not following along with the course of defiled delusions.'"
"Good son! These are the ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva fulfills and perfectly accomplishes the merit of the sublime practice of not following the dyeing of robes. Furthermore, good son!"
Bodhisattvas have ten dharmas which, when fully perfected, lead to the accomplishment of relying on alms-gathering.

What are these ten? First, gathering others through a mind of loving-kindness; second, practicing sequential begging; third, not giving rise to self-affliction; fourth, achieving contentment; fifth, sharing food universally with others; sixth, having no craving for fine foods; seventh, knowing the proper measure in eating and drinking; eighth, swiftly attaining wholesome dharmas; ninth, fulfilling the roots of goodness through aspiration; and tenth, being free from the characteristics of social attachment.
"Noble son! How does a bodhisattva gather beings through a mind of loving-kindness, and even come to distance himself from all signs of composite phenomena? Noble son!"

When a bodhisattva sees sentient beings oppressed by various sufferings and lacking roots of goodness, he seeks to fulfill those roots of goodness for their sake; thus, in accordance with those beings, he gathers them in with a compassionate heart.
To accord with this impartial compassion, the bodhisattva practices alms-gathering in successive order.

When going on almsround, if one arrives at a city or town, one should maintain composed deportment, properly restrain the sense faculties, and remain single-minded without distraction. One should gaze attentively while walking slowly, not exceeding seven paces, dwelling securely in right mindfulness. Regarding the practice of wholesome dharmas, one should not select noble households nor reject those of lowly status; however, to avoid censure and suspicion, one must not go to those who follow evil disciplines or to outcastes (caṇḍālas) and the like.
If one gathers others with a mind of universal compassion, one should never abandon them in the end.

When a bodhisattva practices alms-gathering according to the prescribed sequence, they do not give rise to personal distress; even if they do not obtain food, they do not give rise to anger. In this way, the bodhisattva achieves contentment, accepting whatever is given without discriminating between the fine and the coarse.

Having thus begged for alms in sequence, the bodhisattva carries them before the Buddha or before a stūpa and temple, making offerings with a heart of reverence and respect. Having completed the offering, he returns to his original dwelling and divides the food into four parts:

taking the first part, he waits for those of like spiritual practice (*sabrahmacārin*); with the second part, he gives to the poor and suffering; with the third part, he gives to those in prison; and with the fourth part, he provides sustenance for himself.

Regarding the food he eats, he does not indulge in craving or attachment, but contemplates only the body, maintaining the thought that it is for the purpose of curing illness, even unto the point of enabling the body to remain stable.
When receiving food and drink, one should not take too little, thereby causing oneself to become emaciated and weak, which hinders the cultivation of wholesome deeds;
nor should one take too much, causing the body to become weary and heavy, which increases drowsiness.
By means of this food, one is able to apply diligent effort and swiftly attain wholesome dharmas.
Because a bodhisattva desires to fulfill all roots of goodness that constitute the factors of enlightenment, they should further distance themselves from grasping at the signs of combination.

Having abandoned such signs, they abandon the grasping at a self and achieve non-self; even regarding their own internal and external flesh, blood, and all material wealth, they do not give rise to stinginess, but are able to share them with sentient beings for their common enjoyment.
“Good son! These are the ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva fulfills and perfectly accomplishes the meritorious virtue of the sublime practice of constantly begging for alms. Furthermore, good son!”
Bodhisattvas possess ten dharmas; when these are fully perfected, they achieve the practice of eating while remaining seated for a single session. What are these ten?
First, as all bodhisattvas sit upon the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) in a single sitting;
Second, subduing the enmity of Māra with an unshakable mind;
third, achieving immovability in supramundane concentration;
fourth, achieving immovability in supramundane wisdom.
Fifth, they achieve immovability regarding supramundane wisdom;
sixth, they achieve immovability regarding the emptiness of all phenomena;
seventh, they achieve immovability regarding the realization of the true path.
Eighth, they achieve immovability regarding the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*);
ninth, they achieve immovability regarding the nature of suchness (*tathatā*);
tenth, they achieve immovability regarding omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

"Good son! This 'sitting in one session' refers to sitting in the Dharma; because the Bodhisattva relies upon it to attain immovability, it is said that the Bodhisattva accomplishes sitting in one session."
"Good son! These are the ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva fulfills and perfectly accomplishes the sublime practice and merit of always eating in a single sitting.
*The Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Scroll Thirty-Three."
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha’s Great Vaipulya, Scroll Thirty-Four,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā of Kapiśī by Imperial Decree:
"The Chapter on the Vows and Practices of Samantabhadra Entering the Sphere of Inconceivable Liberation."
"Furthermore, good son, when a bodhisattva possesses ten dharmas, they attain the perfect accomplishment of eating but one meal a day. What are these ten?
First, when obtaining food, one’s nature is free from greedy seeking;
second, when obtaining food, one’s nature is without defiled attachment;
third, whenever food is obtained, one always knows contentment and moderation.
Fourth, one should always eat at the proper time and never fall into eating at improper times;
fifth, if it is for the sake of gain or sustenance, one should not eat at all;
sixth, even if one obtains something sweet and delicious, one should likewise not eat it.
Seventh, if one sees others eating, one does not give rise to anger;
eighth, when seeing others eat, one is likewise free from stinginess and envy;
ninth, until the end of one's life, one always maintains the practice of eating only once a day.
Tenth, at the time of eating, one should conceive the thought that food is medicine.
Son of good family!
These are the ten dharmas that accomplish the meritorious virtue of the sublime practice of eating a single meal.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
If a bodhisattva possesses ten qualities, they will attain the perfection of the dharma of araṇya. What are these ten?

First, accomplishment of long-cultivated pure conduct; second, accomplishment of pure restraint; third, accomplishment of undisturbed faculties; fourth, accomplishment of constant delight in much hearing; fifth, accomplishment of power in all circumstances; sixth, accomplishment of being far removed from self-clinging; seventh, accomplishment of non-attachment to the body; eighth, accomplishment of constant delight in seclusion; ninth, accomplishment of the presence of the true Dharma; tenth, accomplishment of delighting in dwelling alone.
“Good son! How does a bodhisattva long cultivate the pure conduct (brahmacarya), and even achieve delight in dwelling alone? Good son!”
Thus, once this bodhisattva has gone forth, they become fully endowed with the three wheels within the teachings spoken by the Tathāgatas;
their seal of ethical discipline is pure, and they attain skillfulness regarding all precepts, being able to understand them through self-awakening without depending on the instruction of others.
That is to say:
skillfulness in accordance with the meaning, whereby one is able to practice;
and skillfulness in accordance with the letter, whereby one receives and maintains it without forgetting.
He is skillful in following the path of definitive emergence;
he is skillful in repenting and eliminating the five groups of transgressions;
and wherever he dwells and acts, he remains free from all occasions for offense.
Toward all evil persons, his mind is always fearful; even regarding minor transgressions, he does not conceal them.

Regarding all points of training (*śikṣāpada*), whether they involve an offense or not, he is fully able to discern them; he understands the long or short duration of such karmic actions, and how one falls into the three evil destinies or is reborn among humans and devas.
Thus, the Bodhisattva skillfully disciplines the six sense faculties so that they are free from agitation and distraction, and by these means dwells in an araṇya.
He dwells in a place free from affliction and harm, devoid of difficulties and obstacles;

he does not associate with the spheres of ordinary householders, yet he is not far from towns and cities, so that alms-seeking is convenient and medicinal herbs are abundant, with pure springs and flowing streams;
he stays far from wicked beasts, in a secluded and tranquil environment.
Dwelling in such a place, one should apply oneself with diligence to what has been studied and recited.

While chanting, one should regulate the breath, keep the voice free from fluctuations of pitch, and prevent the mind from wandering to external objects. One should focus the thought on retention, contemplate the words and their meaning, remain free from lethargy and agitation, and maintain the union of śamatha and vipaśyanā.

If he sees ministers, brahmins, or others approach his dwelling, he should give rise to a heart of affection and respect toward those who come; he should first inquire after them with a welcoming mind, bid them sit at ease, observe their faculties and dispositions, and preach the True Dharma for them so that they may all be filled with joy, accept it with faith, and practice accordingly.
If one sees a king, one should welcome and attend to him with propriety, skillfully complying with his intentions, and speak thus:
"I pray only that Your Majesty will take a seat upon this spread."
Once the king was seated, he was invited to choose whatever he desired, and everything was provided for him.
At times, if that king’s mind lacked faith or joy, one should use kind words to praise the king’s virtues:
"I observe, Great King, that you have most excellently attained a sublime benefit."
Now, within Your Majesty’s realm, all those who maintain the precepts and possess great learning—namely, all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, the excellent fields of merit—dwell therein;
by the majesty of the King’s power, no thieves or bandits come to cause disturbance;
and through the transformative influence of the King’s virtue, all predatory beasts have completely departed.

Upon hearing these words, the king was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; his faculties were subdued and his mind became tranquil. Being a fit vessel for the Dharma, the Buddha proceeded to proclaim various teachings of the True Dharma: he might expound upon the methods for wearying oneself of birth and death, or he might expound upon the Tathāgata’s merits, vast sovereignty, and profound, wondrous Dharma—in all such ways, he caused him to rejoice.
When a bodhisattva achieves such extensive learning and the power of all-encompassing mastery, they are capable of practicing correct conduct;
when a bodhisattva achieves self-benefit and the benefit of others, they remain far removed from all afflictions of self-clinging;
when a bodhisattva achieves non-attachment to the body, their mind is free from fear while dwelling in an araṇya.
The Bodhisattva achieves constant delight in seclusion and dwells in an araṇya, his mind being tranquil;
the Bodhisattva achieves the manifestation of the True Dharma and completely renounces all worldly things;
the Bodhisattva achieves a delight in solitary dwelling, like a wild deer, free from the fear of predators.
"Noble son! These are the ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva is fully endowed with, and perfectly accomplishes, the merit of dwelling in the sublime practice of the araṇya.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva possesses ten qualities, they will achieve the accomplishment of sitting beneath a tree.

What are these ten? First, not being near a village or settlement; second, not relying on a place too far from a city or town; third, not relying on a place of thorns and brambles; fourth, not relying on a place with many poisonous weeds; fifth, not relying on a tree without branches or leaves; sixth, not relying on a place with many monkeys and langurs; seventh, not relying on a place where flocks of birds gather; eighth, not relying on the dwelling place of predatory beasts; ninth, not relying on a place near enemies or bandits; tenth, not relying on a place where unlawful and evil practices are performed.
One should not rely on such places as these.
However, one should dwell securely in those places that can bring peace, stability, joy, and happiness to body and mind, and where one may cultivate wholesome conduct.
O son of good family!
This is for a bodhisattva to be fully endowed with ten dharmas, thereby perfectly accomplishing the meritorious practice of sitting beneath a tree. "Furthermore, good son!
If a bodhisattva possesses ten qualities, they attain the perfection of sitting in the open air.

What are these ten? First, to endure cold, heat, and rain without seeking warmth or coolness; second, not to rely on walls; third, not to rely on groves of trees; fourth, not to rely on heaps of grass; fifth, not to rely on dangerous places; sixth, not to cover oneself against the cold; seventh, not to cover oneself against the rain; eighth, not to cover oneself against the heat; ninth, not to cover oneself against the wind; tenth, to reside in a dwelling only if one suffers from illness.
A bodhisattva should form this thought:

"If I sit in the open air with right mindfulness present, I shall swiftly eliminate afflictions according to my practice; following the Buddha’s teaching on the merits of the dhūtas, I shall diligently seek them and bring them to fulfillment."
Even when dwelling in a residence, one should not give rise to attachment, nor should one say that this place is good while that is bad; rather, one should think:
"I dwell in this monastery to benefit all sentient beings who cultivate merit."
"Sitting in the open air cannot bring about great benefit;
furthermore, sitting on open ground can only benefit oneself and cannot benefit others.
Yet, although that bodhisattva dwells in a dwelling, day and night he constantly maintains the perception of sitting in the open air.
"Noble son! These are the ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva fulfills and perfectly accomplishes the meritorious practice of sitting in the open air.
Furthermore, noble son!"
If a bodhisattva possesses ten dharmas, they will be able to accomplish dwelling in cemeteries.

What are these ten? First, the perception of revulsion toward the world; second, the perception of the manifestation of the signs of death; third, the perception of the body immediately after death before it has decomposed; fourth, the perception of the manifestation of the livid discoloration of the corpse; fifth, the perception of the manifestation of the bloating of the corpse; sixth, the perception of the flow of pus and the rotting of the corpse; seventh, the perception of the corpse being devoured by birds and beasts; eighth, the perception of the corpse being half-burnt by fire; ninth, the perception of the separation of the limbs and joints; and tenth, the perception of the manifestation of the skeleton.

"Good son! When bodhisattvas dwell among cemeteries, they should constantly abide in a mind of loving-kindness and a mind of benefit toward all sentient beings; they should firmly maintain pure precepts, guard their dignified deportment, purify their bodies, and must not eat meat."
Why is this? Residing in the Śītavana forest, one should guard against two faults:
first, to avoid being reviled and disparaged by non-Buddhists; second, to avoid giving non-human beings the opportunity to cause harm.

"Good son! If that bodhisattva enters a monastery, he should first pay homage to the Buddha’s stūpas and various images, and then prostrate before the superior, middling, and inferior seats as appropriate.

Having completed these acts, he should maintain his dignified deportment and ritual protocols for the sake of those bodhisattvas dwelling in cemeteries who are逆流生死 (flowing against the current of birth and death) and conforming to the noble Dharma."
"Noble son! If that bodhisattva enters a monastery, the resident bhikṣus should invite him to take a seat by offering a couch or mat.
The bodhisattva should examine the situation carefully; if there are obstacles or difficulties, he should reflect upon them according to the circumstances."
"If there is no hindrance or difficulty, you may then take your seat;
you should humble your mind in this way. Good son!"
This is for a bodhisattva to be fully endowed with ten dharmas, thereby perfectly accomplishing the meritorious virtues of the sublime practice of dwelling in cemeteries.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
When a bodhisattva possesses ten qualities, they attain the perfect accomplishment of perpetual sitting (*prahāṇa*).

What are these ten? First, not for the sake of physical fatigue; second, not for the sake of mental affliction or distress; third, not for the sake of indolence or sleep; fourth, not for the sake of the discomfort of standing for long periods; fifth, to fulfill the accumulation of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*); sixth, to cultivate one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*); seventh, to bring the true path (*samyagmārga*) into manifestation; eighth, out of the desire to sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); ninth, out of the desire to benefit sentient beings; and tenth, out of the desire to extinguish and eliminate the afflictions (*kleśa*).
“Good son! These are the ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva fulfills the merit of the sublime practice of constant sitting. Furthermore, good son!”
If a bodhisattva possesses ten qualities, they will attain the perfect accomplishment of following the practice of sitting.

What are these ten? First, regarding whatever seat one encounters, the mind does not harbor attachment. Second, regarding seats already spread by others, one does not personally arrange them. Third, one likewise does not instruct others to set out beds or seats. Fourth, one does not create the conditions for the use of various bedding materials. Fifth, encountering grass, leaves, and the like, one sits at any available time. Sixth, one should avoid places where there are many venomous insects. Seventh, when wishing to lie down, one rests on the ground with the right side downward. Eighth, the mind is free from negligence, maintaining the mindfulness that it is time to rise. Ninth, one fixes the mind upon clarity and sleeps in accordance with the Dharma. Tenth, it is for the sake of spiritual cultivation, so as to bring peace and ease to the body.
"Noble son! These are the ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva fulfills the merit of accomplishing the sublime practice of following the seat. Noble son!"

When a bodhisattva fully accomplishes these twelve kinds of dhūta merits through practice, they are able to bring all the dharmas of spiritual friends to complete purity and are never to regress from those dharmas of spiritual friends.

At that time, having heard such pure and wondrous practices of *dhūta* merit—the various praises of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), the various gateways of bodhisattva conduct, and the manifestation of all Buddha-dharmas—Sudhana’s body and mind became supple;

he leaped for joy with great exultation, and his heart of love and reverence increased rapidly. He prostrated at the feet of the boy and the girl, circumambulated them countless times, gazed up at them with earnest devotion, and departed with single-minded longing.

At that time, the youth Sudhana, his mind moistened by the instructions of his spiritual friends, reflected with right mindfulness upon the practices of all bodhisattvas as he proceeded gradually toward the country of Sāgaratīra.

Recalling his past lives, he remembered that throughout many cycles of birth and death he had failed to practice respectful salutation; immediately, he resolved his mind, deeply reproaching himself, and practiced with diligent effort.
Furthermore, recalling his past lives, he remembered that for a long time he had dwelt in saṃsāra with an impure body and mind; immediately, he resolved his mind:
to exclusively cultivate self-purification, vowing to reach the other shore.
Furthermore, I recall that in past lives, when I followed worldly ways and committed various evil deeds,
I immediately resolved to observe the practices of all bodhisattvas with right mindfulness.
Again, I recall that in past lives, when my mind was shrouded by afflictions and I gave rise to various delusive thoughts, I immediately resolved [to abandon them].

Constantly and correctly contemplating the true nature of all phenomena, he further recalled that the various practices he had cultivated in past lives were intended solely for his own sake; thereupon, he resolved:
"I shall cause my mind to become vast and universal, extending to all sentient beings."
Furthermore, recollecting past lives, when one constantly brought oneself to ruin in the pursuit of sensual objects, one immediately resolved:
"I shall practice the Buddha-dharma and nourish my faculties.
Furthermore, recollecting past lives, when one gave rise to perverse thoughts associated with inversion, one immediately resolved:

Giving rise to the mind of right view and initiating the vows of a bodhisattva, he further recalled his past lives, wherein he had labored day and night committing various evil deeds; he immediately resolved:
"I shall arouse great vigor to bring the Buddha-dharma to fulfillment."
Furthermore, he recalled his past lives as he underwent births within the five destinies, wherein his own body and the bodies of others had brought no benefit whatsoever. At that moment, he resolved:

"May this body bring benefit to sentient beings, may I accomplish the Buddha-dharma, may I arouse the roots of goodness in all sentient beings, and may I serve all spiritual friends, always remaining in harmony with a mind of right aspiration.
Thinking thus, he gave rise to great joy.

Furthermore, one contemplates this body as the constant root of all sufferings—birth, old age, sickness, death, and the separation from those one loves—from the beginningless past. One vows that until the end of the future, one shall practice all the paths of the Bodhisattvas, teaching and bringing all sentient beings to maturity; behold all Tathāgatas as they accomplish the Buddha-dharma; travel through all Buddha-fields; serve all masters who skillfully expound the Dharma; uphold the true teachings of all Tathāgatas; seek out companions for the true Dharma; and, seeing all spiritual friends, gather all the qualities of the Buddhas to act as the causal conditions for the body of the vow-wisdom of all Bodhisattvas.

At the moment of forming this thought, inconceivable and immeasurable roots of goodness rapidly increased. He immediately conceived deep faith and a heart of reverence toward all bodhisattvas, giving rise to the perception of their rarity and the perception of them as Great Teachers.

His faculties became pure and wholesome dharmas increased; he began to offer respectful worship to all bodhisattvas, bowing his body and joining his palms before them all. He gave rise to the perception of all bodhisattvas as the universal eye that beholds the world, and the perception of all bodhisattvas as those who universally keep sentient beings in mind.

He entered the infinite gates of equality of all bodhisattvas, manifested the infinite transformation-bodies of the vows of all bodhisattvas, and produced the pure speech of all bodhisattvas, vowing to adorn all buddha-lands.

They have beheld all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the past and present, their majestic power fully perfected, manifesting the attainment of enlightenment and miraculous transformations in all places; indeed, there is not even a single hair’s breadth where the bodies of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not pervade.
Furthermore, they have attained the pure eye of wisdom-light of all Bodhisattvas, seeing the spheres of activity of all Bodhisattvas:

their minds universally enter the net of lands throughout the ten directions, their vows pervading the void of the Dharma-realm, conforming to all places without exception, universally practicing impartial and non-discriminative conduct throughout the three periods of time, continuing without interruption and without rest, and universally entering all profound Dharma-gates.
All of this was brought about solely by his having accepted the instructions of the spiritual friend with faith.
In this manner— with such reverence, such offerings, such praise,
such observation, such empowerment, such power of aspiration, and such contemplation— Sudhana the youth...
Thus conforming, thus reflecting, and thus giving rise [to realization], he pervaded the infinite realm of wisdom.
Before the Great Pavilion of Vairocana’s Adorned Treasury, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, paying reverent homage;
for a moment, he withdrew his thoughts to contemplate and observe, and gave rise to a profound...
With profound, vast, and great faith-understanding and the power of vast vows, they transform their own bodies so as to pervade all places;
they enter the body of wisdom, abide in the gate of equality, and universally manifest their bodies before all Tathāgatas,
before all Bodhisattvas, before all spiritual friends, and before all stūpas of the Tathāgatas.
Before temples, before the images of all Tathāgatas, before the abodes of all Buddhas and all Bodhisattvas,
before the halls and buildings of all Dharma-jewels, before the shrines and reliquaries of all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas,
before all fields of merit consisting of the noble assemblies, and before all parents and venerable elders.
Before the bodies of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, pervading every place, they perform acts of respect, prostration, and praise as described above; thus, within all conditions,
they fill them completely through the sustaining power of inexhaustible vows and transformations, continuing without rest throughout all places until the end of the future.

Because it is equal to space in its boundless measure; because it is equal to the dharma-realm in its lack of obstruction; because it is equal to the limit of reality in its pervasiveness of all things;

and because it is equal to the Tathāgata in its non-discrimination; because it appears like a shadow following the perceptions of wisdom; because it arises like a dream from thoughts and the like; because it represents all things like a reflected image; and because it issues forth like an echo from favorable conditions;

because there is no birth through mutual arising and passing away; because there is no corresponding movement of the mind; and because there is no intrinsic nature that undergoes transformation according to conditions.
Furthermore, they attain certain knowledge and profound faith and understanding: that all such retributions arise from karma;
and that all such fruits arise from causes; thus they attain profound faith and understanding.
In this way, they develop a profound and deep conviction that all such karmic actions arise from habitual practice;
they develop a profound and deep conviction that all such Tathāgatas appearing in the world arise from faith;
and they develop a profound and deep conviction that all such manifested acts of offering arise from resolute understanding.
In this way, they develop a profound and deep-felt conviction that all these emanation Buddhas of the Tathāgatas arise from a heart of reverence and affection;
in this way, they develop a profound and deep-felt conviction that all these Buddha-dharmas arise from roots of goodness;
and in this way, they develop a profound and deep-felt conviction that all these emanation Buddhas arise from skillful means.
In this way, one develops profound faith and understanding that all such buddha-activities arise from great vows;
in this way, one develops profound faith and understanding that all such practices cultivated by bodhisattvas arise from dedication;
and in this way, one develops profound faith and understanding that all such vast adornments of the entire dharma-realm arise from the sphere of omniscience.
They are free from the view of nihilism because they know how to dedicate [merit];
they are free from the view of eternalism because they know non-arising;
they are free from the view of causelessness because they know the true cause.
They are free from the view of inversion because they know the principle of reality as it is;
they are free from the view of a sovereign creator because they know things do not arise through another;
they are free from the view of self and other because they know things arise from conditions.
They are free from all false views because they understand the power of cause and effect;
they are free from the view of extreme adherence because they understand that the dharma-realm is boundless;
they are free from the view of coming and going because they understand that all things are like reflections.
They are free from views of existence and non-existence because they know there is neither arising nor ceasing;
they are free from views of all phenomena because they know emptiness is unarisen, they know [phenomena] lack self-mastery, and they know they are produced through the power of vows;

they are free from views of all marks because they enter the limit of the markless, knowing that all phenomena arise like sprouts from seeds without being lost or destroyed, and arise in succession like the impression of a seal upon its surface.

They know that substance is like a reflection; they know that sound is like an echo; they know that objects are like dreams; they know that karma is like an illusion; they understand that the world is a manifestation of the mind; they understand that results arise from causes; they understand that retribution is the accumulation of karma;
they understand that all dharmas of merit flow forth from the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of Bodhisattvas;
and they understand that all phenomena and non-phenomena are equal in their manifestation, thereby increasing and perfecting the true realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*).

The youth Sudhana entered into such wisdom, such reflection, and such mental attention; with an upright mind and pure thoughts, he prostrated himself before the pavilion, casting his entire body to the ground in earnest veneration. Inconceivable roots of goodness swiftly manifested and flowed through his body and mind, bringing him coolness, joy, and clarity. Thereafter, rising slowly from the ground, he gazed up at it with single-minded devotion, his eyes never for a moment turning away. He circumambulated the vast and great pavilion, the Universal Adornment Treasury of Vairocana, for immeasurable circuits, reflecting and attending to it, giving rise to a profound resolve.

Bowing low in reverence, he spoke these words: "This great pavilion is the dwelling place of those who have realized the profound emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—the three gates of liberation."
This great celestial palace is the dwelling place of those who have thoroughly realized that the nature of all phenomena is non-conceptual;
this great celestial palace is the dwelling place of those who understand that the fundamental limit of the dharma-realm is equal and without distinction;
this great celestial palace is the dwelling place of those who know that all realms of sentient beings are ungraspable.
This great pavilion is the dwelling place of those who know that all phenomena are without arising, abiding, or ceasing;
this great pavilion is the dwelling place of those who do not cling to anything in the world;
this great pavilion is the dwelling place of those who do not cling to any cave-dwelling or home.
This great celestial palace is the dwelling place of those who take no delight in any village or settlement;
this great celestial palace is the dwelling place of those who do not rely upon or cling to any sensory realm;
this great celestial palace is the dwelling place of those who are able to remain far removed from all signs.
This great celestial palace is the dwelling place of those who can shatter and disperse all false conceptualizations;
this great celestial palace is the dwelling place of those who know that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature;
this great celestial palace is the dwelling place of those who have severed all karma of discursive discrimination.
This great celestial palace is the dwelling place of those who are free from all conceptualizations, mind, mentation, and consciousness;
this great celestial palace is the dwelling place of those for whom all phenomena neither come nor go, neither enter nor emerge;
this great celestial palace is the dwelling place of those who have entered the profoundly deep Prajñāpāramitā.
This great pavilion is the dwelling place of those who, through skillful means, abide in the universal dharma-realm;
this great pavilion is the dwelling place of those who can tranquilly extinguish the fires of all afflictions;
this great pavilion is the dwelling place of those who, by means of supreme wisdom, sever all views, cravings, and pride.

This great celestial palace is the dwelling place of those who sport in all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, attainments (*samāpatti*), and supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*);
this great celestial palace is the dwelling place of those who observe the spheres of samādhi of all great bodhisattvas;
this great celestial palace is the dwelling place of those who dwell in the presence of all Tathāgatas, drawing near to and relying upon them.
This great celestial palace is the dwelling place of those who enter all eons into a single eon and enter a single eon into all eons without destroying their respective characteristics;
this great celestial palace is the dwelling place of those who enter all lands into a single land and enter a single land into all lands without destroying their respective characteristics;

this great celestial palace is the dwelling place of those who enter all phenomena into a single phenomenon and enter a single phenomenon into all phenomena without causing them to become confused or intermingled.

This great pavilion is the dwelling place of those who, by means of a single sentient being, enter into all sentient beings, and by means of all sentient beings, enter into a single sentient being, without destroying their respective characteristics;

this great pavilion is the dwelling place of those who, by means of a single Buddha, enter into all Buddhas, and by means of all Buddhas, enter into a single Buddha, without destroying their respective characteristics;
this great pavilion is the dwelling place of those who, within a single thought-moment, know all of the three periods of time.
This great celestial palace is the dwelling place of those who, in a single thought-moment, travel to all lands;
this great celestial palace is the dwelling place of those who manifest their bodies before all sentient beings;
this great celestial palace is the dwelling place of those whose minds constantly benefit all worlds.
This great pavilion is the dwelling place of those who have attained the power of mastery and are able to reach all places;

this great pavilion is the dwelling place of those who, although they have already transcended all worlds, constantly manifest their bodies therein without ever departing, for the sake of teaching and transforming all sentient beings;
this great pavilion is the dwelling place of those who do not rely on or cling to any land, yet travel through all Buddha-lands in order to make offerings to all Buddhas.
This great celestial palace is the dwelling place of those who, while remaining unmoved from their original location, are able to travel universally to all Buddha-fields to adorn them;
this great celestial palace is the dwelling place of those who are able to approach all Buddhas everywhere yet do not give rise to the notion of "Buddha";
this great celestial palace is the dwelling place of those who are able to rely upon all spiritual friends everywhere yet do not give rise to the notion of "spiritual friend."
This great pavilion is the dwelling place of those who abide within all the palaces of Māra yet do not cling to the realm of desire;
this great pavilion is the dwelling place of those who understand all dharmas of mind, thought, and consciousness, yet are forever free from all mental conceptions, thoughts, and views;
this great pavilion is the dwelling place of those who manifest their bodies among all sentient beings, yet give rise to no dualistic notions of self and other.
This great celestial palace is the dwelling place of those who can universally enter all worlds while perceiving no marks of differentiation within the dharma-realm;
this great celestial palace is the dwelling place of those who vow to abide through all future kalpas while perceiving no notions of length or brevity regarding those kalpas;

this great celestial palace is the dwelling place of those who, without departing from the tip of a single hair, universally manifest their bodies in accordance with all worlds throughout the ten directions.
This great celestial palace is the dwelling place of those who can expound the Dharma that is difficult to encounter;
it is the dwelling place of those who can abide in the Dharma that is difficult to understand and comprehend;
it is the dwelling place of those who can abide in the profound Dharma; it is the dwelling place of those who can abide in the non-dual Dharma.
This is the dwelling place of those who can abide in the dharma of signlessness; this is the dwelling place of those who can abide in the dharma of non-antidote;
this is the dwelling place of those who can abide in the dharma of non-apprehension;
this is the dwelling place of those who can abide in the dharma of non-proliferation; this is the dwelling place of those who can abide in the Great [Vehicle].
It is the dwelling place of those who possess great loving-kindness and great compassion;

it is the dwelling place of those who have already transcended the spheres of knowledge of all followers of the two vehicles; it is the dwelling place of those who have already surpassed all realms of Māra;
it is the dwelling place of those who are already able to remain unstained by any worldly dharmas; it is already...

It is the dwelling place of those who have reached the shore attained by all bodhisattvas; it is the dwelling place of those who have already been able to abide in the dwelling place of all Tathāgatas;
it is the dwelling place of those who, although they have already abandoned all marks, yet do not enter the fixed stage of the śrāvakas.
This is the dwelling place of one who, although having already realized that all phenomena are unarisen, does not abide in the dharmic nature of non-arising;

this is the dwelling place of one who, although having already contemplated the impurity of desire, neither realizes the dharma of freedom from desire nor dwells together with the defilement of desire;
this is the dwelling place of one who, although practicing loving-kindness, neither realizes the dharma of freedom from hatred nor dwells together with the stain of hatred.

This is the dwelling place of those who, although they contemplate all twelve links of dependent origination, do not realize the state of being free from delusion, nor do they dwell in conjunction with delusive ignorance;
this is the dwelling place of those who, although they abide in the four dhyānas, do not take birth according to those meditative states due to the power of their vows of great compassion;
this is the dwelling place of those who, although they abide in the four immeasurables, do not take birth in the form realm for the sake of transforming sentient beings.
