The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s jewel of the sovereign king who has resolved upon bodhicitta is likewise so: wherever the light of omniscience shines, all the various roots of goodness, outflowing and non-outflowing dharmas, and all merits of the devas and humans, as well as those of the two vehicles throughout the three periods of time, cannot equal it.
“Good son! For example, there is a mani-jewel in the ocean called ‘Ocean-Treasury’ (Sāgaragarbha), which universally manifests all the adornments within the ocean;
the mani-jewel of the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is likewise, for it can universally manifest all the adornments of the ocean of omniscience.”
“Good son! For example, among the Jāmbūnada gold of the heavens, there is nothing that can equal it except for the Great Mani Jewel of the Mind-King;
likewise, the Jāmbūnada gold of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s production of the bodhicitta has no equal except for the Great Jewel of the Mind-King of All-Knowledge.
“Good son! For example, suppose there is a person who is skilled in the methods for taming dragons and thus attains mastery over all dragons;

so too is it with the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, who, having resolved upon bodhicitta, attains the method for taming dragons that is omniscience, and thereby attains mastery over all the dragons of the afflictions.”
“Good son! It is like a valiant warrior who, having donned armor and taken up weapons, cannot be overcome by any enemy;

so too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, who, having donned the armor and taken up the weapons of the great mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), cannot be crushed or defeated by any enemies—whether they be karmic afflictions or various evils.

“Good son! For example, if a single *zhu* of the white *candana* sandalwood from the heavens is burned, its fragrance pervades a small thousand-world system (*sāhasra-lokadhātu*), such that the total value of all the precious jewels filling a great trichiliocosm cannot equal it.

The fragrance of the bodhicitta of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: the merit of a single thought-moment pervades the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), such that the merits of all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cannot equal it.”
“Good son! Just as when white sandalwood is applied to the body, it can completely eliminate all feverish afflictions and cause both body and mind to attain universal coolness;

so too is the incense of the bodhicitta of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva. It gives rise to omniscience and universally perfumes the body and mind, able to eliminate all delusions and feverish afflictions—such as false imaginings, discrimination, greed, anger, and ignorance—and causes them to be endowed with the coolness of wisdom.”
“Good son! Just as when sentient beings approach Mount Sumeru, they take on its color;
so too is the mountain of the bodhicitta of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: if anyone approaches it, they all attain the color of universal gnosis (sarvajñatā).”

“Good son! For example, the fragrance of the bark of the Pārijātaka tree and the Kovidāra tree cannot be matched by any of the fragrances of all the flowers in Jambudvīpa—whether they be pāṭalī, campaka, sumana, or saffron—and so forth; the tree of the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is also like this.

The fragrance of the merit of the great vows he has generated cannot be matched by any of the fragrances of the virtues of the two vehicles, such as their untainted morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.”
“Good son! For example, although the pārijātaka tree and the kovidāra tree have not yet blossomed, one should know that they are the source from which immeasurable flowers will emerge.

In the same way, the bodhicitta-tree of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, though it has not yet brought forth the flower of omniscience (sarvajñatā), should be known as the place where the countless flowers of the enlightenment of humans and devas—both with outflows (sāsrava) and without outflows (anāsrava)—are produced.”

“Good son! For example, the fragrance emitted by a garment perfumed for a single day with *pārijātaka* flowers cannot be matched even by *campaka*, *vārṣika*, or *sumana* flowers, even if they have been perfumed for a thousand years.

It is the same with the flower of the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva: the fragrance of all merits perfumed during a single lifetime pervades the presence of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions, such that it cannot be matched by the untainted merits of all those of the two vehicles, even if they were perfumed for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.”

“Good son! Just as the coconut trees growing on an island in the ocean—whose roots, trunks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are constantly harvested and enjoyed by all sentient beings without a moment’s respite;

so too is the Bodhicitta-tree of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva. From its initial arousal of the heart of compassionate vows until the attainment of Buddhahood and the duration of the True Dharma in the world, it constantly benefits all the world without interruption.”

“Good son! It is like a medicinal elixir called *harītaka*; if someone obtains it, one *liang* of it can transform a thousand *liang* of copper, causing it all to become pure gold, yet those thousand *liang* of copper cannot transform this medicine.

A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: by means of the medicine of the wisdom of dedication through the bodhicitta, they universally transform all dharmas such as karma and delusion, causing them all to become the marks of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), yet karma, delusion, and the like cannot transform their mind.”
“Good son! Just as when a small spark of fire is cast onto a heap of dry grass, its flames grow ever more intense as it consumes them;

so too is the fire of the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva: according to the collection of wholesome or unwholesome dharmas upon which it takes its object, it causes the flames of wisdom to increase and flourish further and further.”
“Good son! For example, when one lamp ignites hundreds of thousands of lamps, that original single lamp neither diminishes nor is exhausted;

the lamp of the bodhicitta of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is likewise. It universally ignites the wisdom-lamps of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, yet its own mind-lamp neither diminishes nor is exhausted.”
“Good son! For example, when a single lamp enters a dark room, it can completely dispel the darkness of hundreds of thousands of years, giving rise to light that shines universally upon all things.

The lamp of the bodhicitta of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: entering the dark room of ignorance within the minds of sentient beings, it can extinguish all karmic afflictions accumulated over immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of unspeakable eons, as well as all manner of obstacles, and give rise to the light of all-encompassing great wisdom.”
“Good son! It is like the wick of a lamp: according to its size, it emits light; if fresh oil is added, the brightness will never cease.

The lamp of the bodhicitta of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: with great vows as its wick, it emits the light of wisdom to illuminate the Dharma-realm. By adding the oil of great compassion, it transforms sentient beings, adorns the buddha-fields, performs the works of a Buddha, and manifests great majestic power without rest.”

“Good son! For example, when the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven wears his celestial crown of Jambūnada gold, the radiance of all the ornaments and adornments of the devas in the desire realm cannot outshine it, nor can any of their powers reach its level.

In the same way, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva wears the celestial crown of the great vows—the jewel of omniscience that is the bodhicitta—none of the merits of ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles can reach its level.”

“Good son! Just as when the lion king roars, the lion cubs who hear it all increase in courage and vigor, while other beasts who hear it have their fat and blood depleted and immediately flee and hide;

so too should one know that when the Buddha-lion king roars with the roar of Bodhi, the sound of omniscience acts in the same way: those bodhisattvas who hear it nourish their Dharma-body and increase their merit, while all other sentient beings of false attachments who hear it all retreat and scatter, like ice melting away.”
“Good son! It is like a person who uses a lion’s sinew to make the strings of a musical instrument; once that sound is played, all other strings snap.

In the same way, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva uses the Bodhicitta-sinew from the Tathāgata’s lion-like body of the Pāramitās as the string for the music of the Dharma; once that sound is played, all the strings of the five desires and the various merits of the two vehicles are completely severed.”

“Good son! It is like a person who takes various kinds of milk, such as that of oxen and sheep, and even if they were accumulated until they filled the great ocean, were it to receive a single drop of lion’s milk cast into it, that drop would pass through unimpeded and cause all the other milks to turn sour and spoil at once.

So too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: by applying the lion-like milk of the Tathāgata’s bodhicitta to the karma and afflictions of beginningless time, it passes through them unimpeded and causes them all to be destroyed, never again dwelling in the liberation of the two vehicles.”
“Good son! For example, the kalaviṅka bird of the Snowy Mountains possesses great power within its eggshell that no other birds can equal;

likewise, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, having given rise to the bodhicitta within the shell of saṃsāra, possesses the power of the merit of his great compassion such that no śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha can equal it.”

“Good son! Just as when the prince of the garuḍa is first born, his eyes are clear and sharp, his flight is powerful and swift, and his majestic power and capability surpass all other birds such that none can equal him even after they have grown old;

so too it is with the bodhisattva-mahāsattva. Having resolved upon bodhicitta, he becomes a prince of the garuḍas among all Tathāgatas. With pure wisdom, courageous great compassion, and the majestic power of sovereign spiritual penetrations, he cannot be equaled by any of the followers of the two vehicles, even those who have practiced the path for hundreds of thousands of kalpas.”
“Good son! It is like a strong man who, grasping a sharp spear in his hand, pierces solid and dense armor, passing straight through without obstruction;

so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, who, with courageous diligence, grasps the sharp and keen spear of the bodhicitta and the knowledge of all modes, piercing the dense armor of all latent tendencies of false views, being able to penetrate them all completely without hindrance.”

“Good son! It is like a great nāga, a warrior of immense strength; if he rouses his majestic wrath, a tumor will inevitably appear upon his forehead. As long as that tumor has not yet healed, no one among the multitudes of people in Jambudvīpa can subdue him.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva is also like this: if he gives rise to great compassion, he will certainly give rise to the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta).”

"As long as one has not yet abandoned the mind that is a wound of omniscience, the various māras, their retinues, delusions, karmas, and evil persons throughout all worlds cannot cause harm. Good son!..."

For example, suppose there is a master archer who has several disciples; although they have not yet mastered the teacher’s skills, their wisdom, skillful means, and ingenuity are such that no other person can equal them.

It is the same with a bodhisattva mahāsattva at the initial moment of generating the mind of awakening (*cittotpāda*): although they have not yet mastered the practices for omniscience or the activities of enlightenment, their vows, wisdom, understanding, and aspiration surpass all ordinary worldlings and those of the two vehicles.
“Good son! Just as a person learning archery first steadies their feet and then practices the techniques and various swordsmanship skills—since these constitute the foundation of all martial arts;

so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: wishing to learn the path of the Tathāgata’s omniscience, they must first dwell securely in the bodhicitta, and only thereafter practice all the Buddha-dharmas.”
“Good son! It is like a magician who, when about to perform a magical feat, must first give rise to the intention and recall the magical arts; only then can everything be fully accomplished.

A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: when about to manifest the various supernatural transformations of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, he must first give rise to the great bodhicitta; only then can everything be fully accomplished.”
“Good son! It is like the art of illusion, which manifests forms where there are no forms and can display all manner of transformations;

so too is the mark of the bodhicitta of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva and the illusion of omniscience. Although they have no form and cannot be seen, they are nonetheless able to universally manifest various adornments of merit throughout the dharma-realm of the ten directions.”
“Good son! It is like a wildcat:
as soon as it sees a mouse, the mouse immediately enters its hole and dares not come out again.

So too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who has resolved for bodhicitta: when he momentarily observes all delusive afflictions and karmic actions with the eye of wisdom, they all immediately flee and perish, never to arise again.”
“Good son! It is like a person who wears ornaments made of Jambu-river gold; they outshine the radiance of all other jewels, making them appear like a mass of ink.

In the same way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wears the golden ornaments of the bodhicitta and the wisdom of omniscience outshines the merit-ornaments of all ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles, rendering them entirely lusterless.”
“Good son! Just as a fine magnet, by the power of even a small portion of it, can attract and destroy all firm iron hooks and chains;

so too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: if he gives rise to a single thought of bodhicitta, he is able to utterly destroy all wrong views, the fetters of greed and desire, and the hooks and chains of ignorance.”
“Good son! It is like a magnet:
wherever it may be, if iron sees it, it immediately disperses and vanishes, with nothing remaining behind;

so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva. Having resolved upon the bodhicitta, he observes all things with wisdom; if he even momentarily beholds the various worldly karmas and afflictions, or the liberation of the two vehicles, they all immediately disperse and vanish, with nothing remaining.”

“Good son! It is like a fisherman who has skillfully entered the great ocean; no aquatic creatures can cause him harm, and even if he should enter the mouth of a makara fish, he will not be swallowed by it.

In the same way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has resolved for bodhicitta enters the ocean of birth and death; all karmas and afflictions—the various aquatic creatures—cannot cause him harm, and even if he should enter the mouth of the makara of the true reality (bhūtakoṭi) and liberation of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, he will not be obstructed by them.”

“Good son! For example, if there is a person who drinks the nectar of ambrosia, no poisons whatsoever can cause them harm. It is the same for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: having drunk the nectar-like dharma-juice of the omniscient wisdom of the bodhicitta, they do not fall into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, because they are endowed with the power of vast compassion and vows.”

“Good son! It is like a person who obtains añjana ointment and applies it to his eyes; though he can travel freely through the human world, no ordinary person can see him. In the same way, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva likewise obtains the añjana ointment of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta); by means of the skillful means of aspiration and wisdom, he enters the realm of Māra in accordance with its conditions and travels there freely, such that none of the māras can see him.”
“Good son! Just as a person who relies upon a king has no fear of others, so too it is with the bodhisattva-mahāsattva:
by relying on the sovereign power of omniscience through abiding in the bodhicitta, they have no fear of any worldly hindrances, obscurations, or the perils of the evil realms.”
“Good son! Just as a person dwelling in water does not fear being burned by fire, so too is it with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
dwelling in the water of the roots of goodness of the bodhicitta, they do not fear the fires of the liberative wisdom of all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.”
“Good son! It is like a person who, by relying upon a valiant general, has no fear of any enemies;
so too it is with the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, who, by relying upon the courageous wisdom-general of the bodhicitta, does not fear any enemies of unwholesome conduct.”
“Good son! Just as the Heavenly King Śakra, wielding the vajra-pestle, subdues and overcomes all the hosts of asuras;
so too does the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, grasping the vajra-wisdom pestle of the bodhicitta, subdue and overcome all hosts of māras, externalists, and asuras.”
“Good son! It is like a person who obtains a most supreme medicine; by taking it, they prolong their life, remaining forever robust, neither weak nor emaciated, neither aging nor ill.

In the same way, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva takes the supreme medicine of the wisdom of the bodhicitta; dwelling within birth and death for countless eons while practicing the bodhisattva path, his mind knows no weariness and is free from attachment.”
“Good son! It is like a person who prepares medicinal decoctions; they must first take pure, clear water, which is used equally in all instances.

In the same way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to cultivate all the practices and vows of a bodhisattva must first give rise to the bodhicitta, which can cause all things to be equally moistened.”
“Good son! Just as a person who wishes to protect their body must first protect the life-faculty, so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
in upholding the true Dharma of all Buddhas, one should first guard and protect the bodhicitta.”
“Good son! For example, if a person’s life-faculty is severed, all their endeavors cease and they can no longer benefit their parents or kinsmen;

so it is with the bodhisattva-mahāsattva—if they abandon the life-force of the bodhicitta and omniscience, none of their merits will be accomplished, and they will be unable to benefit all sentient beings.”
“Good son! For example, just as the great ocean cannot be destroyed by any poison;

so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: the ocean of omniscience born from the arousal of the bodhicitta cannot be destroyed by any karmas, afflictions, the minds of the two vehicles, or any poisons whatsoever.”
“Good son! For example, just as the orb of the sun cannot be eclipsed by the light of the stars, so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
the sun of the bodhicitta and the great wheel of wisdom cannot be obscured by the star-like light of the untainted wisdom and merit of all those of the Two Vehicles.

“Good son! Just as when a prince is first born, he is immediately respected by all the elder ministers because of the excellence and sovereignty of his noble lineage; so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.

Having first generated the mind of omniscience for enlightenment within the Buddha-dharma, he is born into the family of the Tathāgata as a Dharma Prince, and is immediately respected by all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who have long practiced the holy life, because of the excellence and sovereignty of the lineage of the Bodhicitta and Great Compassion.”

“Good son! For example, although a prince may be of tender age, all the great ministers pay him homage; yet while this prince respects those ministers in his heart, he should not prostrate before them, for his lineage is superior.

In the same way, although a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has only recently resolved to attain enlightenment and practices the Bodhisattva path, even senior followers of the Two Vehicles who have long cultivated pure conduct should all pay him homage upon seeing him, for he has attained the superiority of the Dharma.”

“Good son! For example, although a prince has not yet attained sovereignty over all his ministers and attendants, no prime minister or high official can equal him, because his birth is of the most exalted and superior status.

In the same way, although a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva has not yet attained mastery over all karma and afflictions, since he has already resolved upon great bodhicitta, no Arhat or Pratyekabuddha can equal him, because he possesses the noble lineage of the Tathāgata.”
“Good son! It is like a pure maṇi jewel, which is seen as impure because the eye is clouded by cataracts;

so too it is with the bodhisattva-mahāsattva. The nature of the great bodhicitta is inherently pure, yet because all sentient beings have eyes clouded by the cataracts of ignorance and lack faith, they deem it impure.”

“Good son! It is like a medicine that is sustained by a mantra; if there are sentient beings who see it, hear it, dwell with it, or even touch it, all their various illnesses will be completely eliminated.

The medicine of the bodhicitta of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this: all roots of goodness, wisdom, and skillful means are collectively sustained by the power of aspiration and knowledge. If there are sentient beings who see it, hear it, dwell with it, follow it, or mindfully recollect it, all the diseases of their afflictions will be entirely eradicated.”
“Good son! For example, if there is a person who constantly consumes ambrosia, their body will ultimately remain unchanged and indestructible;

so it is with the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: if they constantly recollect and maintain the ambrosia of the bodhicitta, they will cause the body of their vows and wisdom to remain ultimately indestructible.”
“Good son! For example, if there is a person wearing a garment made of swan feathers, no mud or water can stain it;
so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: the white swan-feather garment of the pure bodhicitta cannot be stained by any cycle of birth and death, nor by any karmas or afflictions.”
“Good son! It is like a raft made of bamboo and wood, which, when bound together with ropes so that they do not scatter, can travel freely upon a river.

In the same way, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva likewise uses the rope of the great vow and wisdom of the bodhicitta to hold all practices together so that they do not scatter; thus, he travels freely within the swift current of the Dharma, proceeding in accordance with it to enter the ocean of omniscience.”
“Good son! It is like a wooden man:
if it lacks its internal mechanisms, the body will fall apart; though its limbs are complete, they cannot move.
So too it is with the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: if he abandons the bodhicitta, his practice will disperse, and he will be unable to accomplish any of the Buddha-dharmas.”
“Good son! Just as a wheel-turning king possesses a precious sandalwood called ‘Elephant Treasury,’ the burning of which causes his fourfold army to all soar into the air;

so too is the incense of the bodhicitta of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva. If this mind is generated, it immediately causes all the roots of goodness of the Bodhisattva to forever transcend the triple world, proceeding toward the Tathāgata’s wisdom that pervades the inexhaustible dharma-realm of empty space.”
“Good son! For example, just as a diamond is produced only from a diamond or a diamond-bearing site, and cannot be produced from any other place of jewels;

so too is the diamond of the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva. It is produced only from the diamond-site of great compassion that rescues and protects sentient beings, and from the gold-site of the ability to contemplate the realm of all-knowledge, but not from the roots of goodness of other ordinary beings.”
“Good son! It is like a tree named ‘Rootless,’ for which no basis or place of dwelling can ever be found, yet all its branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are in full and flourishing abundance;

so too is the Bodhicitta-tree of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva. Although the nature of omniscience has no basis upon which to rely, it is able to grow forth the branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits of merit, wisdom, spiritual powers, and great vows, benefiting the world and universally covering all things.”
“Good son! Just as a diamond jewel cannot be contained or supported by any inferior, wicked, or cracked vessel, but only by a complete precious vessel made of gold or silver;

so too is the diamond-like wisdom-jewel of the bodhicitta generated by a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. It cannot be contained or supported within the evil vessels of other inferior beings of meager merit—those characterized by stinginess, envy, broken precepts, hatred, laziness, distracted mindfulness, or lack of wisdom—nor can it be contained within the vessels of those who have fallen away from their sublime vows, or those who are distracted and possessed of evil thoughts. It can only be contained within the precious vessel of the Bodhisattva’s profound mind.”
“Good son! Just as a diamond can pierce all manner of jewels, so too is the diamond of the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva; it is able to penetrate through all the jewels of the dharmas.”

“Good son! For example, just as a vajra can shatter all solid mountains of precious gems, so too is the vajra of the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva; it can utterly destroy all mountains of false views.”
“Good son! For example, just as a diamond, though broken and incomplete, still surpasses all other jewels and golden ornaments;

so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: although the jewel of omniscience born of the resolve for bodhicitta may be of inferior aspiration and slightly impaired, it still surpasses all the merits of the two vehicles.”
“Good son! For example, just as a diamond, even if it has flaws or fractures, can still eliminate all poverty and suffering;

so too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: although the jewel of omniscience born from their resolve for enlightenment may have many deficiencies in their observance of the precepts, they will ultimately be able to abandon all of birth and death.”
“Good son! For example, just as even a minute fragment of a diamond can destroy all manner of objects, so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
by giving rise to the bodhicitta, even for a single moment, they immediately shatter all delusions of ignorance.”
“Good son! For example, just as a diamond cannot be obtained by ordinary or inferior people;

so too is the diamond of the bodhicitta—the treasure of omniscience—of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, which cannot be obtained by those of inferior intent, such as ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles.”

“Good son! For example, just as a person who does not recognize jewels does not know the power of a diamond and thus cannot make use of it, so too is it with the diamond of the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva:
those of dull faculties, lacking wisdom, and inferior ordinary beings do not understand its power and cannot utilize it.”
“Good son! For example, just as a diamond cannot be destroyed, so too is the diamond of the bodhicitta of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva; no phenomena whatsoever can destroy it.”
“Good son! Just as a vajra-pestle cannot be held by any of the great strongmen, except for those possessing the power of Mahānārāyaṇa;

so too is the vajra-pestle of the bodhicitta of a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva. Although all followers of the two vehicles possess great power, none can hold it, except for a Bodhisattva’s vast, causal, and firm roots of goodness.”
“Good son! For example, just as a diamond cannot be destroyed by any object, yet can universally destroy all objects without obstruction, and its essential nature is not diminished;

so too is the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva mahāsattva. Throughout countless eons across the three periods of time, it universally teaches and transforms sentient beings and practices austerities—accomplishing all that is beyond the reach of any worldly being, śrāvaka, or pratyekabuddha. Yet this great diamond-mind of omniscience remains ultimately firm and solid, without diminution; it does not give rise to weariness or fatigue, nor does it encounter any obstruction.”
“Good son! For example, just as a diamond cannot be supported by any other portion of the earth except for a foundation of solid, thick diamond;

so too is the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, which no practices or vows of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas can support, except for the firm power of wisdom of great bodhisattvas who are advancing toward the path of sarvajñatā.”
“Good son! Just as a vajra vessel has no cracks or fissures, so that when used to hold water, it never leaks or allows it to be lost;

likewise, the vajra-jewel vessel of the great bodhicitta of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also thus: its essential nature is without outflows, and through firm dedication, it holds the water of roots of goodness, never allowing them to be lost.”
“Good son! Just as the vajra-wheel can support the great earth, preventing it from scattering or breaking apart, and preventing it from sinking;
so too is the bodhicitta of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, which can support all the practices and vows of a bodhisattva, preventing them from falling and sinking into the triple world.”

“Good son! For example, just as a diamond remains in water for a long time without rotting or decaying, so too is the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva; throughout all kalpas, while remaining amidst the karma and afflictions of saṃsāra, it neither rots nor decays.”

“Good son! For example, just as a diamond cannot be burned or heated by any great fire, so too is the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva; it cannot be burned or heated by any fires of the afflictions within saṃsāra.”

“Good son! For example, in this world-system, when all Buddhas are about to attain perfect enlightenment, subdue the four māras, realize all-knowledge, and sit upon the site of awakening, it can only be supported by the adamantine seat at the adamantine foundation of the three-thousandfold world-system; it cannot be accomplished by any other seat.

The seat of the bodhicitta of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is likewise: it can sustain all the bodhisattva’s vows and practices, the various pāramitās, the fulfillment of all patiences, the deep entry into the stages, the perfection of roots of goodness, the various dedications, the reception of the Buddha’s prophecy, the cultivation and increase of all bodhisattva paths, the approaching and making offerings to all Tathāgatas, the receiving and upholding of the great rain-clouds of the Dharma in accordance with them, the rapid growth of firm great compassion, and the accomplishment of all wisdom of vows, even unto the ultimate state of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; it can be sustained only by adamantine wisdom, and cannot be accomplished by any other roots of goodness.
“Good son! Just as when a wheel-turning monarch travels through the four continents, the wheel-treasure leads among his seven treasures;
so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: acting as a Dharma-wheel-turning monarch to benefit all beings, the treasure of the bodhicitta is what leads the way.”
“Good son! For example, among all the weapons used in the world to eliminate enemies, the bow and arrow are the most excellent;
likewise, for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, among all the requisites for practice, the bodhicitta is the foremost, for it is capable of completely eliminating all afflictions, birth, death, and enmity.”
“Good son! For example, among all water-born flowers, the utpala is the most excellent; among land-born flowers, the campaka is the most excellent.”

The bodhicitta of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is likewise so: the essence of omniscience is like the utpala flower, and the mind of great compassion is like the campaka flower, which is foremost because it can extinguish the karma and afflictions of sentient beings.
“Good son! Just as among all vehicles, the ship is foremost because it travels swiftly, brings peace and happiness to the body, and enables one to reach the great ocean and arrive at the other shore;

so too is it with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: among all those of the two vehicles, the Great Bodhicitta is foremost, for it can swiftly transport and deliver sentient beings, bringing them peace and happiness to reach the further shore.”
“Good son! Just as, among all the waters in the world, rainwater is foremost;

so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: among all the waters of samādhi, the bodhicitta is foremost, for it is able to produce the nectar-like flavor of all meditative concentrations and liberations.”
“Good son! For example, among all salts, saindhava salt is the foremost; it can eliminate all illnesses and clarify the eyes.

In the same way, among the eighty-four thousand dharmas, the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is the most supreme, for it can eradicate the afflictions, karma, and grave illnesses of all sentient beings, and give rise to the light of wisdom.”
“Good son! For example, among all milks, cow’s milk is foremost; it can eliminate all diseases and cause people to increase their lifespan.

The bodhicitta of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is likewise: among the ambrosial flavors of all true dharmas, it is the most supreme, for it can eliminate the diseases of the afflictions of sentient beings and cause the life-force of wisdom of bodhisattvas to increase.”

“Good son! This bodhicitta accomplishes such immeasurable and boundless, even unspeakably unspeakable, fully perfected and supreme merits. If there are sentient beings who resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they shall obtain these fully perfected and supreme dharmas of merit.”

"Noble son! You have attained a great benefit and possess an excellent reputation, for you are now able to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and seek the conduct of a bodhisattva, having already acquired such great merit that is difficult to practice and difficult to accumulate."
The Flower Adornment Sutra of the Buddha, Mahāvaipulya, Scroll Thirty-Six;
The Flower Adornment Sutra of the Buddha, Mahāvaipulya, Scroll Thirty-Seven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā of Kaśmīra by Imperial Decree.
In the "Chapter on the Vows and Practices of Samantabhadra for Entering the Realm of Inconceivable Liberation," at that time,
Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the youth Sudhana, saying:
"O son of good family!"
Regarding what you have asked— how a bodhisattva studies the bodhisattva conduct and cultivates the bodhisattva path—
O son of good family!

You may enter this Great Pavilion of Vairocana’s Adorned Treasury and observe it thoroughly; then you will be able to understand all the trainings of bodhisattvas. Having trained in the practices of a bodhisattva, you will be able to carry them out to perfection and accomplish immeasurable merit.
At that time, the youth Sudhana, having respectfully circumambulated Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva three times to the right, addressed him, saying:
"I pray only that the Great Sage will open the gate of this pavilion, so that I may enter."

Then, Maitreya Bodhisattva went before the Vairocana-alaṃkāra-garbha pavilion; he immediately snapped his fingers with his right hand, making a sound, whereupon the door opened, and he commanded Sudhana to enter.
Sudhana’s heart rejoiced; having entered, he closed the door again and beheld that pavilion as vast and immeasurable as space.

Its ground was composed of incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) jewels, and it contained incalculable palaces, incalculable gates, incalculable windows, incalculable stairways, incalculable railings, and incalculable pathways, all fashioned from the seven treasures.
Incalculable banners, incalculable standards, and incalculable parasols were arranged in rows all around.
Countless *asaṃkhyeya* necklaces of various jewels, countless necklaces of white pearls, countless necklaces of red pearls, and countless necklaces of *siṃhamaṇi* pearls hung down everywhere;
they were further adorned with countless crescent moons, countless full moons, and countless silk ribbons;

and they were interlaced and decorated with countless lion-bannered nets, countless *maṇi* jewel nets, countless exquisite golden nets, and countless gold-threaded nets, which were spread out and draped over them.
There were incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) precious bells and incalculable precious chimes that emitted lovely sounds when stirred by the wind;

incalculable varieties of celestial flowers were strewn about; incalculable celestial jewel-garlands and sashes were suspended; incalculable censers of various jewels were arrayed; incalculable fine and exquisite gold dust rained down; incalculable jewel-mirrors were hung; incalculable jewel-lamps were lit; incalculable jewel-robes were spread out; incalculable jewel-canopies were set in rows; incalculable jewel-poles were held aloft; incalculable jewel-seats were prepared, upon which incalculable jewel-silk cloths were spread as coverings;

and incalculable images of boys and girls made of precious Jambūnada gold, incalculable images of various forms made of diverse jewels, and incalculable images of Bodhisattvas made of wondrous jewels filled every place, majestic and magnificent in their splendor.

Countless flocks of birds emitted harmonious and elegant sounds that inspired love and joy; it was adorned with countless precious *utpala* flowers, countless precious *padma* flowers, countless precious *kumuda* flowers, and countless precious *puṇḍarīka* flowers;
countless precious trees were arranged in successive rows;
and countless precious plantain trees provided subtle and exquisite adornment.
There were incalculable jeweled walkways with paths demarcated by golden cords;
incalculable jeweled ponds filled with fragrant water;
and incalculable jeweled bridges with soaring spans constructed like clouds.
Countless *asaṃkhyeya* jewel grounds were interlaced with exquisite pavements;
countless *maṇi* jewels emitted great radiance;
and countless varieties of sublime sounds praised its great merit. With such immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* ornaments as these, it was adorned.

Furthermore, Sudhana saw that within each pavilion there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of pavilions; each and every pavilion was adorned in various ways, exactly as described above—vast, magnificent, and beautiful, all equal to space, appearing with perfect clarity like forms and shadows, mutually reflecting one another without obstruction and without being confused or intermingled.
Within a single location, the youth Sudhana saw all locations;
likewise, he saw all locations within each and every one.
In this manner, without exception, he saw everything within every single object in the same way.

At that time, the youth Sudhana, beholding such various and inconceivable realms of sovereign mastery within the Vairocana-Adorned Treasury Pavilion, gave rise to great love and reverence. He leaped for joy immeasurably; his body and mind became supple, and he was suffused with the moisture of bliss.

He was freed from all conceptualizations, removed all obstructions, and extinguished all delusions. What he saw he did not forget; what he heard he could remember; and what he contemplated remained undisturbed. He entered the dharma-door of unimpeded liberation;
with an unobstructed mind, he universally directed his heart toward making offerings to all.
With unimpeded eyes, they universally beheld all subtle realms;
with unimpeded bodies, they everywhere paid reverent homage to all.
By the majestic spiritual power of Maitreya Bodhisattva, they saw their own bodies pervading all the pavilions, fully perceiving various inconceivable states of sovereign mastery.
That is to say:

some see Maitreya Bodhisattva when he first resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, seeing his name, his clan, and the spiritual friend who awakened him; how he planted such roots of goodness, lived for such a lifespan, encountered such eons, and dwelt in the presence of such Buddhas;
and how, in such adorned lands, he cultivated such practices and made such vows.
He clearly perceives all those Tathāgatas, their respective assemblies, their lifespans, and the duration for which he attended upon and made offerings to them.
Some see Maitreya first realize the Samādhi of Compassionate Mind, from which time forth he is called the "Kindly One" (Maitreya);
some see Maitreya practicing all difficult and wondrous deeds, fulfilling all the Pāramitās;

some see him attain Patience (Kṣānti), or see him dwell in the Stages (Bhūmi); some see him adorning various Buddha-fields, or see him upholding all the Buddha-teachings as a Great Dharma Master, attaining the Patience of Non-arising (Anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
In some instances, they see [the Bodhisattva] at a certain time, in a certain place, in the presence of a certain Tathāgata, receiving the prophecy of unexcelled bodhi;
at other times, they see him acting as a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin), causing all sentient beings to abide in the ten paths of wholesome action;
or he acts as a world-protector (lokapāla) to bring benefit and joy to sentient beings.
Sometimes he becomes Śakra-devendra to rebuke the five desires;
sometimes he becomes the king of the Yāma Heaven to praise non-heedlessness for those devas;
and sometimes he becomes the king of the Tuṣita Heaven to extol the merit of the Bodhisattvas who are in their final birth.
Sometimes he becomes the King of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati), manifesting the bodhisattva’s adornments of transformation;
sometimes he becomes the King of the Heaven of Mastery over Others’ Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin), preaching the dharma of the sovereign mastery of all Buddhas;
or he acts as a Mara King, teaching that all phenomena are entirely impermanent.
Sometimes he becomes a Brahma King, preaching to them the various meditative concentrations and immeasurable joys;
sometimes he becomes an Asura King, preaching for his assembly how to sever all arrogance and intoxication, enter the great ocean of wisdom, and realize that all phenomena are like illusions;
or again, he is seen dwelling in the realm of Yama, emitting great radiance to rescue those suffering in the hells.
In some instances, he was seen in the realm of hungry ghosts, bestowing food and drink to relieve their hunger and thirst;
in others, he was seen in the paths of animals, employing various skillful means to subdue sentient beings;
and yet again, he was seen preaching the Dharma to the assemblies of the World-Protecting Heavenly Kings.
Or again, they see him preaching the Dharma for the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven King;
or again, they see him preaching the Dharma for the assembly of the Yāma Heaven King;
or again, they see him preaching the Dharma for the assembly of the Tuṣita Heaven King.
Or again, he may see him preaching the Dharma to the assembly of the King of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations;
or again, he may see him preaching the Dharma to the assembly of the King of the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations;
or again, he may see him preaching the Dharma to the assembly of all the Mara kings.
Or again, he may see [the Buddha] preaching the Dharma to an assembly of Great Brahma Kings;
or again, he may see him preaching the Dharma to an assembly of various great Dragon Kings;
or again, he may see him preaching the Dharma to an assembly of Yakṣa and Rākṣasa kings.
Or again, he sees [the Buddha] preaching the Dharma to an assembly of Gandharva and Kinnara kings;
or again, he sees him preaching the Dharma to an assembly of Asura and Dānava kings;
or again, he sees him preaching the Dharma to an assembly of Garuḍa and Mahoraga kings.
Or again, he may see him preaching the Dharma to an assembly of all other humans, non-humans, and so forth;
or again, he may see him preaching the Dharma to an assembly of all śrāvakas;
or again, he may see him preaching the Dharma to an assembly of all pratyekabuddhas.
In some instances, he was seen preaching the Dharma for bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds;
in others, he was seen preaching the Dharma for the assembly of bodhisattvas practicing dedication, up to those who have attained the stage of patience and dwell in non-retrogression;
and in yet others, he was seen preaching the Dharma for the assembly of bodhisattvas bound by only one more birth who have already received the empowerment.
In some instances, they saw the praise and exposition of all the most supreme merits of the Bodhisattva’s stages, from the first stage up to the tenth;
in others, they saw the praise and exposition of the fulfillment of all the pāramitās;
and in others, they saw the praise and exposition of entering the gates of the various patiences.
In some places, they saw the praise and exposition of various great samādhi gates;
in others, the praise and exposition of the gate of profound liberation;
and in still others, the praise and exposition of the realms of dhyāna, samādhi, and supernormal powers.
In some places, they see the praise and exposition of the various bodhisattva practices and skillful means;
in others, they see the praise and exposition of the various great vows that give rise to them;
and in yet others, they see themselves together with fellow bodhisattvas who practice in harmony.
They praise and speak of the worldly arts of livelihood and craftsmanship, discussing in all places various supreme skillful means for taming and bringing to maturity all sentient beings;
or they see Maitreya and the bodhisattvas who are bound to one more birth praising and speaking of the gateways of consecration for all Buddhas;
or they see Maitreya practicing with diligence, his body and mind free from weariness for hundreds or thousands of years.
Some see Maitreya walking for meditation, reciting, or copying sutras without ever resting;
some see Maitreya employing various skillful means to preach the Dharma for the sake of the multitude;
and some see Maitreya entering into various meditative concentrations and the four immeasurable minds.
Some entered the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) and the various liberations (*vimokṣa*);
some entered samādhis and, through the power of skillful means, manifested various supernatural transformations;

some beheld all the hosts of bodhisattvas, who had all entered various transformation-samādhis (*nirmāṇasamādhi*), each emitting from every single pore of their bodies clouds of all manner of transformation-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*).
In some places, they saw clouds of celestial hosts appearing;
in others, clouds of nāga hosts appearing;
and in others, clouds of yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, the world-protectors, and universal monarchs appearing.
In some instances, they see clouds of bodies appearing as minor kings, princes, ministers, officials, elders, and householders;
in others, they see clouds of bodies appearing as śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas;
and in others, they see clouds of bodies appearing with the majestic power and virtue of all Tathāgatas.
In some places, they saw the manifestation of clouds of transformation bodies for all sentient beings;
in others, they saw the emergence of all manner of sublime sounds, praising the various Dharma-gates of the bodhisattvas.
That is to say:
some see the gateway of praising the merit of generating the bodhicitta;

others see the gateway of praising the merits of the perfection of giving, as well as the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, aspirational power, and primordial wisdom.

In some instances, they see praises being spoken regarding the various means of integration (*saṃgraha-vastu*), meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa-citta*), as well as the various samādhis, attainments (*samāpatti*), supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), clarities (*vidyā*), dhāraṇīs, eloquence (*pratibhāna*), truths (*satya*), knowledges (*jñāna*), tranquility and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), conditions (*pratyaya*), and the gateways of merit based on various supports;

or they see praises being spoken regarding the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), right efforts (*samyak-prahāṇa*), bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, the vehicle of the bodhisattvas, the stages (*bhūmi*), the patiences (*kṣānti*), the practices (*caryā*), and the vows (*praṇidhāna*)—that is, all such gateways of merit;
or again, within these, they see various Tathāgatas in diverse assemblies, surrounded by great multitudes.

Furthermore, he clearly perceives all the birthplaces, lineages, physical forms, lifespans, lands and eons, names, sites of enlightenment, assemblies, the benefits of their preaching, and the duration for which their teachings remain—all of these being diverse and distinct.
At that time, the youth Sudhana again beheld within those various pavilions inside the Vairocana-alaṃkāra-garbha a single pavilion,
lofty, vast, and exquisitely beautiful; it encompassed all the magnificent adornments of every other pavilion,
being supreme and peerless before them, and within it he saw entirely the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system.
In this world— within ten billion sets of four continents, ten billion Jambudvīpas, and ten billion Tuṣita heavens— in each and every one,
the Bodhisattva Maitreya descends from the womb of a lotus treasury to be born;
the Śakra and Brahmā kings receive him by supporting his head, and he walks seven steps, observing the ten directions as a Great Master.
He uttered the lion’s roar, appearing as a youth dwelling in palaces and sporting in gardens;
for the sake of all-knowledge, he leaped over the city walls to leave the household life, manifested various ascetic practices, showed himself receiving the milk-gruel,
proceeded to the site of enlightenment, subdued all demons, and attained equal and perfect awakening.

One observes that the Brahma Kings who entreated the Bodhi-tree Buddha to turn the wheel of the sublime Dharma, his ascension to celestial palaces to expound the Dharma, the number of kalpas and the span of his lifespan, the assemblies and their adornments, the Buddha-fields he purified, the practices and vows he cultivated, the majestic power he manifested, the skillful means he employed to teach and mature all sentient beings, and the distribution of his relics and the preservation of his bequeathed teachings—all of these were entirely different.
At that time, Sudhana saw his own body there, serving and making offerings to all those Tathāgatas;

he also saw, within all those great assemblies and great maṇḍalas, all the Buddha-activities, which he retained in memory without forgetting. By the power of empowerment, he attained unimpeded penetration, seeking with diligent vigor, and dwelt securely on the ground of wisdom.

Furthermore, I heard that within all the pavilions, the jeweled nets and bells, as well as all the musical instruments, were all resonating with the inconceivable, subtle, and wondrous sounds of the Dharma, expounding various teachings.

That is to say: some speak of bodhisattvas generating the mind of enlightenment; some speak of practicing the perfections (*pāramitā*); some speak of various vows; some speak of the stages (*bhūmi*); some speak of the practice of mastery over supernormal powers and the mind; some speak of reverently making offerings to the Tathāgatas; some speak of adorning the buddha-fields; and some speak of the differences in the Buddhas' preaching of the Dharma. Of all such Buddha-dharmas as mentioned above, he hears their sounds entirely, understanding them thoroughly and explaining them with clarity.

Furthermore, one hears that in such-and-such a place, within such-and-such a world, there is a certain bodhisattva who, having heard a certain dharma-gate and being exhorted by a certain spiritual friend, has resolved upon the bodhicitta and is being led to cultivate sublime practices.

In a certain kalpa, at a certain place, in the presence of a certain Tathāgata, within a certain assembly, they heard of the such-and-such merits of a certain Tathāgata; they gave rise to such-and-such a mind, planted such-and-such vows, and cultivated such-and-such vast roots of goodness. Having practiced the bodhisattva path for a certain number of kalpas, after that duration of time, they shall attain Buddhahood with such-and-such a name, such-and-such a lifespan, and such-and-such a land, fully adorned with all merits. Fulfilling such-and-such vows, they shall be able, by means of such-and-such supreme skillful means, to teach, transform, and subdue such-and-such sentient beings, as well as such-and-such assemblies of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma remained in the world for as many kalpas as these, benefiting such immeasurable sentient beings.

Some heard that in a certain place, within a certain world, a certain bodhisattva was extensively cultivating the practice of the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), being able to relinquish what is difficult to give; likewise, they cultivated the perfections of pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), patience (*kṣānti*), diligence (*vīrya*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Others heard that in a certain place, within a certain world, a certain bodhisattva, for the sake of seeking the Dharma, renounced his royal throne, as well as all precious jewels, wife, children, retinue, head, eyes, hands, feet, and every part of his body, without any sense of stinginess.

Or they may hear that in a certain place, within a certain world-system, there is a certain bodhisattva who protects the True Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata, acting as a great Dharma teacher, extensively practicing the gift of Dharma, loftily erecting the banner of Dharma, blowing the great conch of Dharma, beating the great drum of Dharma, raining down the great rain of Dharma, constructing Buddha-stūpas and temples, fashioning images of the Buddha, adorning them with various exquisite and magnificent ornaments, and bestowing all instruments of happiness upon sentient beings;

or they may hear that in a certain place, within a certain world-system, a certain Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment during a certain kalpa, in such a land, amidst such an assembly, with such a lifespan, preaching such a Dharma, fulfilling such vows, and transforming such immeasurable sentient beings, manifesting the realization of unsurpassed Bodhi before their very eyes.

When the youth Sudhana heard such inconceivable and subtle sounds of the Dharma, his body and mind were filled with joy, becoming supple, serene, and radiant; he immediately attained immeasurable gateways of dhāraṇī;

he immediately attained immeasurable gateways of eloquence, various dhyānas, various patiences, various great vows and practices, various pāramitās, various supernormal powers, various clarities, as well as various liberations and gateways of samādhi.
Furthermore, within all the precious mirrors, he saw the manifestation of immeasurable varieties of forms and images, namely:
some were assemblies of Buddhas at their sites of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa),
and some were assemblies of Bodhisattvas at their sites of enlightenment.
In some cases, they see the assembly circles of the śrāvakas;
in others, they see the assembly circles of the pratyekabuddhas;
and in others, they see pure worlds.
Some see impure worlds; some see both pure and impure worlds;
some see both impure and pure worlds.
Some see Buddha-worlds; some see worlds without Buddhas; some see small worlds.
Some see intermediate worlds;
some see great worlds; some see subtle worlds.
Some see vast worlds; some see Indra’s net worlds; some see inverted worlds.
Some see worlds turned upward;
some see worlds on their sides; some see level worlds.
In some cases, they see worlds inhabited by hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts;
in others, they see worlds filled with devas and humans.
Within such various worlds, they see countless great bodhisattvas, either walking or sitting, engaged in various activities.
Some were seen practicing dhyāna;
some were cultivating wisdom;
and some were giving rise to great compassion and pitying sentient beings.
Some compose various treatises to benefit the world;
some instruct their disciples;
and some personally uphold [the teachings].
Whether writing, reciting, questioning, or answering, they performed repentance during the three periods of the day and dedicated their merit through the making of vows.

Furthermore, they saw from within all the jeweled pillars the emission of great nets of light from *maṇi* kings—light that was blue, yellow, red, white, crystal-colored, quartz-colored, indranīla-colored, rainbow-colored, or the exquisite true-gold color of Jāmbūnada, or appearing in the colors of all various radiances.
Furthermore, he saw images of maidens made of Jambūnada gold and various precious jewels, some holding clouds of flowers,
some holding clouds of garments,
and some holding banners and streamers.
Some held flower garlands and canopies;
some carried various kinds of ointments and powdered incense;
and some held exquisite nets of mani jewels.
Some hang golden chains;
some drape necklaces;
some raise their arms, holding up ornaments of adornment.
Some lowered their heads, their maṇi crowns hanging down; they bowed their bodies in reverent gazing, their eyes never for a moment leaving him, as they stood with palms joined.
Furthermore, he saw that from those pearl necklaces there constantly issued fragrant water, endowed with the eight meritorious qualities, flowing forth without end.

Lapis lazuli necklaces emit hundreds of thousands of rays of light that shine forth simultaneously; banners, streamers, nets, canopies, and all such articles are all adorned with the treasury of the sovereign maṇi-jewels and various precious gems, causing all who behold them to rejoice.

Furthermore, he saw various lotus ponds filled with *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers, each producing immeasurable blossoms—some as large as a hand, some as long as a cubit, and others as wide and broad as a chariot wheel.
Within every single flower, various forms and images were manifested as ornamental adornments.
That is to say:

the forms of men, the forms of women, the forms of boys, the forms of girls, Śakra, Brahmā, the World-Protectors, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all bodhisattvas—all such various and wondrous forms—each with palms joined, bowed their bodies in reverent salutation.
I also saw the Tathāgata sitting cross-legged, his body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
Furthermore, upon that ground of pure lapis lazuli, within every single step, there appeared inconceivable varieties of forms and colors.
That is to say:
the forms and images of worlds, the forms and images of bodhisattvas, the forms and images of Tathāgatas, and the forms and images of the adornments of various pavilions.
Furthermore, within each and every thing—the branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits of the jewel trees—they all behold various kinds of half-body forms and images.
That is to say:

the half-body forms of Buddhas; the half-body forms of Bodhisattvas; and the half-body forms of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, the World Protectors, universal monarchs, minor kings, princes, ministers, high officials, elders, householders, boys, girls, and the fourfold assembly.
Their various forms and appearances were such that some held flower garlands; some held necklaces;
and some held all manner of ornamental accessories.
Some bowed their bodies with palms joined in reverence, gazing up at him with single-minded devotion, their eyes never wavering for a moment;
some offered praises;
others entered into samādhi, their bodies all adorned with the primary and secondary marks, universally radiating various kinds of colored light.
That is to say:

golden light, silver light, coral-colored light, *duṣara*-gold light, indranīla-blue light, the light of the color of the Vairocana-maṇi-king jewel, the light of the colors of all manner of jewels, and the light of the *campaka* flower—such lights as these all issue forth from the thirty-two marks of his own body.
Furthermore, he saw from within all those crescent-shaped ornaments on the towers emerge the various radiances of incalculable suns, moons, and stars, universally illuminating the ten directions.

Furthermore, he saw all manner of exquisite pavilions and various palaces, with walls and four sides made of many jewels in diverse colors. Within every single step, all kinds of precious gems served as adornments; within each and every gem, there appeared Maitreya practicing the bodhisattva path throughout past kalpas—whether giving away his head or eyes, or giving away his hands, feet, lips, tongue, teeth, ears, nose, flesh, blood, skin, marrow, and even his nails and hair—sacrificing all such things without exception;
as well as his wives, concubines, sons, daughters, slaves, servants, entertainers, handmaidens, and all his retinues, along with cities, towns, villages, palaces, and gardens.
Whether it be the sovereignty of Jambudvīpa or the four continents, with their various riches, pleasures, honors, and powers;
or the status of great and small kings; or various requisites, timely food and drink, and exquisite couches for rest and repose;
or exquisite jeweled vessels;
Whether it be chariots drawn by four horses or whatever else they may require, he gives them all as alms.
For those in prison suffering various hardships and calamities, he causes them to escape; for those whose bodies are bound and who face execution, he brings about their liberation.
For those who are afflicted and entangled by various illnesses, he provides medical treatment and bestows medicine so that they may be cured;
for those who have entered onto wrong paths, he shows them the correct path;
or he acts as a mariner to enable them to cross the great ocean, ensuring that all sentient beings do not lose their way at the ferry crossing.
Sometimes he becomes a horse-king to rescue all sentient beings, causing them to escape all the evil perils of rākṣasas;
sometimes he becomes various great wise seers, skillfully expounding various treatises to benefit sentient beings;
or sometimes he becomes a wheel-turning monarch, exhorting them to cultivate the ten wholesome paths of action.
Some become kings of physicians, skillfully treating all manner of illnesses;
some are filial and obedient toward their parents, reverently making offerings to them;
some draw near to virtuous friends, following and listening to their teachings.
Sometimes they appear as śrāvakas, sometimes as pratyekabuddhas, sometimes as bodhisattvas, or sometimes as tathāgatas, teaching and subduing all sentient beings;
or they manifest various supreme birthplaces to bring to maturity all sentient beings within those birthplaces;

or they act as Dharma masters, carrying out all the teachings of the Tathāgata through various modes of deportment, receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting them, observing them minutely, and reflecting upon them according to principle; they establish Buddhist stūpas and fashion images of the Buddha, adorning each one with precious ornaments and various decorations, whether making offerings themselves or encouraging others to do so—using ointments, scattered flowers, oil lamps, garlands, and canopies, arranging various offerings, and performing prostrations with reverence—continuing such deeds without interruption.

Or they may see [the Buddha] seated upon a lion throne, extensively expounding the Dharma, exhorting all sentient beings to dwell securely in the ten wholesome paths of action, to single-mindedly take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, to receive and uphold the five precepts and the eightfold fast-day precepts, to leave the household life to hear the Dharma, to receive, uphold, read, and recite it, to maintain right mindfulness and mental attention, and to practice in accordance with the truth; even seeing Maitreya Bodhisattva seated upon a lion throne, proclaiming the essentials of the Dharma and revealing the bodhi of all Buddhas.
Furthermore, he saw Maitreya, throughout hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asamkhyeya kalpas, practicing all the perfections in every form.

He also saw all the spiritual friends whom Maitreya had previously served, all adorned with every merit; he likewise saw himself in the presence of each of those spiritual friends, drawing near to them and making offerings, receiving and practicing their instructions, even until he reached the stage of consecration (abhiṣeka).
At that time, all his spiritual friends addressed Sudhana with gentle words, saying:
"Welcome, young man!
As you now behold these inconceivable deeds of the Bodhisattva, do not give rise to weariness or distaste."
At that time, the youth Sudhana attained the power of unforgetting right mindfulness;
he attained the pure eye that perceives the ten directions;
and he attained the unhindered wisdom of skillful observation.
Because they have attained the sovereign wisdom of all bodhisattvas;
because they have attained the vast understanding of all bodhisattvas who have already entered the stage of wisdom;
and because within each and every object of the various pavilions, they see all such things as well as other immeasurable, inconceivable, and sovereignly adorned realms.
For example, suppose there is a person who, while dreaming, sees various things, namely:
all cities, villages, palaces, gardens, mountain forests, rivers, ponds, clothing, food and drink, and even all manner of articles for sustaining life;
or they see all kinds of delightful songs, praises, music, assemblies, and various diversions.
Or they may see their own parents, brothers, and inner and outer relatives;
or they may see the great ocean, Sumeru, the king of mountains, and even all the celestial palaces and the affairs of the four continents, such as Jambudvīpa;
or they may see their own bodies reaching a vast size of hundreds of thousands of yojanas, with dwellings, clothing, and various meritorious qualities—all adornments being perfectly proportionate.
That is to say:

during the daytime, for immeasurable periods, he remains neither sleeping nor reclining, experiencing all manner of peace and bliss, fully endowed with every sovereignty. Upon awakening from sleep, he realizes it was a dream; he is far removed from all notions of peace and bliss, and there is no longer any perception of the duration of time. Yet, he is able to clearly remember the events he witnessed, following them all in accordance with reality without ever forgetting.
The youth Sudhana was likewise thus: because he was sustained by the majestic spiritual power of Maitreya Bodhisattva;
because he knew that all phenomena of the three realms are like dreams;
and because he had extinguished the narrow and inferior conceptions of all sentient beings.
Because they have attained vast understanding free from obstruction;
because they abide in the supreme realm of all bodhisattvas;
and because they have entered the inconceivable wisdom of skillful means.
One is able to see all such majestic and sovereign realms of these great bodhisattvas, understanding and discerning them in accordance with their subtle observations.
It is like a person about to die who sees the signs of the retribution they will receive according to their karma:
those who have committed evil deeds see all the realms of suffering belonging to hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts.
In some instances, they see hell-wardens holding weapons in their hands, who—either in a fit of rage or with insults—seize and lead them away;

they also hear the sounds of all sentient beings in the hells crying out and lamenting in grief. They may see the River of Ashes, or the Cauldron of Boiling Water, or the Mountain of Knives, or the Forest of Swords; they may see fierce flames blazing and glowing intensely, or see surging waves as boiling water gushes forth, undergoing various forms of oppression and suffering.

Those who have performed virtuous deeds see all the celestial palaces of the devas, the immeasurable devas, and the various retinues of celestial maidens fully adorned with diverse garments; they see palaces, gardens, lotus ponds, rivers, and various jewel mountains and precious kalpavṛkṣa trees, all of which are exquisitely beautiful for them to enjoy at will. Although their bodies have not yet died, they see such things through the power of their karma.
The youth Sudhana was likewise thus; by the inconceivable power of his bodhisattva karma, he beheld all the adorned realms.
It was as if there were a person possessed by a spirit who saw various things, forms, and retinues, and who was able to answer everything according to whatever was asked.
The youth Sudhana was likewise so.
Because he was sustained by the wisdom of a bodhisattva, he beheld all those various adornments; and if anyone were to question him, there was nothing he could not answer.

For example, suppose there is a person who, possessed by a nāga, considers himself to be a nāga; he enters a nāga palace and sees the nāga retinue, and in a short period of time, he considers that many days, months, years, and ages have already passed.
The youth Sudhana was likewise thus: because he dwelt in the perception of the bodhisattva’s wisdom,
and because he was sustained by the sovereign power of Maitreya Bodhisattva,
a short period of time seemed to him like immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas.

It is like the Brahma palace named "Treasury of Supreme Adornments of All Sentient Beings," within which all the various distinct images of everything in the trichiliocosm are seen without any confusion.
In the same way, the youth Sudhana, within the tower, universally beheld all the various distinctions of the adorned realms, which mutually interpenetrated;
yet each was distinct, without being confused with one another.

For example, when a bhikṣu enters a universal base concentration (kṛtsnāyatana-samādhi), whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, the object of the concentration he has entered manifests before him.

In the same way, the youth Sudhana entered the tower; all the profound realms of experience manifested through its various adornments were perfectly in accord with his faculties, and he understood them all with complete clarity.
It is, for example, as if someone were to see a city of the gandharvas in the midst of space, complete with all its adornments, perceiving it clearly and without any obstruction.
The youth Sudhana was likewise thus: he beheld all those adorned realms as profoundly harmonious, clearly understood, and unimpeded.
It was like the palaces of yakṣas and the palaces of humans being situated in the same place without mingling, yet without obstruction, each seeing differently according to their respective karma.
It is like the great ocean, within which the forms and images of all things in the trichiliocosm are reflected.
It is like a master illusionist who is well-versed in the arts of illusion; by the power of illusion, he manifests various illusory phenomena and diverse activities, accomplishing them all.

The youth Sudhana was likewise; by the majestic spiritual power of Maitreya Bodhisattva, by the power of inconceivable knowledge of illusion, and by attaining the sovereign powers of all bodhisattvas, he beheld within the pavilion the sovereign realm of all its adornments.
The Flower Ornament Sutra of the Buddha’s Great Vaipulya, Scroll Thirty-Seven;
The Flower Ornament Sutra of the Buddha’s Great Vaipulya, Scroll Thirty-Eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Prajñā of Kapiśī, by Imperial Decree.
The Chapter on the Vows and Practices of Samantabhadra for Entering the Realm of the Inconceivable Liberation.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya entered the pavilion, withdrew his supernormal powers, snapped his fingers to make a sound, and addressed Sudhana, saying:
"Son of good family, arise!"
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is thus: this is the characteristic of the manifestation of the causal conditions for a bodhisattva’s wisdom that knows all phenomena.
Such intrinsic natures are entirely unestablished; they are like illusions, like dreams, like shadows, and like reflections.
At that time, upon hearing the sound of a finger-snap, Sudhana arose from his samādhi. Maitreya said to him:
"Good son, do you see the sovereign power of liberation and the majestic spiritual might of the Bodhisattva?"
Do you see the power of the outflow of all the bodhisattva’s aids to enlightenment?
Do you see the power of the gathering of manifestations produced by the bodhisattva’s vow-knowledge?
Do you see the variously adorned and wondrous palaces of the bodhisattva?
Do you see the various powers of practice accumulated by the Bodhisattvas?
Do you see the lands adorned with the various merits of the Bodhisattvas?
Do you see the various powers within the ten stages of the Bodhisattvas?
Do you see the inconceivable fruits of the bodhisattvas' various pāramitās?
Do you see the inconceivable power of the bodhisattvas' various samādhis?
Do you see the power of the Tathāgatas' various most supreme great vows?
Have you heard of the various gates of liberation through which Bodhisattvas are born?
Do you accord with and understand the inconceivable liberations of the Bodhisattvas?
Do you accord with and joyfully accept the samādhis of the Bodhisattvas?
Sudhana replied, “Indeed, I have seen it;
this is due to the power of the spiritual benefactor’s empowerment, the power of his mindfulness, and the power of his majestic virtue.”
"Noble One! What is the name of this gate of liberation? Maitreya replied:
“This gate of liberation is named ‘The Adorned Treasury of the Wisdom of Unforgetting Recollection that Enters All Realms of the Three Times.
Good son! A bodhisattva in their final birth attains such gates of liberation as these, which are unspeakably unspeakable in number.”
Sudhana said, "Noble One! Where has this array of adornments gone?"
Maitreya replied: "It goes to where it comes from. He asked:
"From where have you come?
He replied, "I have come from the wisdom-power of all bodhisattvas; I abide by relying upon the wisdom-power of all bodhisattvas."
There is not the slightest place of coming or going;
there is no accumulation, no increase, no accomplishment, and no establishment; it does not rely on earth, nor does it rely on space, being far removed from everything.
Good son! It is like a dragon king: the various clouds and rains do not emerge from his body, nor do they emerge from his mind; they have no accumulation, establishment, or growth.
Yet, solely by the power of the dragon king’s mental intention, they pour down in torrents, pervading the entire world.
This is the inconceivable realm of the dragon kings. Good son!
Those matters of adornment are likewise so.
It does not abide within, nor does it abide without;
yet, through the sovereign majestic power of the Bodhisattva and the strength of your own roots of goodness, it is not that you do not see it.
Son of good family!

For example, when a magician performs various illusory feats, they come from nowhere and go nowhere; they have no movement, no entry, no concealment, and no manifestation, yet through the power of illusion, these embellishments appear with perfect clarity.

It is the same with this [Buddha-field]: it comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; it is neither accumulated nor established. Nevertheless, through the power of inconceivable illusory wisdom cultivated through habituation, and by the power of past great vows, it appears in such a manner.
The youth Sudhana said: "O Great Sage!
From where have you come?"
Maitreya replied: "Good son!
All bodhisattvas come without coming and go without going; it is in this manner that they come."
Without activity and without abiding, thus they come;

without location, without fixedness, without perishing, without arising, without dwelling, without shifting, without moving, without originating, without attachment, without clinging, without karma, without retribution, without origination, without cessation, without interruption, and without permanence—thus they come.
"Furthermore, good son! Bodhisattvas come from the state of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), for they pity, protect, and subdue all sentient beings;
they come from the state of great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), for they rescue and guard sentient beings oppressed by suffering."
They come from the state of pure precepts, for they arise with sovereign mastery according to their inclinations;
they come from the state of great vows, for they are sustained by the power of their past aspirations;
they come from the state of supernormal powers, for they manifest wherever they wish in all places.
They come from the state of immovability, because they do not abandon the immovable essence of the Tathāgata;
they come from the state of neither grasping nor rejecting, because they do not cause body or mind to engage in coming and going;
they come from the state of wisdom and skillful means, because they turn in accordance with all sentient beings.
They come from the place where transformations are manifested, for they appear as illusory reflections.
Furthermore, noble son, regarding what you have asked— "from where do you come?"— noble son:
I have come here from my birthplace, the village of Ambaṣṭha in the country of Mālava.

There is an elder there named Gopaka; in order to transform him and lead him into the Buddha-dharma, and furthermore, to teach the Dharma according to the capacities of all the people in that land, as well as to expound the Mahāyāna for the sake of my parents, relatives, kinsmen, and Brahmins so that they may enter it, I remain there and have come from that place.
Sudhana said, "Noble One! What is the birthplace of a bodhisattva?"
Maitreya replied: "Good son, there are ten kinds of birthplaces for bodhisattvas."
What are the ten? They are as follows:
generating the bodhicitta is the birthplace of a bodhisattva, for it causes one to be born into the family of bodhisattvas;
The profound mind is the birthplace of the bodhisattva, for it gives birth to the family of spiritual friends;
the stages are the birthplace of the bodhisattva, for they give birth to the family of the perfections;
the great vows are the birthplace of the bodhisattva, for they give birth to the family of sublime practices.
